СтраницаPage 1 · Detailed robotics programme: M1-M24
Detailed robotics programme: M1-M24


This programme consists of 24 modules, each 15 pages long. This volume brings them together in
365 pages, with a contents list and PDF bookmarks for navigation. The practical work focuses on
measuring, calculating, designing and testing robotic systems.
The plan develops the topics and goals of M1-M24 in the supplied roadmap.pdf. Every module
specifies assigned reading, essential concepts, equipment and software. Worked mechanics
examples connect the theory to leg, body and finger motion, and to robot locomotion.
Start with sensor data and a single joint. Progress through mathematics, electronics, leg
mechanics, control, ROS and simulation. After perception and autonomous behaviour, build a
quadruped and extend the tested design into a hexapod. The hand examples teach shared
principles; building the hand and working with tactile sensors belong to the separate OPT stage.

How to use this edition
Before each module, check the equipment and software list: identify what you already have, what
the experiments require, and how to verify that the environment is ready. Read the robot motion
fundamentals on page 15; in M1, the introduction also appears on page 13. Explain the concepts in
your own words and reproduce the calculation. Each reading list identifies the relevant sections.
This work is included in the module's 75 hours.
Use PDF bookmarks to move between sections. The ZIP archive contains 24 separate documents,
M01-M24. The contents tables give the original schedule dates and each module's starting page in
this volume. This English edition retains the detailed tasks, worked examples, references,
definitions and equipment stages of the edited Russian edition.

Study hours

 Programme component                     Hours         Included work

 24 modules at 75 hours each             1,800         Theory, practical exercises, verification and recording the
                                                       results.

 G1-G4 at 35 hours each                  140           Subsystem integration, fault correction and readiness
                                                       checks before the next stage.

 OPT after M17                           120           Building the robotic hand and working with tactile sensors.

 Complete programme                      2,060         11 Oct 2026-22 Dec 2028; the original scheduling rules
                                                       are retained.

These documents provide the detailed plans for M1-M24. The G1-G4 checkpoints and the OPT hand
project have separate time allocations. Completing the full programme requires the modules and
these additional stages.

What counts as progress
Support each learning outcome with working software, a calculation, a measurement or a
repeatable experiment. The stated criteria guide the learning process; verify the allowable loads
and operating conditions of the actual hardware separately. Record simulation results and physical
robot tests as distinct forms of evidence.

СтраницаPage 4 · Schedule and readiness to progress
Schedule and readiness to progress


Organising study sessions
The original schedule allocates 2 hours each weekday, Monday to Friday, and 10 hours of practical
work on Sunday; Saturday is free. During a holiday block, only its first Sunday remains a study day.
Breaks are excluded from study time. In M1, one of the programme's 12 additional hours is
assigned to 2 November 2026.
The remaining modules use three 20-hour blocks and a final 15-hour block: 35 hours of study and
analysis, and 40 hours of practice. Complete these blocks in sequence on the available days,
allowing for holidays. They need not coincide with four calendar weeks.
One module may end on the day the next begins. Divide that day's available time between them;
count each hour only once. The cover pages retain the original dates. This edition does not replace
the roadmap with a new hour-by-hour calendar. Allocate additional hours and Sunday sessions
according to the overall plan without counting them twice.

Checkpoints

 Stage      Dates                        Main readiness question

 G1         22 Mar-04 Apr 2027           Have electronics, mechanics, measurements and fault responses been
                                         checked before connecting the actuator?

 G2         15-25 Oct 2027               Are the leg model, controller and ROS interfaces consistent, and has
                                         their integrated operation been demonstrated?

 G3         27 Nov-10 Dec 2028           Have autonomous behaviour, perception, data, trained models and
                                         their intended operating conditions been evaluated?

 G4         10-22 Dec 2028               Have all requirements been met, and can the final result be
                                         reproduced?

The source plan contains two sequencing mismatches. G2 requires HIL tests that are developed
later in M13; that requirement remains open until the tests are completed. G3 appears after the AI
modules and serves as a final audit, so each model must be evaluated before it is used. The
decision to buy a Jetson or hardware for learned locomotion belongs to G3. Successful simulation
alone does not establish readiness for that purchase.

What to retain at the end of each module
Save the versions of code, CAD models and configurations, raw data with units, and commands for
repeating experiments. Mark completed requirements and unresolved issues. For hardware, record
power settings, loads and fault responses. If parts have not arrived, continue modelling and
preparing documentation, and mark the corresponding hardware tests as pending.

СтраницаPage 5 · Robot motion fundamentals: learning
Robot motion fundamentals: learning
sequence


The sections on robot motion connect the individual subjects into an understanding of the complete
robot. In M2-M24, the model and exercise appear on page 15. M1 introduces the foundations on
pages 13 and 15. The reading and calculations are included in each module's study hours.

 Stage          Essential understanding                                  Evidence of understanding

 M1-M3          Links, joints, configuration and state; vectors,         Draw a mechanism, calculate a point's
                coordinates, derivatives and measurement                 position and velocity, and assess the effect
                error.                                                   of sensor error.

 M4-M7          Motion sampled at fixed intervals; statics,              Explain the sampling-rate choice, calculate
                torques, transmissions and actuator power.               the torque under load, and estimate heating.

 M8             Forward and inverse kinematics, coordinate               Calculate foot position from joint angles,
                frames, Jacobians, singularities and forces.             solve IK, and verify velocities and work.

 M9             Inertia, energy, Newton-Euler and Lagrangian             Derive and verify equations of motion;
                methods, forward and inverse dynamics, and               explain forces and accelerations.
                contact.

 M10-M13        Feedback, state, stability, physical models and          Trace how a command produces measured
                model validation.                                        motion, and validate the model.

 M14-M17        Perception geometry, body motion,                        Express a target in the robot frame,
                trajectories, finger contact and grasping.               calculate a trajectory, and verify a grasp.

 M18-M21        Identification, centre of mass, support forces,          Explain balance, feasible forces and the
                floating-base dynamics and learning.                     physical meaning of a learned model's
                                                                         commands.

 M22-M24        Measured loads, support transitions, hexapod             Compare predictions with measurements
                locomotion and verification of calculations.             and explain the model's limits.

Practical progression: from one link to a step
Begin with a link whose base is fixed. Calculate leg position from joint angles, link velocities and the
acting forces. Account for inertia and prescribe motion over time. Then introduce ground contact,
body movement and changes of support. Apply the same principles to a finger, adding checks of
grasp forces and transmission behaviour.

When to move on
Before the next topic, check that you understand the notation, coordinate frames, units and
modelling assumptions. Solve a simple example by hand, then verify it with software or an
experiment. Assess separately whether the target pose is reachable, whether the actuator can
supply the required torque, and how accurately the controller follows the command.

ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M01  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

M1 Robot software foundations

M1 • 11 Oct 2026 - 03 Nov 2026 • 75 hours
Python, C++ and Rust: a body, one joint, observation and fault investigation

Deliverable: telemetry-core v1.0. One repository with a shared IMU and joint data structure,
three command-line utilities (CLIs), a Python analyser and a main C++ processor. A generator
produces data; the test bench displays roll and joint-angle error, detects invalid rows and
interrupted transmission, and saves a log for repeating the experiment. This prepares you for legs
and fingers; actuators and physics simulation are not yet needed.

 Block      Dates in 2026             Analysis     Practice         Deliverable

 1          11-16 October             10 h         10 h             Environment, snapshot and Python

 2          18-23 October             10 h         10 h             C++ and logger

 3          25-30 October             10 h         10 h             Faults, tests and Rust

 4          1-3 November              5 h          10 h             Streaming, timeout and replay

 Total      M1                        35 h         40 h             75 hours

Calendar. Four Sundays of 10 h and 17 weekdays of 2 h give 74 h. One of the programme's 12
additional hours is assigned to Monday 2 November: 3 h; the source does not date this hour.
Saturdays are free. In the source, M2 also starts on 3 November, with no boundary specified by
hour; its calendar is not recalculated. Detailed dates and tasks are on pp. 11-12.

Work rhythm and scope
Weekdays: 120 min - restore context 10, read 45, work through an example 35, explain 20, record
results 10. Sunday: five 2 h blocks - readiness criterion 10, implementation 90, verification 20 min.
Breaks of 15-30 min and lunch are outside the 75 h. Reading, glossary work and setup are
included.
Keep one task on a board labelled 'Next / In progress / Verified'. Log the date, minutes, scenario,
random-number generator seed, axes, units, commit, parameters and command. After 30 min
without progress, simplify the example; after 60 min, describe the problem and change sources.
Update README at each block's end. The main processor is C++; cut extensions before core tests.

Acceptance checks: evidence to save
Provide an axes and joint-zero diagram, rest and 15° roll recordings, q_ref and q plots, and a
NO_RESPONSE event without guessing its cause. Check all three CLIs and count gaps, rejected and
dropped separately. The watchdog must trigger during silence; duplicates must not refresh its
timer, and FAULT must not clear itself. Include raw-recording replay; GDB, ASan/UBSan, and TSan
or its limitations; a clean Ubuntu build; timing measurements, CLI medians, p50/p95/p99; queue
sizes and deliberately slow logging.

Save six scenarios, expected results calculated by hand, plots, events, a report and commands. Total your
hours and identify three skills, two mistakes and unfinished tasks; repeat the experiment independently after AI
assistance. Multiple joints will require names and aligned timing. Balance, kinematics, state estimation,
physical constraints and torque control come later.
Motion fundamentals are compulsory from M1: link, joint, degree of freedom, configuration and state; the
distinction between kinematics, dynamics and control. Explanations are on p. 13 and the first mechanism
calculation on p. 15. It belongs to the 'axes, units, RobotState' block on 11 October.

СтраницаPage 7 · A body and one-joint test bench
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M01  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

A body and one-joint test bench

A shared state snapshot: from reading fields to observing a robot

Mechanism and coordinates
The model has a body with an IMU and one revolute joint, such as a leg's knee or a finger joint. Use
the IMU accelerometer readings, namely specific force. Its axes align with the body axes: x
forwards, y left, z upwards, forming a right-handed frame. Measure specific force in m/s², joint
angle in radians and current in amperes. Draw and label the joint zero and positive direction in
README.
A snapshot contains one generator step's data. All fields share the timestamp t_us; this is a
test-bench simplification. Real IMUs and encoders may have different rates and clocks. Here,
current i_a is merely a recorded signal; it is not actuator torque. q_ref_rad is the requested angle
and q_rad the encoder measurement.

seq,t_us,ax,ay,az,q_ref_rad,q_rad,i_a
0,0,0.0,0.0,9.81,0.0,0.0,0.2
1,10000,0.0,0.0,9.81,0.01,0.008,0.2

Data and error contract
Use unquoted UTF-8 CSV with the exact header and 8 fields. seq and t_us are ASCII integers in
0…2^63-1. Other fields are finite decimal numbers; signs, decimal points and exponents are
allowed. Reject hex, underscores and NaN/Inf. Trim surrounding whitespace and require complete
parsing. Both angles of the teaching joint are limited to [-1; 1] rad.
For accepted snapshots, seq and t_us increase strictly. An invalid row does not update the
accepted state. A seq gap is a diagnostic event, not a reason to reject the next snapshot. Resetting
the counter requires a new recording; M1 does not require automatic reset detection.

 Check                     Result

 Header, file              Stop with code 2 if the header is wrong or the file cannot be read.

 Row or fields             Reject as blank, field_count, number, nonfinite, joint_range, sequence or timestamp,
                           in that priority order.

 CLI result                Code 0: all rows valid; 1: some rejected. JSON to stdout, reasons to stderr.

 Summary                   rows_total, accepted, rejected, errors_by_reason; first/last_t_us; mean_ax/ay/az;
                           max_abs_joint_error. Empty metrics: null.

Experiment set
Create separate files of 1 000 snapshots at 10 000 µs intervals: rest; static 15° roll; smooth
joint motion; no response after seq=200; seq=40…49 gap; bad rows. Use a separate
streaming test with a pause to test real clock progression. Verification files contain no noise; noise
with seed=42 is an additional experiment.

All language implementations read the same files. Calculate expected results for small experiments by hand.
Integers and error reasons must match exactly; metrics use an absolute tolerance of 10^-9 for these data.
Shared layout: python/, cpp/, rust/, scenarios/, fixtures/, tests/, reports/.

СтраницаPage 8 · Linux and reproducible experiments
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M01  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Linux and reproducible experiments

Learn to run and investigate a robotics experiment

Topics to study
• Files and the shell. Paths, working directory, permissions, environment variables, quoting,
stdin/stdout/stderr, redirection, pipes and exit codes. Commands: pwd, ls, cd, mkdir, cp, mv, less,
head, tail, rg, chmod, env.
• Processes. PID, foreground and background execution, ps, top, SIGINT/SIGTERM. Learn how to
stop the generator while allowing the logger to close its file, and why kill -9 prevents normal
cleanup.
• Python environment. Interpreter, virtual environment, pyproject.toml, uv.lock, uv run and
dependency restoration. The project needs numpy, matplotlib and pytest.
• Git. Index, commit, diff, branch and merge; Pro Git 2.1-2.5, 3.1-3.2. Preserve the history of
scenario parameters and changes to sensor-data processing.

Workstation setup
On an Apple Silicon Mac, use the planned Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64 in UTM for primary runs. If Ubuntu
is already available, use it. You need a terminal, Git, uv/Python, a C++ compiler, CMake, GDB,
clang-format and Rustup/Cargo. These experiments require neither ROS nor a physics simulator.
Record versions, architecture and commands in README. Add .venv, build, target, caches and
large results to .gitignore. Keep small verification recordings in Git; generate large ones. For every
experiment, save the scenario, axis and unit configuration, seed, commit and result.

Practical tasks
L1 Run an experiment. Generate a stationary-robot recording, analyse it, and save the JSON
summary and errors separately. Repeat from another directory using explicit paths. Then supply a
missing file: this must produce a clear error rather than an empty successful report.
L2 Process lifecycle. Make the generator emit one row every 10 ms with an explicit flush; actual
intervals may vary. Pipe it into a simple Python logger. Stop the generator with SIGINT, wait for EOF
and check the last saved row. The final multithreaded logger comes later.
L3 Configuration history. Create a branch to correct the y-axis sign in the tilt scenario. Change
the data and expected result together, explaining why in the commit. Create a threshold-value
conflict in a separate practice configuration file, resolve it and rerun the relevant test.
L4 Replay. In a project copy, restore dependencies from the lockfile and repeat the 'no response'
experiment. The command, data version and result must match. A VM snapshot helps restore the
environment, but does not replace project history and an experiment description.

Connection to later robotics work
These skills matter when a sensor or driver runs as a separate process, an experiment runs on an
onboard computer, and a fault must be reproduced on a laptop. Save a reproducible experiment
folder and explain what happens when each process stops.

ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M01  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Python and motion diagnostics

Five tasks using body and joint data

Study before practice
Python: functions, dataclass, dict/list, generators, with, modules, exceptions, argparse, pathlib and
JSON. NumPy: arrays, shape/dtype, columns, masks, abs, mean, max, isfinite, sin/cos and arctan2.
Matplotlib: Figure/Axes, multiple lines, labels, legends and savefig. Apply each construct to a
RobotState snapshot.

P1 Generate data for known motion
For rest, set f=(ax,ay,az)=(0,0,9.81), q_ref=q=0, i=0.2. For static roll φ=15°: f=(0,g·sinφ,g·cosφ),
g=9.81; convert φ to radians for sin/cos. The joint is stationary in both experiments. These are ideal
data with known answers.
For joint motion, set q_ref=min(0.8, 0.002·seq), q=max(0, q_ref-0.02), i=0.2. In the 'no response'
variant, after seq=200 hold q at its value at 200 while q_ref keeps changing. Record this boundary
in the configuration. This is a predefined motion trace, not a physical motor model.

P2 Read and validate a snapshot
Implement parse_row and sequence validation separately. Stream the file using with, recording
rejection reasons and maintaining accepted+rejected=rows_total. Distinguish an unrepresentable
number, a packet gap and mechanically suspicious behaviour: these are different events. Update
the last valid state only after all checks.

P3 Plot body data
Plot ax, ay, az and the specific-force magnitude against time. In static experiments, estimate roll as
φ_est=atan2(ay,az): expect 0° and 15°, with a 0.1° tolerance without noise. Add an artificial 2 m/s²
to ay for the stationary body and demonstrate the false tilt. Conclude that linear acceleration and
vibration interfere with accelerometer-only tilt estimation; yaw cannot be determined this way.

P4 Detect a joint that does not respond
Plot q_ref and q, then e=q_ref-q. Find max|e| and mean |e|. Flag NO_RESPONSE if, in a
10-snapshot window with consecutive seq values, every |e|>0.1 rad and max(q)-min(q)≤0.005 rad.
Restart the window after a gap. These are teaching thresholds; 10 samples specify a sample set,
not an exact duration.
Compare the event with the scenario label. q alone cannot distinguish a frozen encoder, a jammed
mechanism and a disconnected motor: report 'no expected response'. Plot current alongside as an
additional observation, but do not treat it as proof of the cause.

P5 Find transmission gaps
Remove seq=40…49 from a clean file: 990 of 1 000 snapshots remain, with 10 seq numbers
missing. Next corrupt one row without removing it: rejected=1. A number missing among accepted
snapshots does not prove transmission packet loss: validation may have rejected a row. Account
for these cases separately.

Deliverables: a JSON summary, body and joint plots, events.json with seq and reason, and expected results
calculated by hand for every experiment. Python analyses events; C++ and Rust implement the shared
contract, not the entire analysis.

СтраницаPage 10 · Modern C++ and resource management
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M01  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Modern C++ and resource management

Object lifetime, resource ownership and porting the data parser

Study in this order
• Building a programme. Source, header, translation unit, object file and linking. Examine one
compilation error and one linking error in the sensor processor. Study declarations and definitions,
include guards or pragma once.
• Values and references. Initialisation, automatic lifetime, scope, const, passing by value and by
const T&. Compare pointers and references. Understand why a reference to a local variable
becomes invalid.
• RAII. The constructor establishes a valid state; the destructor releases the resource. A file closes
both on function exit and on an exception. Usually express ownership with an object, std::vector or
std::unique_ptr; use shared_ptr only when shared ownership is actually needed.
• Standard library. std::string, std::vector, std::array, iterators, range-for, algorithms and
std::optional. Determine when modifying a vector invalidates references. Study string_view as a
non-owning view with a limited lifetime.
• Copying and moving. Understand copy/move behaviour before studying std::move. It permits
move selection but does not itself transfer bytes. Do not build a complex class hierarchy for a
RobotState structure containing a few numbers.

Practical tasks with robot data
C1 State snapshot. Create RobotState with the contract's eight fields. Put the parser, structure
and CLI in separate files. Pass a snapshot by value and by const reference; explain who owns it and
why a consumer must not retain a reference to a reused sensor buffer.
C2 Data reception. Port snapshot validation from Python, including the angle range and seq
ordering. Run rest, motion and corrupted recordings. Accepted rows, counters, mean ax/ay/az and
max|q_ref-q| must match; NO_RESPONSE analysis remains in Python.
C3 Logger resource. Wrap the output file in a RAII object. Save 10 snapshots; exit via return,
then via an exception after the fifth. Verify that the object is destroyed and the error remains

CMake, debugging and diagnostics

Reproduce an error, find its cause and verify the fix

Topics to study
In the official CMake Tutorial, study building an executable and a library, separating subdirectories,
target commands, and Testing and CTest. Understand the relationship between add_library,

entire CMake language.
The project needs a telemetry library, a CLI and a test build target. Enable -Wall -Wextra
-Wpedantic for GCC/Clang. Use Debug for debugging and Release for speed comparisons.
clang-format establishes a consistent style; formatting does not establish programme correctness.

cmake -S cpp -B build/debug -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug
cmake --build build/debug
ctest --test-dir build/debug --output-on-failure
cmake -S cpp -B build/release -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build/release
These commands assume a configured CMakeLists.txt. Describe GoogleTest integration and
test-data paths in README; pin the dependency version for reproducible builds.

Debugging a concrete scenario
D1 Incorrect units. In a practice analyser version, pass 15 as radians instead of 15°. In GDB, set a
breakpoint at the q_ref check, inspect the value and stack, and practise run, next, step, print and
backtrace. The range check must reject this command; fix the conversion and add a test. Small unit
errors may remain within range, so this check alone is insufficient.
D2 Corrupted snapshot. In a separate faulty C++ version, access q after receiving a row with
too few fields. Examine the crash stack and diagnostic-tool message, then check the length before
accessing fields. Save the input file and test. Study core dumps using this example; if dump saving
is disabled, debug directly in GDB.

ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M01  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Data streaming and update monitoring

Distinguish slow disk writes from an interrupted robot stream

Programme model and study topics
Study threads, shared memory, mutexes, RAII locks and condition_variable with a predicate. A
reader thread receives snapshots; a writer thread logs them through a queue of K=64. latest_state
stores the accepted snapshot and host_received_at. Read and update all shared state under one
mutex; perform file I/O outside the lock.
On normal EOF, close the queue: set closed, wake threads, write the remaining entries and join. A
writer error wakes a blocked reader and ends the experiment with an error. The monitor runs in the
main thread. Disable the watchdog for file processing; in streaming mode, normal EOF disables
commands and stops the monitor before draining the queue.

Q1 Logger overload
In blocking mode, the reader waits for space; a slow disk also slows reception of new snapshots. In
drop newest mode, a new record cannot enter a full queue, but the reader continues updating
latest_state. The log can therefore lose rows while the monitor still sees new snapshots. Report
missing log entries and reception delays separately, explaining their causes.
For verification file processing, use blocking mode without losses. For streaming, compare K=4 and
K=64 with a slowed writer. Check saved seq order and capacity. After normal completion,
accepted=enqueued+dropped and enqueued=processed. Count invalid rows separately; after an
error, also report unprocessed snapshots.

Q2 Monitor updates independently of packet reception
Roughly every 10 ms, the main thread calls tick(now) and checks now-last_new_valid_receive. After
more than 100 ms, it logs FAULT and disables simulated command sending. Before the first
snapshot, state is INIT and commands are disabled; timing starts when reception begins. A first
valid snapshot before timeout changes INIT to OK. Duplicates, old seq values and invalid rows do
not refresh the time. The 10/100 ms limits are teaching settings, not real-time guarantees.
In the streaming test, stop updates while the reader keeps waiting. The watchdog must trigger
without another message. A new valid snapshot after failure does not automatically clear FAULT:
allow reset separately, and only with a current accepted snapshot. No commands are sent to actual
actuators; test the command_allowed variable and event log.

Q3 Required checks
• Update RobotState as a whole: angle and time belong to one snapshot. Run TSan if supported.
• Test empty input, EOF with queued entries, a slow writer and write failure. Hold the writer with an
explicit signal to fill the queue.
• Source silence, duplicates and NaN cause FAULT when the valid snapshot becomes too old. Test
the 100/101 ms boundary with controlled clocks.

The watchdog measures time since receipt of a new snapshot at the host. It does not establish measurement
freshness: data may have been delayed before reaching the reader. Clock synchronisation and source-delay
estimation will be needed later.

Replay and processing latency

Repeat a failure and check whether monitor updates arrive on time

E1 Reprocess a motion recording
Save complete original scenario files and a separate cleaned log of accepted snapshots. Original
data are needed to reproduce input errors. Write numbers without losing precision: in C++, use
max_digits10 for double or preserve the original fields. Compare values and ordering, not CSV
bytes.
Fast mode reads the file without waiting. Reanalysing raw data produces the same rejected and
NO_RESPONSE events at the same seq values; analysing the cleaned file produces the same
accepted states. Snapshots dropped by the queue are missing from the cleaned log but remain in
the original scenario file. They cannot be recovered from the cleaned log alone.

E2 Check timing characteristics

 Metric                           Measurement boundary and meaning for the robot

 Source interval                  Difference between consecutive t_us values; 10 000 µs in the clean scenario.
                                  Gaps differ from host interval variation (jitter).

 Age at monitoring                now_host-last_new_valid_receive_host. The watchdog uses this to detect
                                  channel silence.

 Queueing and writing             t_done-t_enqueue on one monotonic clock. Shows logger queue accumulation.

 Three-CLI runtime                From launch to completion on one file: includes runtime startup, parsing,
                                  reading and summary generation.

 p50 p95 p99                      Sort n latency values; take element ceil(p×n), counting from 1;
                                  p=0.50/0.95/0.99. Empty sample: null.

Clocks: Python perf_counter_ns, C++ steady_clock, Rust Instant. Subtract readings from the same
clock: do not subtract t_us from host now. A 'nanosecond' unit does not imply that accuracy; a VM
provides no hard deadline guarantee.

E3 Take measurements
• Generate one file of 100 000 motion snapshots; record SHA-256, seed and versions. First verify
equivalence of the three CLIs. Use Release builds of C++/Rust without diagnostic tools.
• Use an external Python programme for 2 warm-ups and 10 measurements of each CLI,
alternating languages. Save individual runtimes, median and range. Compare the implementations
without claiming general language superiority.
• For C++, compare normal and slowed writers, K=4/64 and blocking/drop newest. Show maximum
queue size, dropped, latencies and watchdog events. Collect at least 10 000 individual latency
measurements for p99.
• In a 1-2 page report, explain whether history was retained, whether the monitor received
updates, what limited processing, and whether the data allow the failure to be repeated.

Optional: replay 100-1000 snapshots at a specified rate: deadline_s=start_s+(t_us-first_t_us)/(1 000
000×speed), speed>0. Wait until each specified absolute time and record lateness. Control clocks in watchdog
tests.

Assigned reading by task

Programming references and the compulsory first mechanism analysis

The plan and definitions are in English; references include English-language materials. Read the
assigned passage before its task, then test the idea in code. You need not buy four books or read
them cover to cover. Core reading is identified; consult the reference book when stuck.

Core reading
1. Scott Chacon, Ben Straub - Pro Git, 2nd ed. English edition. Sections 2.1-2.5: creating a
repository, recording changes, history, undoing and remotes; 3.1-3.2: branching and merging. For
L3/L4: axis-correction branch, threshold conflict and versioning a reproducible experiment.
2. Steve Klabnik, Carol Nichols and the Rust community - The Rust Programming
Language. Rust Book. Chapters 4-6 and 9: ownership and references, structs, enum/match and
errors for R1/R2. From 11-13: tests, CLI, file reading and iterators for R3/R4. Read chapters 3 and 8
selectively for syntax and collections; skim 16. Defer async, unsafe and FFI.
3. Anish Athalye, Jon Gjengset, Jose Javier Gonzalez - The Missing Semester of Your CS
Education, MIT, 2020 course. Course notes. 'Course Overview + The Shell', 'Command-line
Environment', 'Debugging and Profiling': redirection, processes, diagnostics and measurement for
L1/L2, D1/D2, E3. Use relevant parts of 'Metaprogramming' for builds and dependencies.

C++ reference: specific sections
4. Bjarne Stroustrup - A Tour of C++, 3rd ed. Author and contents. §1.5-1.7: lifetime, const,
pointers and references; §3.2 and 3.4: separate compilation and arguments; §6.2-6.3: copy/move
and resources for C1-C3. §10.2-10.3 and 12.2: string, string_view and vector for C4. §18.2-18.4:
threads, shared data and waiting for Q1-Q3. The book assumes programming experience; begin
after P1/P2. Use the C++17 subset; modules and coroutines are unnecessary here.

Documentation for individual steps

Python Tutorial: Control Flow, Data Structures, Modules, Input/Output, Errors and Exceptions, Classes, Virtual
Environments for P1/P2. Follow task-page links for NumPy/Matplotlib and testing tools. REP-103 (Units, Axis
Orientation) and REP-145 (Data Sources) explain axes and accelerometers; reading them requires no ROS
installation.

Motion fundamentals: what the programme describes

A link is a mechanism part treated as rigid in the model. A joint defines allowed relative link motion: a revolute
joint permits an angle, a prismatic joint a displacement. A degree of freedom is one independent local
motion. A fixed-base leg with an open link chain and three independent revolute joints has three; actuator
count and degrees of freedom can differ.
Configuration q determines relative link placement; for a single fixed pivot it is an angle. A second-order
mechanical model's state also includes velocity: x=(q, q_dot), where q_dot is angular velocity in rad/s. The
same pose at different velocities gives different states. M1 RobotState is an observation snapshot, not the
complete physical state.
Kinematics relates coordinates, velocities and accelerations without calculating forces. Dynamics explains
changes in motion through mass, inertia, forces and torques. Control selects an input to achieve a goal. An
inverse-kinematics angle does not establish that the motor can perform the motion. Further detail: M8, M9,
M10.
Read before P1: Kevin Lynch, Frank Park, Modern Robotics, §2.1: configuration and degrees of freedom and
§2.2: joints. Study definitions, joint types and the mechanism diagram; the general mobility formula comes in
M5.

ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M01  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

M1 key terms

Definitions for the data schema, resource ownership and stream processing

Telemetry. Transmission of measured quantities and diagnostic events to observe a system; it does not itself
control motion.
State snapshot. A consistent set of values for one step; in M1, eight fields share a t_us timestamp.
Coordinate frame. An origin and oriented axes relative to which vector components are expressed; here x
forwards, y left, z upwards.
Radian. A unit of plane angle: arc length divided by radius. One revolution is 2π rad; θ_rad=θ_deg·π/180.
Specific force. Ideal accelerometer output: f=a−g; a is motion acceleration and g gravitational acceleration,
expressed in the same frame. At rest with z upwards, f_z≈+9.81 m/s².
Roll. Body rotation about the longitudinal x axis; the static estimate atan2(ay,az) is distorted by linear
acceleration and cannot determine yaw.
Position error. Difference between requested and measured angles, e=q_ref−q, in radians; these quantities
describe the command and observation respectively.
Timestamp. Event time on a chosen clock; source t_us and host time cannot be subtracted without aligning
their timescales.
Monotonic clock. A timescale that never goes backwards; suitable for intervals within one time source, but it
does not specify a calendar date.
Invariant. A condition that must hold in valid programme states; for example, accepted+rejected=rows_total
after file processing.
Ownership. Responsibility for a resource's lifetime. The owner ensures release; a non-owning reference does
not extend the resource's lifetime.
RAII. Tying a resource to a C++ object's lifetime: the destructor releases it. Object destruction does not prove
a successful write.
Borrowing. Rust access through a reference without ownership transfer, limited by lifetime and compatibility
rules for mutable and immutable access.
Dangling reference. A reference to an object whose lifetime has ended or whose address has become invalid;
using it violates programme correctness.
Mutex. A mutual-exclusion mechanism that protects shared state from simultaneous conflicting access when
all threads use it consistently.
Data race. Unsynchronised, conflicting thread accesses to the same memory, with at least one write; in C++,
these cause undefined behaviour.
Backpressure. Slowing a producer when a consumer cannot keep up: in blocking mode, the reader waits for
space in a full queue.
Watchdog. Periodic checking of the time since a new valid snapshot was received, using the host clock;
silence causes FAULT without another message.
Latency. Time between two defined events, such as enqueue and write completion. Specify the boundaries
and clock source before measuring.
p99 quantile. A value at or below which approximately 99% of observations lie; here, take element
ceil(0.99·n) of the sorted sample, counting from 1.
Replay. Reprocessing saved input; raw rows are needed to reproduce rejections that are absent from the
cleaned log.
SHA-256 hash. A 256-bit content fingerprint for checking file equality; it does not itself establish authorship or
authentic provenance.
Check yourself: why is az≈g at rest; why does constant q not establish a fault's cause; why are dropped,
rejected and seq gaps separate counters?

M1 equipment and setup

Prepare before L1, C1 and R1; setup time is included in the 75 hours

Equipment and purchases
Available: 1 MacBook Pro M4, a terminal and the existing 3D printer; choose its profile later using
the exact printer model. M1 needs no printing. Required purchases: none. No IMU, MCU, motors,
batteries, robot or GPU is needed: the Python generator supplies data. Borrow the C++ book from a
library if available; purchase is optional.

Install before the first practical session: 11 October
On macOS ARM: an editor such as VS Code for Apple Silicon, and UTM. Use Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64
as the guest OS; choose the arm64 image and ARM virtualisation, rather than x86 emulation. Use
an existing suitable Ubuntu installation if available. Allocate VM resources according to the Mac's
memory and disk capacity; check free space and responsiveness before experiments.
In Ubuntu ARM64: Git, terminal and shell, ripgrep; uv and Python; numpy, matplotlib and pytest
dependencies in one project. Pin Python and dependencies in pyproject.toml/uv.lock, and record
commands in README. Do not install experiment packages in system Python. Save plots as PNG so
experiments also run without a GUI.

Before C1: 18 October; before R1: 25 October
C++ in Ubuntu: GCC/G++ or Clang with C++17, CMake, make/Ninja, GDB, clang-format; a pinned
GoogleTest version for tests. Ubuntu packages: build-essential, cmake, gdb, clang-format; record
compiler choice and versions. Use a separate Debug configuration for ASan/UBSan; build TSan
separately and only where the environment supports it.
Rust in the same Ubuntu: rustup, rustc, Cargo, rustfmt and Clippy. Pin the toolchain and
Cargo.lock. Add serde/serde_json for R3 as needed. Native macOS builds are an additional check;
take comparison measurements for all three CLIs in one Ubuntu environment.

Installation checks and optional additions
Record guest architecture (aarch64) and versions. Make a Git commit; use uv to import
NumPy/Matplotlib/pytest and save a plot; build and run a C++17 example through CMake/CTest
and stop at a GDB breakpoint; run cargo test, cargo fmt --check and cargo clippy. Restore
dependencies from the lockfile in a clean copy and repeat L1/L4. The environment is ready for a
task once its corresponding tool passes verification.

Optional: Docker only if isolation beyond the VM becomes necessary; M1 does not need it. Defer ROS 2,
Gazebo and the GPU stack to their modules. Apple M4 does not support CUDA. A VM does not guarantee hard
real time; check graphics and USB before later hardware experiments. Delivery time for subsequent purchases
is outside study hours.
Basis: roadmap.pdf, physical p. 3 for the calendar; pp. 19-21 for M1 objectives. The RobotState schema,
scenarios, teaching thresholds and acceptance checks were developed for this detailed plan. Installation and
environment checks: p. 15.

First motion calculation: before generator P1

A planar link L=0.20 m pivots at the origin: x right, y upwards; q is measured anticlockwise from +x. Endpoint:
p=(L cos q, L sin q). At q=0, obtain (0.20; 0) m; at q=0.50 rad, (0.17552; 0.09589) m. Mass is unnecessary for
this calculation: it is forward kinematics.
In block 2 on 11 October, replace part of the RobotState analysis with 30 min for definitions and a diagram, and
30 min for calculation and plotting. Save mechanism.md and the figure; check ||p||=L and q=-0.50. Why can q
and L alone not determine motor torque? Retain the CSV, [-1;1] rad limit and 75 hours.

СтраницаPage 21 · Mathematics of robot state and motion
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M02  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Mathematics of robot state and motion

M2 • 03 Nov 2026 - 29 Nov 2026 • 75 hours

What you should achieve by the end of M02
Learn to turn a simple leg or finger problem into quantities, equations and a verifiable calculation.
For example: find a force's moment arm from a support point's position; recover an angle from
encoder counts; obtain velocity from a trajectory; predict a compliant support's motion from mass,
stiffness and damping. The main deliverable is robot-math, a collection of numerical and
geometric checks reusable in later modules.
The scope is deliberately limited: vectors and matrices, linear systems and least squares,
derivatives and integrals, and ordinary differential equations. Introduce the Jacobian as a table of
sensitivities and eigenvalues as properties of a simple linear transformation and system. Do not yet
implement full 3D robot kinematics, spatial velocities, controllers or a Kalman filter.

Starting model and preparation
Use Python, NumPy, Matplotlib and SciPy in the M01 environment. Create notebooks/01_vectors,
02_calibration, 03_motion and 04_odes; move repeated functions into robot_math/. Each notebook
must contain a problem statement, axes diagram, parameters with units, calculation, error plot and
conclusion. Keep raw and computed data separately; pin dependency versions and the
random-number generator seed.
The shared teaching object is a link of length L=0.12 m with one revolute joint and a support point
at its tip. Masses, forces and other numbers in this document are calculation-example parameters,
not authorisation to test a future design. The second object is a compliant support with mass
m=0.5 kg, stiffness k=50 N/m and viscous damping coefficient c=1 N·s/m. M02 investigates motion
only through calculation.

Entry diagnostic: within the first two hours
Without references, convert 120 mm to metres, 90° to radians and 10 ms to seconds; find sin(π/2),
a rectangle's area and the solution of two linear equations. In Python, create an array of shape
(100,3), select one coordinate and calculate its mean. If unit arithmetic or trigonometry is difficult,
spend up to 90 minutes of block A addressing that specific gap and reduce decorative plotting
work.
Starting criterion: explain in your own words the difference between a number, a vector component
and a physical quantity. Record one M01 error that mathematics could detect: a reversed axis sign,
milliseconds used instead of seconds, or a false velocity jump from a missing packet. This becomes
your first regression example.

СтраницаPage 22 · Allocating 75 hours and recording
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M02  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Allocating 75 hours and recording
calculations

Four study blocks
A - hours 1-20: 10 h of theory and hand calculations, 10 h of practice. Topics: units, vectors,
bases, dot and cross products, matrices and rank. Deliverable: force diagrams and a library of
verifiable point and vector transformations.
B - hours 21-40: 10 h of theory and 10 h of practice. Topics: Gaussian elimination,
overdetermined systems, residuals, QR, conditioning and eigenvalues. Deliverable: encoder
calibration with a separate validation set and an unsuccessful experiment example.
C - hours 41-60: 10 h of theory and 10 h of practice. Topics: derivatives, integrals, partial
derivatives, gradients and an introductory Jacobian. Deliverable: link-trajectory analysis, work done
by a force and sensitivity of the endpoint position to angle.
D - hours 61-75: 5 h of theory and 10 h of practice. Topics: initial-value problems, explicit Euler,
semi-implicit Euler, RK4, stability and step-size error. Deliverable: mass-spring-damper, pendulum
and convergence report. Total: exactly 35 h of analysis and 40 h of practice.

Session rhythm
Divide each 10 h of theory into five two-hour sessions: 15 min reviewing the preceding idea, 35 min
reading, 40 min hand calculations, 20 min Python verification and 10 min recording conclusions.
Theory in the final block takes 2+2+1 h. Divide the ten-hour practical into five 2 h sessions:
formulation, implementation, cross-checking, error analysis and presentation. Breaks are outside
study hours.
The calendar window on the first page comes from the roadmap. A boundary date may belong to
two modules; rest days, holidays and integration stages remain as in the original plan. Numbered
work steps fill available sessions sequentially without recounting hours. Do not add an extra hour to
every module.

When to move from reading to practice
After each section, close the text and explain which quantity you are calculating, why the operation
is valid and how you will verify the answer. One correct example and one deliberately faulty
example are more useful than a second lecture on the same topic. Use these log fields: robot task;
model; assumptions; prediction before running; result; error; next check.
If behind schedule, first remove animation styling and a second language implementation, then
reduce parameter sweeps. Retain four notebooks, both dynamic objects, unit checks and method
comparisons. Full QR proofs and derivation of RK4 from Taylor series can wait; explanations of
residuals, time steps and causes of discrepancies are compulsory.

СтраницаPage 23 · Vectors, bases and forces on a link
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M02  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Vectors, bases and forces on a link

Topics to study
Study point and free-vector coordinates, length and normalisation, force addition, bases and
projections. The dot product a·b connects components to angle; for unit direction n, the force
projection is F·n. The cross product r×F gives torque about a chosen origin. Measure r in metres, F
in newtons and torque in N·m; its direction follows the right-hand rule.
Study matrix-vector multiplication as a coordinate transformation, matrix product order,
transposition and the meaning of an inverse matrix. For planar rotation, use R(θ) with first row
[cosθ, −sinθ] and second row [sinθ, cosθ]. State the convention explicitly: an active anticlockwise
vector rotation in a fixed frame. The reverse transformation uses R(θ)ᵀ; do not confuse the two
operations.

Task 1. Loading a finger or shank
Input: r=(0.12;0;0) m, F=(0;0;−5) N. First draw a side view and predict the torque direction. Then
calculate r×F by hand and with NumPy, find its magnitude and project F onto the link axis. Rotate
the force by 30° in the same plane and repeat. Deliverable: diagram and table of four positions,
labelling axes, units and signs.
Check: in the first case, torque is (0;0.6;0) N·m; collinear r and F give zero. Doubling the
moment-arm length must double torque magnitude. Faulty case: enter 120 instead of 0.12 and
explain the exact thousandfold discrepancy. This checks the unit model; it is not a physical motor
test.

Task 2. Sensor coordinates on a rotated body
Input: three unit vectors and ten arbitrary points in the plane. Implement R and rotate the set by
0°, 90°, 180° and back. For an offset-mounted sensor, distinguish p_body=R·p_sensor+t from the
direction transformation v_body=R·v_sensor. Do not add translation t to force, acceleration or
direction.
Save a plot of original and transformed axes, a norm test and a reverse-transformation test. For
float64 numbers of order one, use a teaching absolute tolerance of 10⁻¹²; also explain the scale
choice. Test the zero vector without normalising it and an angle in degrees mistakenly passed as
radians. Be able to state by hand the result of rotating (1,0) by 90°.



































M2 • 03 Nov 2026 - 29 Nov 2026 • 75 hours                                                                           3 / 15
СтраницаPage 24 · Linear systems and encoder calibration
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M02  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Linear systems and encoder calibration

From equation to solution
Study A·x=b: each row defines a constraint and each column an unknown's contribution. Work
through Gaussian elimination on a 2×2 system, row swaps for a poor pivot, and nonexistent or
nonunique solutions. Rank is the number of independent constraints. The inverse matrix is useful
conceptually; solve numerically with solve or lstsq rather than inverse(A)·b.
For calibration q=a·u+b, u is the encoder count and q is in radians. Construct A from a column of u
values and a column of ones. With more observations than parameters, minimise the sum of
squared residuals r=A·x−q. QR separates the problem into an orthogonal transformation and a
triangular system; understand this role and one 3×2 example without writing a general QR
implementation.

Task 3. A teaching body with two supports
A 2 kg body rests on two points at horizontal positions x=0 and x=0.3 m; its centre of mass is at
x=0.12 m. Write vertical force and torque equilibrium equations; find support reactions by hand
and in Python. With g=9.81 m/s², reactions must sum to 19.62 N, and opposing moments about the
left support must balance.
Move the centre of mass from 0 to 0.3 m. A negative reaction outside the segment means the
contact model, which can only push, is invalid. Do not present it as a feasible leg force. Save a
reaction-force plot and mark the model's validity boundary; balance control comes later.

Task 4. Find encoder scale and zero
Create 21 u positions evenly spanning the teaching range −1000…1000. Generate q with known
a=0.001 rad/count, b=0.03 rad and small noise with fixed settings; save the ground-truth
parameters separately. Reserve some points for validation. Estimate the parameters, plot residual
against u and calculate RMSE=sqrt(mean(r²)) in radians. First check noise-free data: parameters
must be recovered to machine precision.
Then restrict inputs to around u=500 and compare parameter sensitivity to a small change in one
observation. A small error within a narrow region does not establish good calibration across the full
range. Deliverables: coefficients.json, raw CSV, training and held-out error plots, rank of A and an
explanation of units. Failure cases: identical u values, an empty set, NaN and a duplicate
mistakenly counted as a new independent measurement.

































M2 • 03 Nov 2026 - 29 Nov 2026 • 75 hours                                                                        4 / 15
СтраницаPage 25 · Conditioning and eigenvector directions
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M02  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Conditioning and eigenvector directions

Skills needed before M03 optimisation
The condition number describes how much input error can be amplified in the answer for a
specified norm and scale. A large value warrants examining the formulation, units and data
diversity. It is not a universal good/bad switch: parameters in millimetres and metres have different
scales. Compare normalised formulations and always show the actual change in the answer.
Under a matrix transformation, an eigenvector remains on the same line; its eigenvalue is the
multiplier. For a diagonal stiffness matrix K=diag(40,100) N/m, the directions are obvious. If
off-diagonal terms couple the axes, compute the directions. For now, use a symmetric 2×2 matrix
and check K·v=λ·v; leave complex modes, spectral control and general multilink mechanics for
later months.

Task 5. Nearly identical support measurements
Use A=[[1,1],[1,1+ε]] and b generated from known x=(1,2). Set ε=10⁻¹, 10⁻⁴, 10⁻⁸. For each case,
save cond(A), the residual and the error in recovered x. Add the same small relative perturbation to
one b component and repeat. This illustrates two nearly duplicate constraints when determining a
robot's state.
Check: a small residual can coexist with a large x error. Demonstrate this numerically, then replace
the second equation with an independent one and repeat. Deliverable: six-run table and a
conclusion identifying an additional measurement that resolves the problem. Do not insert a
pseudoinverse without explanation: it belongs to M03 and cannot create missing information.

Task 6. Stiff and compliant support directions
For K=[[80,20],[20,50]] N/m, use eigh to find eigenvalues and normalised eigenvectors. Draw
original axes and eigenvector directions. Apply an equal teaching force along each direction and
find displacement from K·x=F. A greater stiffness λ produces less displacement for the same force
magnitude.
Check orthogonality of the two directions, each eigen-equation's residual and reconstruction of the
original matrix. Set stiffness along one axis to zero: this model no longer determines static
displacement along the free direction. Save it as an expected solve failure caused by a singular
system. Additional 20-minute experiment: rotate K using orthogonal R and verify unchanged
eigenvalues.

































M2 • 03 Nov 2026 - 29 Nov 2026 • 75 hours                                                                         5 / 15
СтраницаPage 26 · Derivatives, integrals and motion sensitivity
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M02  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Derivatives, integrals and motion sensitivity

Theory connected to motion
The time derivative of position is velocity; the derivative of velocity is acceleration. For angle q,
units are rad, rad/s and rad/s². Study derivatives of sums, products and sin/cos, and the chain rule
for q(t)=A·sin(ωt), with ω in rad/s. Integrating velocity gives coordinate change; integrating force
along a path gives work in joules, and over time gives impulse in N·s. Label the integration variable
for every integral.
A partial derivative describes how a function changes when one argument varies and the others
remain fixed. The gradient collects these derivatives for a scalar function; a vector function's
Jacobian arranges them with outputs in rows and inputs in columns. Do not call every
multidimensional array a Jacobian: first specify the function, input/output dimensions and each
element's units.

Task 7. Encoder velocity and noise
Generate 5 s of motion q=0.4·sin(2πt) rad with a 0.01 s step. Derive exact velocity and
acceleration. Implement forward and central differences; compare central differences only at
interior samples and state the time assigned to each forward-difference estimate. Add angle noise
and plot velocity error. Compare two time steps with both noise-free and noisy input.
Save q, dq/dt and absolute-error plots with RMSE over the same time window. Noise-free error
should decrease for sufficiently small steps, while differentiating a noisy signal too frequently can
worsen the estimate. Remove one sample and use actual timestamps: division by constant dt at
that point becomes a deliberate error case. M04 covers filtering in detail.

Task 8. Link-endpoint sensitivity
For p(q)=(L·cos q,L·sin q), derive J(q)=(−L·sin q,L·cos q)ᵀ. With L=0.12 m and q=30°, estimate
Δp≈J·Δq for Δq=0.1°, 1°, 10°. Compare with exact p(q+Δq)−p(q); the error magnitude shows
where the linear approximation loses accuracy. Deliverables: tangential-displacement diagram and
error table in millimetres.
Separately integrate a known velocity with the trapezoidal rule and check that the angle returns
after a full period. Calculate work done by a constant torque of 0.2 N·m through 30°: W=τ·Δq, with
angle in radians. Do not confuse torque with energy even though both have dimensional product
N·m: their physical meanings and operations differ.

































M2 • 03 Nov 2026 - 29 Nov 2026 • 75 hours                                                                          6 / 15
СтраницаPage 27 · ODEs: a compliant leg and a free pendulum
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M02  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

ODEs: a compliant leg and a free pendulum

Formulating an initial-value problem
For a spring-supported mass with displacement measured from equilibrium, m·x″+c·x′+k·x=F(t).
Introduce v=x′ and state y=(x,v); then x′=v and v′=(F−c·v−k·x)/m. Initial values x(0) and v(0) are
compulsory parts of the problem. Measuring from equilibrium removes constant gravity; with
another coordinate definition, explicitly restore gravity with the correct sign.
Explicit Euler evaluates the derivative at the step's start. Semi-implicit Euler updates v first, then
uses the new v to update x. RK4 evaluates four intermediate derivatives; implement it for general
y′=f(t,y). It has a fixed step and fourth-order accuracy for sufficiently smooth problems; library
RK45 uses a different scheme and adaptive control, so it is not the same algorithm.

Task 9. Mass-spring-damper
Use the parameters on page 1, x(0)=0.02 m, v(0)=0 and F=0, for 5 s. Implement the three
methods and a reference solve_ivp calculation with stricter tolerances. For each method, test steps
0.04; 0.02; 0.01 s and compare x and v at common times. In a separate undamped experiment
with c=0, track E=mv²/2+kx²/2.
Save state, energy and error-versus-step plots. For c>0 without external force, energy must
decrease in the continuous model. Energy growth may indicate numerical instability or a sign error.
A decay plot alone is insufficient: check equilibrium x=v=0 and compare with the analytical
solution for c=0.

Task 10. Pendulum model of a free link
Set θ″=−(g/L)·sinθ, L=0.3 m, θ(0)=0.1 rad, ω(0)=0. Measure the period between zero crossings in
the same direction and compare with T≈2π·sqrt(L/g). Increase the initial angle to 1 rad and
demonstrate the small-angle approximation's limitation. Energy E=mL²ω²/2+mgL(1−cosθ) must
remain constant in the ideal continuous model.
Test θ=0, a negative initial angle and an excessively large step. Reject negative m or L before
integration. Save solver settings and an error estimate; agreement between two equally faulty
implementations cannot replace an independent analytical reference. Actual foot impacts, joint
friction and backlash are not yet part of this model.





































M2 • 03 Nov 2026 - 29 Nov 2026 • 75 hours                                                                         7 / 15
СтраницаPage 28 · The shared robot-math test bench and error
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M02  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

The shared robot-math test bench and error
checks

Connect all notebooks through one scenario
Scenario: a virtual encoder produces u(t), calibration converts it to q(t), geometry computes the
link endpoint, a numerical derivative gives velocity, and an independent pendulum model supplies
reference motion. Define each stage's input/output contract. Data include t_s, encoder_count,
q_rad, p_x_m and p_z_m; settings include L_m, a_rad_per_count and b_rad.
First generate a trajectory from the ODE, then convert q to u through inverse calibration and
quantisation. The analyser must recover motion with the expected precision loss. Combine existing
functions; a separate large project is unnecessary. In the report, distinguish model, quantisation,
calibration and numerical-differentiation errors: the same final RMSE can have different causes.

Six required scenarios
1. Wrong units. Pass a length in millimetres to an interface expecting metres; a schema or scale
check must explain the failure. 2. Zero vector. Normalisation must return a clear error rather than
propagate NaN through the remaining calculation. 3. Singular calibration. All u values are equal;
the report identifies insufficient rank and does not produce an unsupported scale coefficient.
4. Poor conditioning. Nearly identical equations give a sensitive answer; the programme must
not present a small residual as proof of accuracy. 5. Missing time sample. A removed packet
must not cause an artificial doubling of velocity through a hard-coded dt. 6. Unstable step.
Detect energy growth in an ideal spring and reduce it by adjusting the method or step.

Numerical and geometric checks
For exact noise-free examples, combine absolute and relative tolerances: |a−b|≤atol+rtol·|b|.
Absolute tolerance matters near zero; relative tolerance matters when scale changes. Choose
tolerances before viewing results and label their units. For integration methods, the main check is
convergence over a series of steps, rather than one fortuitously accurate value.
In test_report.csv, record test name, input scenario, expectation, observation, threshold and
pass/fail. Expected failures are valid: a test passes if the programme recognises an invalid
formulation. Save at least one plot each of a faulty and corrected version. For the final run, remove
computed results and recreate them from raw data using one recorded command sequence.


































M2 • 03 Nov 2026 - 29 Nov 2026 • 75 hours                                                                         8 / 15
СтраницаPage 29 · Step-by-step work: hours 1-40
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M02  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Step-by-step work: hours 1-40

Block A: coordinate and force mathematics
Hours 1-2. Complete the entry diagnostic, create a quantity log and define axis conventions. Solve
two unit-conversion examples and resolve a force into components by hand. Deliverable:
assumptions.md with a link diagram and correctness criteria.
Hours 3-4. Study length, normalisation, dot/cross and projections. Calculate torque by hand, then
check with a library function. Hours 5-6. Study matrices, product order and transposition. Draw a
rotation's effect on a basis; explain the result before running code.
Hours 7-8. Study points, directions and shifting the coordinate origin. Hours 9-10. Solve a simple
force system by hand and check dimensions. If these topics are easy, use a more complex force
orientation while retaining the same object and a clear manual check.
Hours 11-20 - practical. First 2 h: tasks 1 and 2 by hand; next 2 h: transformation functions; 2 h:
basis and torque plots; 2 h: zero vector, degrees and radians, and reverse transformation; final 2 h:
tests and a short explanation without code. Finish when every drawing and number can be related
to one chosen coordinate frame.

Block B: calibration and numerical stability
Hours 21-22. Apply Gaussian elimination to support reactions, then repeat with solve. Hours
23-24. Study rank and overdetermined systems; construct the calibration matrix on paper. Hours
25-26. Study residuals, least squares and QR's role; compare a prediction with the observed point.
Hours 27-28. Explore conditioning with two nearly identical equations and understand solution
error versus residual. Hours 29-30. Study stiffness-matrix eigenvector directions. Avoid proofs for
arbitrary-size matrices until you can explain the 2×2 example.
Hours 31-40 - practical. 2 h: supports and reaction plot; 2 h: encoder generator and calibration;
2 h: held-out validation and a narrow range; 2 h: conditioning and eigenvector directions; 2 h:
documenting coefficients and tests. Checkpoint: recover parameters from noise-free data, then
deliberately create an unidentifiable calibration.
Before proceeding, write three short answers: why inverse is not a replacement for a normal solve
call; why a small residual does not guarantee an accurate parameter; why more identical
observations do not resolve insufficient input diversity. If you cannot answer, replace some plot
styling with another hand-worked example.


































M2 • 03 Nov 2026 - 29 Nov 2026 • 75 hours                                                                          9 / 15
СтраницаPage 30 · Step-by-step work: hours 41-75
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M02  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Step-by-step work: hours 41-75

Block C: motion as a function of time
Hours 41-42. Review derivatives and velocity units for linear and angular motion. Hours 43-44.
Study sin/cos and the chain rule; derive reference q, ω and α. Hours 45-46. Study forward and
central differences, the time assigned to an estimate and boundary handling.
Hours 47-48. Study integration as accumulation, work done by torque and the trapezoidal rule.
Hours 49-50. Derive partial derivatives and one column of the link-endpoint Jacobian. The
derivation is short, so reproduce it unaided.
Hours 51-60 - practical. 2 h: trajectory and exact derivatives; 2 h: finite-difference comparison; 2
h: noise and missing time sample; 2 h: p(q) sensitivity and integral check; 2 h: error plots and
conclusions. Do not change noise and step size together without a control run, or you cannot
explain the RMSE change.
Deliverable: a table of 'method / step / noise / time window / RMSE / maximum error' and two
illustrations: the tangent to the endpoint trajectory and angle recovery by integration. Use three
different Δq values for the linear approximation; one small perturbation cannot reveal the model's
limit.

Block D: dynamics, integration and presentation
Hours 61-62. Convert the second-order equation into a first-order system; check each term's
units. Hours 63-64. Write explicit Euler, semi-implicit Euler and RK4 updates, and calculate one
step by hand for x=0.02 and v=0. Hour 65. Study local and accumulated error, stability, initial
conditions and library-solver tolerances.
Hours 66-75 - practical. 2 h: mass-spring and equilibrium check; 2 h: method and energy
comparison; 2 h: pendulum, period and large angle; 2 h: combined
encoder→angle→position→velocity processing; 2 h: clean reproducible run, six failures and oral
explanation.
Reserve the last 30 minutes for a new variant without copying: change link length, initial angle and
step size; predict the direction of period change before running. Then explain what changed in the
model and what stayed the same. List two omitted real-leg effects and a measurement that would
allow each to be added later.
If integrators take extra time, retain one short file with the shared interface step(f,t,y,h) and
remove interactive elements. Do not cut force-sign checks, the analytical comparison or the
step-reduction experiment: these establish that the mathematical model has been checked,
beyond merely running its code.

Acceptance checks and handover to later
modules

What to save in robot-math
Four completed notebooks; a function module with clear units; input CSVs; parameter
configurations; calibration coefficients; test table; norm, residual, derivative and energy plots; and
README with execution order. State the formula and seed for synthetic data; store reference
values separately. Label the 'raw measurements' field synthetic until a real sensor is used.
Begin each notebook with a robotics question and end with an engineering conclusion. 'The code
ran' is not a conclusion. Suitable statements include: 'the length-scale error increased torque a
thousandfold'; 'the narrow encoder range prevents stable scale estimation'; 'the chosen Euler step
increases this oscillator's energy'. Fill in all numerical results after your own run.

Passing criteria
1. Each of ten practical tasks has an input, result, independent check and edge case. 2.
Parameters, columns and plot axes have units. 3. Analytical and numerical answers are compared
over the same time interval. 4. ODE results cover at least three step sizes and both objects. 5.
Singularity and instability are explicitly identified. 6. A clean run reproduces conclusions without
manually editing intermediate files.
Passing many tests does not replace understanding. For the oral review, choose six questions
below at random and answer each with a small diagram or calculation. You may consult NumPy
syntax; explain the underlying torque, linear-calibration and ODE formulae independently.

Self-check questions
Why does shifting the coordinate origin affect a point but not a direction? When is r×F zero? What
does a negative support reaction mean? How does an overdetermined system differ from an
inconsistent one? Why are residual and coefficient error different quantities? How do units affect
numerical conditioning?
How do you obtain link-endpoint velocity from joint velocity? Why does numerical differentiation
amplify noise? What is a 'linear approximation in angle'? Which initial conditions does a pendulum
require? Why is energy conservation useful as a test? How does fixed-step RK4 differ from RK45 in
solve_ivp?

Subsequent use
M03 uses the same calibration and Jacobian for uncertainty estimation. M04 uses the noisy encoder
and derivative to study filtering. M05 uses torque, reactions and eigenvector directions as
preparation for mechanics. Preserve the functions' public interface, but do not claim real-robot
accuracy from synthetic data. Physical test-bench validation follows electronics and mechanical
preparation.

СтраницаPage 33 · Glossary: terms and definitions
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M02  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Glossary: terms and definitions

Vector. A geometric quantity with direction and magnitude; its components depend on the chosen
basis, while the quantity itself does not.
Basis. A set of linearly independent vectors in terms of which every vector in the space has a
unique representation.
Coordinate frame. An origin together with a basis; point coordinates change when the origin
shifts or the axes rotate.
Rotation matrix. A matrix describing an orthonormal basis's orientation; a proper rotation
satisfies RᵀR=I and det R=1.
Cross product. In three dimensions, a vector perpendicular to both operands; its direction follows
the right-hand rule and its magnitude is the parallelogram's area.
Torque. The vector r×F about a chosen point; it describes a force's rotational effect and is
measured in N·m.
Rank. Number of independent matrix columns or rows; it determines how many independent
constraints a linear system contains.
Residual. The difference A·x−b for a proposed solution; a small residual alone does not guarantee
accurate unknown parameters.
Least squares. Choosing parameters to minimise the sum of squared residuals; fits a model to
redundant, usually inconsistent measurements.
Conditioning. Sensitivity of a problem's result to small input changes; depends on its formulation,
units and scaling.
Eigenvector direction. Direction of a nonzero vector v satisfying A·v=λv. The matrix scales the
vector while preserving the line on which it lies.
Derivative. Limit of the ratio of function increment to argument increment; differentiating position
with respect to time gives velocity in m/s.
Integral. Accumulated contribution of a function over an interval; integrating velocity over time
gives displacement with consistent initial conditions.
Jacobian. Matrix of partial derivatives of output coordinates with respect to inputs; approximately
maps small input changes to output changes.
Ordinary differential equation (ODE). Equation relating an unknown function of one variable to
its derivatives; a motion model also requires initial conditions.
Time step. Time interval for one numerical state update; affects trajectory error, stability and
computation cost.
Numerical stability. Property of a numerical scheme in which perturbations do not grow
unacceptably for the problem and chosen integration step.

СтраницаPage 35 · Motion fundamentals: from joint angle to
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M02  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Motion fundamentals: from joint angle to
foot velocity

Compulsory, within 75 hours. Use 1 h from session 49-50 and 2 h of practice 51-60 already
allocated to p(q) sensitivity and checks. This connects tasks 2 and 8; it does not add tasks beyond
the plan. Before starting, convert 30° to π/6 rad and explain why m/s differs from rad/s.

Why joint velocity differs from point velocity
Consider a rigid link of length L=0.12 m with one revolute joint. Frame A is fixed: its origin is on the
joint axis, x points right, y upwards, and positive q is anticlockwise from x. The foot point has
coordinates p_A(q)=(L cos q, L sin q). Length is constant; backlash and deformation are excluded.
This requires geometry, not link mass.
For a small rotation, endpoint displacement is approximately tangent to the circle. By the chain
rule, v_A=dp_A/dt=J(q)·q̇, where J=(−L sin q, L cos q)ᵀ, in m/rad. Thus |v_A|=L|q̇| and p_A·v_A=0.
The Jacobian depends on configuration: equal angular velocities at different q give equal endpoint
speed but different directions. Even at constant q̇, velocity changes direction: acceleration
a_A=−p_A·q̇² points towards the joint. This last equality assumes q̈=0.

Numerical example and change of fixed frame
At q=π/6 rad and q̇=0.5 rad/s, p_A=(0.103923; 0.060000) m, v_A=(−0.030000; 0.051962) m/s and
|v_A|=0.060000 m/s. Over a short time Δt=0.01 s, tangential displacement is approximately 0.6
mm; distinguish distance travelled in this interval from a change in one coordinate.
Let R_BA=[[0,−1],[1,0]] describe A's axes in another fixed frame B, and t_BA=(0.20;0.10) m be A's
origin position in B. Then p_B=R_BA·p_A+t_BA=(0.140000;0.203923) m, but
v_B=R_BA·v_A=(−0.051962;−0.030000) m/s. The derivative of a constant translation is zero. A
moving B introduces additional terms; that case is not modelled here.

Two checks using existing functions
1. In robot-math, compute the central difference [p(q+q̇h)−p(q−q̇h)]/(2h), h=10⁻⁴ s, and compare
with Jq̇. For these noise-free float64 values, use a teaching tolerance of 10⁻⁸ m/s on the error norm.
Save a table for q=0, π/6, π/2; check tangency, speed magnitude and inverse coordinate
transformation.
2. On the leg diagram, label angle, both frames and the v arrow. Predict doubled speed when L
doubles and a reversed arrow when q̇ changes sign. Deliverables: one drawing and tests for tasks
2/8. These check kinematics; they do not establish the existence of a motor capable of producing
the motion.
Read before calculating: Lynch, Park, Modern Robotics: chapter 5 introduction, deriving ẋ=Jq̇;
§3.3.1, changing coordinate frames. Spatial velocities are studied in M08.

Uncertainty: how much to trust a sensor

M3 • 29 Nov 2026 - 27 Dec 2026 • 75 hours

This month's deliverable
In M02, you obtained an angle, force or position as a number. M03 adds variability, error sources
and conditions under which a conclusion remains valid. Deliver a portfolio of uncertainty and
optimisation work: a 30-repeat measurement experiment, encoder and IMU noise models,
calibration through optimisation, poor-conditioning diagnostics and a report on link-endpoint
position uncertainty.
This month's questions are practical: does encoder jitter differ from actual motion; how should two
angle estimators be compared; how much independent information does a long recording contain;
why did an optimiser produce a plausible but incorrect scale; how far does joint error move a foot
or fingertip? Do not yet build a Kalman filter, machine-learning model or QP controller: first learn to
check the assumptions they will require.

Shared object and data
Continue with the M02 link L=0.12 m, p(q)=(L cos q,L sin q) and calibration q=a·u+b. Create
data/synthetic, data/measured, experiments, calibration, uncertainty and report. In the data
manifest, record each file's source, units, random-number generator seed, date, independent-run
identifier and how ground truth was obtained. Keep synthetic ground truth separate from algorithm
inputs.
The physical experiment needs no actuator: place a stationary IMU in the same fixture thirty times.
An existing phone that exports raw readings also works. If no sensor is available, first practise the
procedure with synthetic data; the real-measurement section remains incomplete until the
experiment is done. Generated noise does not replace measured device repeatability.

Prerequisites and scope
You need array means, matrices, least squares, derivatives and the meaning of the Jacobian from
M02. In the first two hours, explain the differences between true value, measurement, model
residual and numerical error. Review why the calculated 'velocity' of a stationary encoder can
fluctuate. M03 adds ways to describe these fluctuations and assess the robustness of conclusions.
Begin with definitions: a random variable models possible outcomes; a sample is the data actually
obtained; a parameter is an unknown distribution characteristic; an estimator is a rule for
computing from a sample. One distribution plot does not prove normality, and optimiser success
does not establish physically correct calibration. Both distinctions must appear in your checks.
