75 hours: experiments, analysis and
reproducibility

Four work blocks
A, hours 1-20: 10 h theory + 10 h practice. Random variables, distributions, expectation,
variance, covariance, correlation, independence, conditional probability and Bayes' rule. Practical
deliverables: encoder quantisation and IMU noise models, and diagnosis involving a rare event.
B, hours 21-40: 10+10 h. Sampling plans, confidence intervals, effect size, outliers, robust
summaries, hypotheses, repeatability and data leakage. Deliverables: a 30-repeat protocol, raw
recordings and a comparison of two estimators across independent runs.
C, hours 41-60: 10+10 h. Objective functions, constraints, gradients, Hessian meaning, gradient
descent, line search, local minima, least squares and regularisation. Deliverables: calibration with
scipy.optimize, held-out validation and residual analysis.
D, hours 61-75: 5+10 h. SVD, pseudoinverse, poor conditioning, covariance propagation through
a Jacobian, Monte Carlo and bootstrap. Deliverable: an endpoint uncertainty region and checks of
linear-approximation limits. Total: 35 h of theory and analysis plus 40 h of practice.

Organising short and long sessions
Divide each 10 h of theory into five two-hour sessions and the final 5 h into 2+2+1. Each 2 h
session should cover one concept, one hand-worked example and one decision about the
forthcoming experiment. Schedule 10 h practical blocks in available Sunday or holiday sessions
from the original plan; divide each into five 2 h segments and count breaks separately.
The calendar window follows the original plan. A boundary date may coincide with a neighbouring
module; holidays, rest and integration stages are preserved. Allocate step hours sequentially to
available sessions, without double counting or adding another 'compensation' hour.

Experiment log
Before collecting data, record the question, primary metric, unit of independent repetition,
recording-exclusion criterion and stopping rule. Afterwards, add actual deviations from the
protocol. Do not delete an inconvenient recording because it worsens the mean: retain it with a
reason and, if necessary, present analysis with and without exclusion.
If time is short, remove optional CVXPY comparison and complex interactive plots. Retain 30
repeats, basic calibration, splitting data by run, SVD diagnostics and Monte Carlo calculation.
Another book cannot replace the measurement work. Being able to say 'these data do not yet
establish the claim' is a valid laboratory outcome.

Probability and sensor-noise models

Topics to study
Study discrete and continuous random variables, interval probabilities, probability density and
cumulative distribution functions. For sensors, use a normal distribution as a working model of
small disturbances, a uniform distribution as a quantisation simplification, and a Bernoulli
distribution for 'packet lost'. Expectation describes the centre; variance is the mean squared
deviation; standard deviation has the same units as the measurement.
Covariance describes joint variation of two channels; correlation normalises it by their standard
deviations. Zero correlation alone does not establish independence. Consecutive stationary-IMU
samples can be dependent because of internal filters and drift. A thousand samples therefore need
not equal a thousand independent experiment repeats.

Task 1. Encoder quantisation
Input: true angle q within −0.5…0.5 rad and quantisation step Δ=0.001 rad. Compute rounded
q_meas, error e=q_meas−q, a histogram and empirical cumulative distribution function. For
uniform coverage of quantisation intervals, compare variance with Δ²/12. Then take a stationary
angle exactly between two codes and explain why this distribution model need no longer describe
the observations.
Deliverables: generator, two different input trajectories and a table of mean, standard deviation
(SD) and maximum error. Check |e|≤Δ/2 under the chosen rounding convention, apart from stated
numerical tolerances. Failure case: the model saturates beyond range; an error does not become
uniform merely because the data came from an encoder.

Task 2. Shared noise on two IMU axes
Generate 5000 synthetic error pairs by adding each axis's independent noise to a shared
component. Record the covariance matrix and explain its units: for acceleration, (m/s²)². Plot the
point cloud and compare it with independent data having the same per-channel variance. Equal
axis standard deviations do not imply equal uncertainty in their sum.
Check covariance symmetry and nonnegative eigenvalues, allowing for rounding. Add slow shared
drift and compare the recording's first and second halves. Deliver three point clouds and explain
the effect shown by each. The aim is to recognise when constant-noise assumptions fail, rather
than force a 'correct' distribution onto the data.

СтраницаPage 39 · Conditional probability and diagnostic
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M03  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Conditional probability and diagnostic
reliability

Bayes' rule for a clear robot event
Study P(A|B), the law of total probability and Bayes' rule using a frequency table. Example: A is a
genuine foot-contact failure; B is a threshold diagnostic trigger. Sensitivity P(B|A) and the
probability of a real failure after a trigger P(A|B) answer different questions. The latter also depends
on event prevalence.
For the teaching example, use failure probability 1%, sensitivity 95% and a 5% false-trigger
probability without failure. These are illustrative calculation values, not properties of an actual
sensor. Among 10 000 virtual episodes, expect 95 true and 495 false triggers; about 16.1% of all
alerts are true. Check using a probability tree or table.

Task 3. Rare events and thresholds
Create an episode generator with a known label and diagnostic feature. Calculate TP, FP, FN, TN,
then precision=TP/(TP+FP) and recall=TP/(TP+FN). Show how both metrics and trigger frequency
change across several thresholds. If a denominator is zero, return 'undefined' rather than silently
assign a perfect score.
Repeat with event probabilities 0.1%, 1% and 10%, retaining the feature's conditional distributions.
Deliver a table and short note identifying the more consequential error type for this test bench.
Here, diagnostics only create log events; this model does not verify a robot's actual protective
functions.

Task 4. Why independence needs checking
Generate white noise and a correlated series e_t=0.95·e_(t−1)+η_t. Scale them to approximately
equal SD; compare time plots and adjacent-sample correlation. Average over equal-length windows
and measure variation of means across non-overlapping windows. Equal sample counts do not
guarantee equal improvement.
Control check: shuffle the correlated series and repeat. Shuffling preserves the marginal
distribution but destroys temporal structure. Save two plots and explain why randomly splitting
rows of one recording can yield an overly optimistic algorithm evaluation. Exact
effective-sample-size theory is optional; the meaning of an independent run must be understood
now.

Statistics: a real 30-repeat experiment

Write the protocol before recording
Task 5 assesses the repeatability of a stationary IMU repositioned in the same fixture. Choose a
device that exports timestamps and raw accelerometer and gyroscope readings; record its settings
and available rate. Perform 30 separate placements, keeping the device still each time, waiting the
same predetermined settling interval and recording for the same duration. Choose a duration
supported by export; the teaching guideline is 2 s after settling.
The repeat unit is one independent run after repositioning, not one CSV row. Record run_id, fixture
orientation, time, temperature if available, observed interference and setting changes. Within each
run, calculate the axis mean and SD; across 30 runs, examine variation of these means.
Repositioning adds geometric uncertainty, so describe the result as repeatability of the whole
procedure.

Calculations and interpretation
For the 30 means, find the mean, median, SD and interquartile range. If assumptions are
reasonable, construct a 95% t-confidence interval for the mean: mean ± t·s/sqrt(n). This interval
concerns the procedure's mean; it is neither a range covering 95% of future individual readings nor
a promise to cover a particular sensor's true angle.
If run independence or stability fails, show a time plot and limit the conclusion. Do not treat 30 as
universally sufficient: justify this pilot sample size using available time and desired interval width,
then estimate the additional independent repeats needed to halve the interval width under the
same assumptions.

Task 6. Outlier robustness and effect size
Compare two constant-level estimates on the same 30 runs: within-recording arithmetic mean and
median. Add labelled individual outliers to copies of several recordings. Calculate the change in
error relative to the clean copy and paired estimate differences, rather than choose an algorithm
from histogram appearance. Express effects in physical units and relate them to the robot task.
Deliverables: protocol.md, 30 raw-data files or one CSV with run_id, a summary table and a plot in
test order. Edge cases: empty run, gaps, changed sampling rate and noticeable device motion.
Define exclusion criteria before viewing results. Without independent ground truth, compare
robustness and repeatability without claiming absolute IMU accuracy.
To introduce hypothesis testing, state H0: the mean paired difference between the two estimates is
zero. Discuss false rejection of H0 and missing a real effect; statistical significance does not say
whether an effect is useful to the robot. Report the difference in physical units and its interval in
the main conclusion, rather than a p-value alone.

СтраницаPage 41 · Calibration optimisation: from error to
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M03  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Calibration optimisation: from error to
parameters

Minimum theory
A loss function answers a specific question: how far do model predictions differ from
measurements? Parameters θ may include encoder scale and zero; constraints express meaningful
admissible values. The gradient gives the local direction of increasing loss; the Hessian describes
local curvature. Begin with a two-variable quadratic bowl that can be drawn and whose derivatives
can be checked by hand.
Gradient descent updates θ_new=θ−α·grad. Excessive α can increase error; too small an α slows
progress. Learn backtracking line search: reduce the step until the objective decreases by the
required amount. Distinguish stopping criteria based on step, gradient and loss; a small step may
indicate poor scaling rather than a good minimum.

Task 7. Implement descent for scale and zero
Using M02 calibration, scale u to a comparable magnitude and derive the sum-of-squares gradient
with respect to a and b. Check it with central finite differences at five parameter points. Run
descent from three initial guesses with two step strategies; save the loss curve, iteration count and
final coefficients.
On noise-free data, compare with linear lstsq. For poorly scaled u, explain elongated contours and
slow convergence. Deliverables: short implementation, contour plot and table. Edge case: wrong
gradient sign; a test must detect increasing loss and stop the run. Choose the gradient-check
threshold relative to function scale and finite-difference step.

Task 8. Constrained nonlinear model
Use the teaching model q=a·u+b+c·u² with normalised u. Prepare independent calibration and
verification series; generate a small known nonlinear component. Pass the residuals vector, not
total loss, to scipy.optimize.least_squares. Specify bounds, initial guess and parameter scales;
compare ordinary least squares and robust loss with labelled outliers.
Regularise c by adding residual sqrt(λ)·c after choosing a dimensionless scale. Compare several λ
values on the validation set, then evaluate the result once on the test set. Show a case where the
linear model performs better on held-out data despite greater training error. The optimum is an
estimate within the chosen model; still check residual dependence on position and motion
direction.

SVD, pseudoinverses and uncertainty
propagation

Core concepts
SVD factors A=U·Σ·Vᵀ into orthogonal input/output directions and stretch factors. A very small
singular value indicates a parameter direction weakly represented in the data. A pseudoinverse
selects a solution of a singular problem according to a defined rule; it cannot recover information
the experiment never measured.
For p=f(x) and small uncertainties near x̄, use Σ_p≈J·Σ_x·Jᵀ. Σ_x is input covariance; evaluate J
specifically at x̄. Covariance has squared units of the corresponding output quantities. This is a
local approximation, so compare with nonlinear Monte Carlo calculation, especially near geometric
singularities or with large variability.

Task 9. Weakly determined calibration
Take the calibration matrix for a wide u range and the same matrix with inputs restricted to a
narrow band. After applying the same scaling, compare singular values, cond and parameter
changes under a small q perturbation. Find the right singular vector for the smallest singular value:
it identifies the parameter combination least distinguishable in the data.
Save a plot of the uncertain parameter direction and predict which u values a new experiment
should add. Then add extreme positions to the synthetic data and verify improvement. Test: all u
values identical; pinv may return a solution, but the report must identify insufficient rank and
nonunique physical calibration.

Task 10. Foot-position variability
Use L=0.12 m, q=30° and teaching standard uncertainties σ_L=0.0005 m and σ_q=0.005 rad.
Repeat with large noise σ_q=0.3 rad; set nonzero correlation ρ=0.6 while keeping covariance
positive semidefinite. Let x=(L,q), and derive J for p=(L cos q,L sin q). First assume independent
errors, then add admissible nonzero covariance. Compute Σ_p, its eigenvector directions and a 10
000-point Monte Carlo cloud.
Compare coordinate SDs and covariance from the linear prediction with sample estimates. Repeat
for small and large angle noise; record relative discrepancies while avoiding division by nearly zero
covariance. The ellipse visualises the assumed uncertainty model, not a guaranteed real-robot
position region. Negative sampled length requires revising the distribution model rather than
silently deleting inconvenient points.

Integrated laboratory and six validity checks

Assemble the final package
Combine calibration and uncertainty: input encoder_count passes through the chosen q(u,θ) model,
then geometry p(L,q). For each validation run, save predicted position, estimated variability and
actual error if independent ground truth exists. Synthetic experiments have known ground truth;
the real stationary-IMU experiment usually establishes only repeatability.
Create three scenarios: nominal noise, correlated drift and outliers. Split independent series into
training (train), validation and test sets. Choose the model, λ and threshold using train and
validation; open test only after fixing settings. If you subsequently change the solution, mark the
test set as used and prepare a new independent check: repeated tuning removes test
independence.

Required error checks
1. Leakage. Compare random row splits with whole-run splits under slow drift; show why the
former appears better. 2. Pseudoreplication. Duplicate each row 100 times; the reporting
algorithm must not count these as new independent experiments. 3. Outlier. Add one large spike
and compare mean, median and robust loss without deleting the original.
4. Singularity. Nearly constant u must trigger a weak-identifiability warning regardless of solver
success. 5. Nonlinearity. Large q noise invalidates linear covariance propagation; Monte Carlo
must reveal the discrepancy. 6. Nonstationarity. Different means at the start and end require a
separate drift discussion rather than one 'sensor σ'.

Bootstrap: an additional interval check
Resample with replacement from the 30 independent run results and estimate intervals for the
median or paired difference. Record resample count and seed; repeat with another seed to observe
computational variation. Do not resample correlated individual rows as independent observations.
Temporal dependence requires another scheme, such as block bootstrap, which is sufficient to
identify as a later topic.
Distinguish observation and interpretation on every report page. A useful format is: 'between-run
SD is … under these conditions; it includes repositioning; no independent absolute reference is
available'. Do not fill numerical fields in advance. Save metrics with units, interval bounds,
independent-repeat count and specific applicability limits.

Session sequence: hours 1-40

Block A - build a noise model and identify its limits
Hours 1-2. Review error, true value and estimator definitions; prepare the data structure. Hours
3-4. Study distributions, expectation and variance; calculate probabilities of three discrete-encoder
outcomes by hand. Hours 5-6. Study covariance and correlation with two channels. Hours 7-8.
Study conditional probability and Bayes' rule through a diagnostic table. Hours 9-10. Study
independence, temporal dependence and the experimental unit.
Hours 11-20 - practice. 2 h: quantisation and Δ/2 check. 2 h: independent and shared IMU noise.
2 h: rare event, TP/FP/FN/TN. 2 h: white and correlated series. 2 h: plots, generator tests and
conclusions. For each plot, state the sensor assumption built into the generator and a real effect it
does not yet describe.
Hour 20 checkpoint: explain to someone without statistics training why high diagnostic sensitivity
can coexist with many false alarms, and why 5000 adjacent samples do not equal 5000
repositionings. If you cannot, revisit the frequency table and temporal-dependence plot.

Block B - make a justified comparison
Hours 21-22. Study sampling and estimation; choose the measured quantity. Hours 23-24. Write
the 30-repeat protocol and exclusion criteria. Hours 25-26. Study SD, standard error and a
t-confidence interval for the mean. Hours 27-28. Study outliers, median, IQR and effect size.
Hours 29-30. Study training, validation and test sets, paired comparison and repeatability.
Hours 31-40 - practice. 2 h: fixture preparation and pilot export; 2 h: 30 measurement runs with
metadata; 2 h: integrity checks and individual-run summaries; 2 h: intervals and estimator
comparison; 2 h: report and excluded-recording review. If longer recordings are necessary, reduce
styling and use prepared summary scripts while retaining the independent-repeat count.
Checkpoint: another person can understand the dataset's experiment boundaries, what remained
stationary, the coordinate frame used and why some recordings are marked doubtful. Without this
information, measurements cannot support rigorous calibration comparisons in later months.











































M3 • 29 Nov 2026 - 27 Dec 2026 • 75 hours                                                                         9 / 15
СтраницаPage 45 · Session sequence: hours 41-75
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M03  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Session sequence: hours 41-75

Block C - optimise and verify calibration
Hours 41-42. Write the loss function for q=a·u+b and check dimensions. Hours 43-44. Derive
and numerically check the gradient; draw curvature in two parameters. Hours 45-46. Study fixed
steps and backtracking. Hours 47-48. Study nonlinear-model residuals, constraints and initial
guesses. Hours 49-50. Study regularisation and model selection using validation data.
Hours 51-60 - practice. 2 h: implement descent and compare with lstsq; 2 h: least_squares with
bounds; 2 h: outliers and robust losses; 2 h: several λ values and independent series; 2 h: gradient
checks, model saving and residual analysis. For every run, retain status, evaluation count, initial
guess, objective value and physical coefficients.
In the last two-hour segment, deliberately create a problem with local minima, such as periodic
zero-offset ambiguity in sin(u+b), and start from different b values. This briefly introduces local
minima and period ambiguity; do not add this complexity to the main calibrator. Conclude that
results depend on the model and observational information, not merely the algorithm's name.

Block D - uncertainty in the result
Hours 61-62. Study SVD geometry and truncation of small singular values; check a diagonal
example by hand. Hours 63-64. Derive J with respect to L and q, and propagate Σ. Hour 65. Study
Monte Carlo, bootstrap, and measurement uncertainty versus computational variation in an
estimate.
Hours 66-75 - practice. 2 h: poor calibration, SVD and a revised measurement plan. 2 h:
analytical endpoint covariance. 2 h: Monte Carlo and large noise. 2 h: bootstrap by run and
consolidated report. 2 h: six error checks, a fresh run and defending conclusions.
Final half-hour task without copying: specify two noise models with equal SD but different
cross-axis dependence. Before running, predict which gives greater variation in a chosen
foot-position projection. Check using the covariance formula and simulation. If the prediction was
wrong, correct the explanation and preserve the mistake as a useful finding.
Do not measure success by method count. The required minimum is one explainable calibrator,
one real experiment with justified conclusions, one poor-identifiability example and one
error-propagation check. Rust/C++ may read M01 logs, but reimplementing all statistics in three
languages is outside the 75 h.

ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M03  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Laboratory acceptance and the future robot

Verifiable deliverables
The package must include ten tasks with initial conditions, a 30-repeat protocol, labelled real and
synthetic data, distribution models with limitations, calibration configurations, splits by series,
residual plots, SVD diagnostics, covariance and Monte Carlo calculations. Record commands,
library versions and report-reproduction order in README.
Every substantial number must answer: 'which data?', 'what unit of repetition?', 'what physical
units?' and 'which metric?'. A mean without run count or an interval without a calculation method
fails acceptance. Do not report more significant figures than uncertainty supports; preserve full
machine precision separately for reproduction.

Check your understanding
Explain variance versus SD; independence versus zero correlation; random spread versus
systematic bias; repeatability versus absolute accuracy. Use a table to distinguish P(failure|alarm)
from P(alarm|failure). Why can you not narrow a confidence interval simply by copying rows?
For optimisation: what goes into residuals; why normalise parameters; why is success insufficient;
what does a small singular value reveal; what does regularisation change, and what does it not
know about the robot? For uncertainty: where is J evaluated; what are Σ's units; when does linear
propagation fail; which units should bootstrap resample?
Practical assessment: take a new independent synthetic series with a seed unknown to you,
calibrate and compare estimates with saved ground truth. Add drift and state which assumptions
fail. For real data, show one supported conclusion and one requiring a different reference or
experiment.

Handover
Pass M04 the actual sampling rates, gaps, noise summaries, original recordings and corrupted
copies for filtering work. Pass M05 length-and-angle error propagation as an example connecting
tolerances to foot position. Later filters and multi-joint calibration can reuse these functions, but a
sensor's numerical covariance must be remeasured after mounting or settings change.
Keep open questions about temperature drift, vibration dependence, axis correlation, reverse
mechanism travel and reference accuracy. For each, describe the smallest future experiment that
could test it. This makes the laboratory a foundation for later hardware tests, beyond a collection of
one-off plots.

Assigned reading: a short route

Read only the specified passages before the corresponding experiment. References are mainly in
English; keep explanations, glossary and report in English. Reading and preparation fit within the
existing 75 hours; whole books are not required.

Core reading
1. Allen B. Downey, Think Stats, 3rd online edition. Chapters 2, 4, 7, 8: Distributions;
Cumulative Distribution Functions; Relationships between variables; Estimation. Tasks 1-6 need
distributions, relationships and estimation uncertainty; adapt the examples to your measurements.
2. NIST/SEMATECH, e-Handbook of Statistical Methods. §1.3.5.2 Confidence Limits for the
Mean: interval from 30 independent runs; §1.3.5.11, skewness and kurtosis: noise-shape reference.
Write interval assumptions before inserting numbers.
3. Stephen Boyd, Lieven Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization (2004). §4.1, §6.1, §6.3,
§9.2-9.3. Problem formulation; norm approximation; regularisation; descent and gradient methods.
In tasks 7-8, connect loss, constraints and parameter scale to physical calibration. General-case
proofs are optional.

Compact implementation references
SciPy optimize. least_squares: fun, jac, bounds, x_scale, loss. Before task 8, check stopping
criteria and output fields. A success status does not replace unit, bound and held-out-data checks.
NumPy. svd: Returns, Notes. For task 9, reconstruct A from U,S,Vh, then compare the
pseudoinverse with pinv. Explain what changes when a small singular value is truncated.
SciPy stats. bootstrap: data, statistic, paired, method. Resample independent runs; use paired
only for paired comparisons. Optional constrained least-squares comparison: CVXPY example.
Reading sequence. First distributions and the 30-repeat plan, then estimates and intervals, then
optimisation and SVD. Deliver one sheet of experiment assumptions and one defining the
calibration problem.

СтраницаPage 48 · Glossary: terms and definitions
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M03  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Glossary: terms and definitions

Random variable. A numerical function of a possible random-experiment outcome; its distribution
specifies probabilities of values or ranges.
Independence. Property of events or variables whereby information about one does not change
the probability distribution of the other.
Conditional probability. Probability of A given B: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B), provided P(B)>0.
Sample. The particular set of observations obtained; under temporal dependence, its size is not
the number of independent observations.
Parameter and estimate. A parameter characterises an unknown model; an estimate
approximates it from a particular sample using a specified rule.
Bias. Difference between an estimator's expectation and the true parameter. Averaging does not
remove constant sensor bias.
Variance. Expected squared deviation from the mean; describes variability and has squared units
of the measured quantity.
Standard deviation. Square root of variance; describes individual-value variability in original
units, such as rad or m/s².
Standard error. Standard deviation of an estimator's distribution over repeated samples;
describes estimation uncertainty rather than individual-reading variability.
Covariance. Mean product of centred deviations of two quantities; its sign describes the direction
of their joint linear variation.
Correlation. Normalised covariance; describes linear association, but zero generally does not
imply independence.
Confidence interval. Interval produced by a procedure that, over repeated experiments, covers a
fixed parameter at the specified frequency.
Bootstrap. Estimation of a statistic's distribution by repeated sampling with replacement. The
resampling unit must match the original experiment's independent unit.
Loss function. Scalar measure of model-data discrepancy; its choice determines which errors
have greater influence on calibration.
Gradient. Vector of a scalar function's partial derivatives; gives the local direction of greatest
increase for the chosen coordinates and metric.
Regularisation. An additional preference or penalty in estimation that limits unstable solutions at
the cost of possible systematic bias.
SVD (singular value decomposition). Factorisation A=UΣVᵀ for a real matrix; singular values
describe amplification along mutually orthogonal directions.
Identifiability. Ability to distinguish parameters from available observations and inputs; repeating
the same experiment can preserve model ambiguity.

Equipment, installation and checks

Complete preparation within the first study blocks in place of another general overview. The
budget remains 75 hours; delivery waiting time is excluded. Statuses below specify actions for you
to take, not purchases or installations already completed.

Use existing equipment
Use the MacBook Pro M4 and M02 Python environment with pinned NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib,
pytest and the chosen notebook environment. For physical work, use an existing phone with
raw IMU data or an existing IMU, a stable fixture and a way to repeat placement. Perform 30
separate placements and runs, not 30 adjacent samples.

Purchases if needed
No new mandatory M03 purchases. A motor and separate new IMU board are unnecessary
before M06. If the phone cannot supply the required data, use an available existing sensor;
synthetic work can begin immediately, but the real experiment remains open until 30 physical
repeats are completed.

Install now
On the phone: an app exporting original accelerometer readings, timestamps and units; for
example, phyphox, Acceleration with g. Check sensor availability on your model. Choose readings
including gravity; do not describe 'linear acceleration' after hidden processing as a raw channel.
On macOS ARM: no new mandatory packages; use scipy.stats and scipy.optimize from M02. If the
file format requires another package, add only that package and update the lockfile. Install CVXPY
solely for the optional constrained-calibration comparison, not as an M03 passing requirement.

Readiness checks
Before the series, export one pilot CSV containing time in seconds, three axes, units, run identifier
and sensor-mode name. Check finite values, timestamp ordering, gaps and duration. On a
stationary support, raw accelerometer magnitude should be near g; this checks mode and scale,
not full calibration.
Open the CSV after restarting the notebook. On synthetic data with a known seed, calculate mean,
SD and an interval; recover known a,b with least_squares and check SVD matrix reconstruction.
Save software versions and the data manifest. Successful optimisation does not replace checking
ground truth and run independence.

Before the next stage
The raw-data archive must contain 30 identifiable physical repeats or explicitly mark that part
incomplete. Keep export settings and synthetic data separately; assess laboratory readiness
against the original M03 criteria without adding hours.

СтраницаPage 50 · Motion fundamentals: how angle error moves
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M03  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Motion fundamentals: how angle error moves
the foot

Compulsory, within 75 hours. Use 1 h from 63-64 and 4 h from block 66-75 already allocated to
analytical covariance and Monte Carlo in task 10. No new measurements or equipment are
required. Entry check: explain zero-offset error, random variability and standard error of the mean.

Displacement direction depends on the error source
Use the task 10 link: L=0.12 m, q=π/6 rad, in a fixed planar frame with x right and y upwards; p=(L
cos q,L sin q). Parameters u=(L,q) have small independent zero-mean errors: σ_L=0.0005 m,
σ_q=0.005 rad. This is a specified teaching model, not a claim about real-encoder accuracy.
A small length error moves the endpoint along the link: ∂p/∂L=(cos q,sin q)ᵀ. Angle error acts
tangentially: ∂p/∂q=(−L sin q,L cos q)ᵀ. Assemble these columns into J to obtain δp≈Jδu. Here u
denotes the parameter pair, not encoder_count in the calibration model.
Covariance transforms as Σ_p≈J·diag(σ_L²,σ_q²)·Jᵀ. Independent input errors do not imply
independent x and y: both outputs depend on L and q. Standard spread along the link is 0.5 mm
and across it Lσ_q=0.6 mm; these are ellipse semiaxes at one standard uncertainty, not a
guaranteed foot-position region.

A calculation you can check by hand
At 30°, Σ_xx=0.2775 mm², Σ_yy=0.3325 mm², Σ_xy=Σ_yx=−0.047631 mm². Thus σ_x≈0.5268 mm
and σ_y≈0.5766 mm. The matrix trace is 0.61 mm², the sum 0.5²+0.6²; rotating axes changes
components but preserves this trace.
Now add a constant zero-offset error Δq=+0.01 rad. The linear mean shift J_qΔq≈(−0.600;1.039)
mm has length 1.2 mm. The exact change p(q+Δq)−p(q)≈(−0.605;1.036) mm. Repeating one
position can reduce uncertainty in the estimated mean, but does not remove this constant
geometric shift.

Verify task 10 and decide what to calibrate
1. Using the same 10 000-point Monte Carlo cloud, compare both variances and covariance with
the calculation, then rotate axes by 90° and check trace and eigenvalues. Save a drawing of the
link, ellipse and cloud. Do not use relative error of nearly zero covariance as the sole metric; allow
for Monte Carlo's own variability.
2. Add Δq separately and show the cloud-centre shift; then restore the task's large σ_q=0.3 rad.
Explain why a tangent describes the arc less accurately. In the report, state what needs correcting:
zero offset, length or random-error model. M03 phone repeatability alone does not calibrate a
future leg's geometry.
Read before calculating: NIST/SEMATECH, §2.5.5: propagation of error, sensitivity coefficients;
Lynch, Park, Modern Robotics, chapter 5 introduction: Jacobian.

СтраницаPage 51 · Electronics and signals for a robot sensor
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M04  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Electronics and signals for a robot sensor
node

M4 • 27 Dec 2026 - 31 Jan 2027 • 75 hours

What you will build
M04 delivers a low-voltage electrical experiment log and a sensor-signal filtering report.
The first part teaches assembly and measurement of simple future-robot circuits: a status
indicator, analogue-input divider, digital contact and a switch for a small inductive load. The second
explains why functioning electronics do not guarantee usable data: sampling rate, quantisation,
aliasing and delay change the observed motion.
These tasks directly support leg and hand design. A foot-contact sensor or limit switch must
produce a defined logic level. An analogue position sensor requires a suitable voltage range. A
body-mounted IMU sees both useful tilt and vibration. Filtering may suppress jitter, but delayed
angles can degrade later feedback. Measure this tradeoff in M04 before programming the M06
controller.

Equipment and monthly scope
You need an adjustable supply with current limiting and a suitable low-voltage output, a
multimeter, breadboard, wires, resistors, LEDs, small capacitors, a switch and switching-circuit
components. Frequency experiments may use simulation; an oscilloscope or logic analyser allows
physical measurement but does not replace circuit understanding. First record available equipment
specifications, then select compatible components.
Battery packs and high currents are outside the plan before checkpoint G1. Here, use bench
circuits with limited stored energy; leg power drives, loaded motors and whole-robot power come
later. A small relay coil with known specifications and unloaded contacts is sufficient for the
inductive experiment. Derive current limits and fuse ratings from the actual components rather
than copy universal values.

Preparation after M02-M03
Retain M03 noisy encoder and IMU recordings, timestamps and the 30-repeat protocol. Create
circuits/, measurements/, signals/ and filter_report/. Link every measurement to a circuit revision,
component values, probe locations and instrument mode. State which results were calculated,
simulated or physically measured.
Initial check: distinguish voltage and current, convert mA to A and µF to F, and solve I=V/R for a
known resistor. If electronics is entirely new, devote the first two hours to circuit diagrams and the
multimeter; use familiar Python for software work. Working ESP32 firmware is not yet required this
month.

ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M04  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Allocating 75 hours and laboratory
procedures

Four blocks
A, hours 1-20: 10 h theory + 10 h practice. Voltage, current, resistance, power and energy;
Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws; series and parallel branches; multimeter use. Deliverables: LED and
loaded divider with predictions and measurements.
B, hours 21-40: 10+10 h. Capacitors, diodes, BJT/MOSFET and flyback diode; pull resistors, logic
levels, ground and supply decoupling; wires, connectors, crimping and fuses. Deliverables: verified
low-power switch and wiring diagram for a future sensor node.
C, hours 41-60: 10+10 h. Sampling, Nyquist, aliasing and quantisation; low-pass, high-pass and
notch filters; moving average, IIR and complementary estimation. Deliverable: reproducible
encoder and IMU processing with error checks.
D, hours 61-75: 5+10 h. Frequency response, bandwidth, phase, FFT, vibration spectrum,
ADC/PWM and sensor delay. Deliverables: noise-versus-delay table, aliasing experiment and final
presentation. Total: 35 h of analysis and 40 h of practice.

Scheduling sessions
Divide ten theory hours into five two-hour sessions and the final 5 h into 2+2+1. Divide each 10 h
practical into five parts: circuit and prediction, assembly, measurement, edge cases and
documentation. For electrical experiments, calculate and draw wiring first, assemble without
power, then measure only after checking.
First-page dates follow the original plan. Boundary dates may overlap a neighbouring module;
holidays, rest and integration stages are not recalculated. Work steps fill available sessions
sequentially without double counting. Time spent merely waiting for recording or printing does not
add study hours.

Required measurement sequence
Before power-up, check polarity, pinout, component limits, common return and accidental shorts.
Measure voltage across a circuit section; measure current in series with its branch; measure
resistance and continuity only on an unpowered circuit with discharged capacitors. After current
measurement, return the probe to the voltage socket. Do not test incorrect ammeter connection by
creating a real short circuit.
Before the physical inductive experiment, check the circuit against component documentation and,
if inexperienced, review it with someone who can assemble such circuits. Without the necessary
review or equipment, perform calculation and simulation and mark the physical work pending. A
simulator screenshot cannot replace real-circuit acceptance. If behind schedule, reduce filter
variants while retaining basic circuits and delay measurement.

СтраницаPage 53 · Direct current: indicator and analogue input
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M04  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Direct current: indicator and analogue input

Study before assembly
Voltage is potential difference; current is charge flow; resistance relates them in an ohmic element:
V=I·R. Power P=V·I is measured in watts; energy E=P·t at constant power is measured in joules.
Kirchhoff's current law expresses current balance; the voltage law expresses loop-voltage balance.
Choose arrow directions beforehand: a negative calculated value indicates the reverse direction.
Study series and parallel connections, open-circuit voltage and loading. An LED is not a constant
resistor: its forward voltage depends on current and temperature. Calculate the limiting resistor for
permissible current and the worst combination of supply voltage and forward drop, then check
resistor power.

Task 1. Node status indicator
Input: supply and LED with manufacturer documentation, and two suitable resistors. A teaching
calculation for 5 V, Vf≈2 V and 5 mA gives about 600 ohm; this illustrates arithmetic, while the
actual value depends on your components and margin. Draw the loop, label voltage drops and
current, then assemble LED and resistor with the supply disconnected.
After checking the circuit, enable power with the calculated limit. Measure supply, LED and resistor
voltages; compute current as V_R/R and, if needed, compare with a correctly connected direct
measurement. Deliverables: schematic, photograph, component values and a
predicted-versus-measured table. Check voltage balance. Study reversed polarity and a missing
resistor in a diagram or simulation without exposing components to damage.

Task 2. Divider as a position-sensor model
Build a divider from two known resistors. Predict V_out=V_in·R2/(R1+R2), then measure without an
added load. Add a third resistor parallel to the lower leg and recalculate using equivalent
resistance. This demonstrates the practical meaning of the next device's input resistance.
Compare three positions of a model resistive sensor; plot voltage against divider-leg ratio. Deliver
an error table accounting for resistor and instrument tolerances. Edge case: divider output exceeds
the future analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) input limit; identify incompatibility during
calculation. Do not treat a divider as a complete voltage regulator or universal input protection.





































M4 • 27 Dec 2026 - 31 Jan 2027 • 75 hours                                                                          3 / 15
СтраницаPage 54 · Components, ground and logic levels
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M04  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Components, ground and logic levels

From passive components to switching
Study capacitors through Q=C·V and energy C·V²/2, and RC charging/discharging with time
constant τ=R·C. A diode conducts mainly in one direction and has current and voltage limits. A BJT
is controlled by base current; a MOSFET by gate-source voltage and gate charge. On-state losses
and switching transients matter, beyond the component name.
Distinguish VGS(th) from the voltage at which the manufacturer specifies RDS(on): threshold does
not mean a fully enhanced power switch. Study the selected package's exact pinout. For a digital
input, compare source VOH/VOL with receiver VIH/VIL and absolute limits. A '3.3 V' board label
does not make all pins 5 V compatible.

Task 3. Foot contact and pull-up resistor
Model the contact with a normal switch connecting the input to ground. A pull-up resistor connects
the input to a suitable logic supply. Before attaching a controller, measure open/closed contact
levels with a multimeter and calculate pull-up current. For teaching values 3.3 V and 10 kohm,
closed-contact current is about 0.33 mA; verify the final value against the input and wire length.
Try two resistor values and compare prediction with measurement. A broken wire must have a
defined logic meaning for future diagnostics, though this need not distinguish it from an open
contact. Deliver a state table for 'open, closed, broken wire' and an explanation. First observe or
simulate switch bounce; firmware debouncing comes in M06.

Task 4. RC circuits, decoupling and return current
Build an RC circuit in a simulator, apply a step and predict the time to approximately 63% of final
voltage. With a suitable instrument, measure the transient in a circuit with little stored energy.
Double R or C and compare the timescale. Save a plot and τ-estimation error; account for
instrument input resistance.
Draw supply-current paths for the sensor and a separate load. Explain why decoupling capacitors
sit near supply pins and why a long shared return wire can introduce interference. Do not
disconnect ground while powered to 'demonstrate failure'. Model shared-wire resistance and show
the added voltage drop caused by load current.





































M4 • 27 Dec 2026 - 31 Jan 2027 • 75 hours                                                                         4 / 15
СтраницаPage 55 · Protected switching and sensor-bench
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M04  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Protected switching and sensor-bench
connections

Task 5. Small inductive load
Choose a low-power, low-voltage relay coil with known rated voltage, resistance and current. Leave
relay contacts unloaded. Draw a low-side switch: coil between positive supply and drain or
collector, source or emitter to common ground. Connect the flyback diode across the coil so it is
reverse-biased in the normal energised state; on a standard positive rail, its cathode connects to
the positive side.
First calculate coil current, switch losses, control-level compatibility and diode-rating margins.
Study any ULN2003A option through its documentation: connect the clamp-diode common pin
correctly, and do not assume the whole breadboard assembly can carry the IC's rated currents.
With a MOSFET, ensure a defined off-state gate voltage and check RDS(on) at the actual drive
voltage.

Experiment sequence and acceptance
1. Check the circuit on paper and in simulation. 2. Verify components and pinouts. 3. Assemble
unpowered after selecting the supply current limit and fuse. 4. Start with static on/off operation. 5.
Measure coil supply and switch voltage drop. 6. If an oscilloscope is available and its ground
connection is understood, compare the measured transient with the model.
Deliver a log of currents, voltages, calculated losses and turn-off response. The coil must reliably
de-energise, current must remain within component limits, and wiring must show no overload
signs. Perform the no-flyback-diode experiment only in simulation. A multimeter cannot establish
absence of a brief voltage spike; explicitly state if fast transients were not measured.

Task 6. Wiring, connector and fuse
List connection details: wire length and cross-section, contact type, connector current rating,
retention method and labels. Calculate ΔV=I·R across outgoing and return wires. Select fuse rating
together with its time-current characteristic, operating and inrush currents, voltage and the
weakest section's allowable conditions; 'slightly above current' is insufficient.
On an unpowered sample, inspect crimps visually and apply a light controlled pull according to
contact instructions; check continuity of each conductor and isolation from adjacent ones. Prepare
a pin→signal→voltage→wire_colour table and photographs of both ends. Edge cases: mirrored
connector pinout and reversed polarity. Detect these before powering rather than rely on
protection after an error.

СтраницаPage 56 · Sampling: when a sensor reports different
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M04  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Sampling: when a sensor reports different
motion

Theory
Sampling converts a continuous signal into values at time intervals. fs=1/dt is measured in hertz. A
band-limited signal requires a sampling rate above twice its highest frequency, plus practical
margin for an antialiasing filter's transition band. Once frequencies have aliased, an ordinary digital
low-pass filter applied after recording cannot reliably separate them.
ADC quantisation limits amplitude resolution; sampling limits temporal resolution. Study saturation,
missing samples and uneven timestamp intervals separately. PWM is a pulse train with a defined
on-time fraction; its frequency differs from command-update frequency and does not automatically
produce a precise analogue voltage.

Task 7. Vibration becomes apparent motion
Generate ground truth on a dense time grid: a useful 2 Hz sinusoid plus 70 Hz vibration. Sample at
100 Hz and show the false 30 Hz component; repeat at 250 Hz. All numbers are teaching examples.
Compare time plots and spectra, labelling true and observed frequencies.
Next, apply a suitable antialiasing filter to the dense recording before downsampling, and compare
with 'downsample first, filter afterwards'. Deliver three spectra and explain operation order. Edge
case: a sinusoid at fs/2 with an unsuitable phase; a few samples cannot reliably recover its
amplitude. Do not test the Nyquist criterion only at the exact boundary.

Task 8. ADC and actual timestamps
Model conversion of voltage 0…Vref to an N-bit ADC integer code with explicit rounding and
saturation rules. Calculate the quantisation step for the chosen model, plot error during a slow
voltage change and check the smallest distinguishable change in a model joint position.
Add timestamp-interval variation (jitter) and one missing sample. Compare angle derivatives using
constant dt and actual intervals; incorporate M01 checks. Deliver a CSV with raw_code, t_s,
voltage_V, angle_rad and flags. Do not silently treat irregular samples as uniform before FFT: for
this laboratory, select a uniform segment or explicitly resample onto a grid and describe the
procedure.




































M4 • 27 Dec 2026 - 31 Jan 2027 • 75 hours                                                                         6 / 15
СтраницаPage 57 · Filters for encoders and body tilt
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M04  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Filters for encoders and body tilt

Required concepts
A low-pass filter preserves slow components and attenuates high frequencies; a high-pass filter
attenuates DC and slow components; a notch filter suppresses a narrow band. A moving average
uses a finite sample window; an IIR uses previous state. A simple low-pass filter is
y[k]=α·x[k]+(1−α)·y[k−1], with 0<α≤1. Smaller α gives stronger smoothing and slower response.
Study causality: a real-time filter cannot access future samples. Forward-backward processing such
as filtfilt is useful for recorded-data analysis, but cannot establish a streaming algorithm's delay.
Define initial filter state and behaviour after missing samples separately.

Task 9. Encoder noise versus delay
Input: a slow reference trajectory with a stationary section and a step, followed by a copy with
noise and outliers. Implement causal moving averages with windows 3, 5, 11 and IIR filters with
three α values. Calculate SD on the same stationary section, motion RMSE and time to reach 50%
of the step relative to the reference. Distinguish step delay from 10-90% rise time.
Deliver a parameter table, time plots and a chosen tradeoff for the future joint monitor. Edge
cases: first packet, NaN, a long gap and restart. NaN handling must allow valid IIR state to recover.
State the policy for each case: reject, reset or continue with a flag; the policy must be visible in
output data.

Task 10. Complementary tilt estimation
Generate a synthetic body-tilt trajectory in one plane with known θ(t). One input is angular velocity
to integrate, with a small constant bias; the other is a noisy accelerometer angle estimate
assuming small translational acceleration. Implement θ_est=β·(θ_prev+ω·dt)+(1−β)·θ_acc and
check rad and s units. For the initial discrete approximation, use β=τ/(τ+dt), with chosen time
constant τ in seconds; recalculate β when dt changes and check the response.
Compare each separate estimate and their combination at rest, during tilt and during artificial
linear acceleration. The last case must reveal the accelerometer-angle limitation. Do not add full
3D orientation, quaternions or automatic calibration here. Deliver drift/noise plots and describe
conditions in which this simplified complementary filter is suitable.

СтраницаPage 58 · Frequency response and latency budget
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M04  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Frequency response and latency budget

What a vibration spectrum means
FFT converts a finite, uniformly sampled recording into frequency components. Study recording
length, frequency spacing fs/N, DC component, window functions and spectral leakage. Spectrum
amplitude and power spectral density are different quantities; acceleration PSD has units
(m/s²)²/Hz. Welch's method helps estimate a noise spectrum, but window parameters affect
resolution.
A filter's frequency response describes amplitude and phase changes at each frequency. For a
sinusoid, time delay relates to phase, but one delay constant may not describe an arbitrary signal.
Do not approve a filter for future control from one smoothed plot: relate bandwidth and phase to
task dynamics.

Task 11. Measure the frequency tradeoff
Pass a set of sinusoids through the task 9 causal filter. After the initial transient, measure
amplitude ratio and phase shift; compare with scipy.signal.freqz. Add one synthetic vibration peak
and calculate PSD with Welch's method. If using a notch filter, first specify centre frequency and
suppressed bandwidth, then verify that nearby useful components remain intact.
Deliver amplitude/phase response plots and a three-variant table. For each setting, report
stationary SD, motion RMSE, step delay and attenuation of the selected vibration. Define
acceptance thresholds from the teaching monitor's requirements; the conclusion does not establish
suitability for balancing a real robot.

From ADC to computed state
Draw the timing sequence: physical event → wait for sampling → conversion and internal sensor
filter → transmission → processing → publication. List ADC sampling rate, output-message rate,
PWM update rate and computation time separately. '100 Hz' does not describe the whole chain.
Some times come from manufacturer documentation, some are measured and some remain
unknown.
Add a known message delay to the test-bench model and compare physical-change time with
filter-output time. If source and receiver clocks are not synchronised, their timestamp difference is
not a reliable one-way latency. M04 needs one shared simulation timebase and a separate list of
future M06-M07 hardware measurements.

Work sequence: hours 1-40

Block A: understand multimeter readings
Hours 1-2. Inventory equipment, study modes and convert units. Hours 3-4. Ohm's law, power
and LED calculations. Hours 5-6. Kirchhoff's laws and series/parallel branches. Hours 7-8.
Divider, loading and instrument input. Hours 9-10. Draw correct probe placement for all
forthcoming measurements and check circuits.
Hours 11-20 - practice. 2 h: unpowered LED assembly and checks; 2 h: LED measurements and
voltage balance; 2 h: unloaded and loaded divider; 2 h: repeat measurements and account for
tolerances; 2 h: log, photographs and error review. Do not spend the practical buying equipment:
prepare it before the relevant session.
At hour 20, choose a new resistor pair and predict divider output before measuring. Explain
deviations from nominal-value calculations: tolerances, actual supply, instrument loading or
connection errors. Identifying testable causes is more useful than adjusting an answer to an ideal
number.

Block B: from contact to small coil
Hours 21-22. Capacitors, diodes and RC transients. Hours 23-24. BJT/MOSFET, pinouts and
turn-on specifications. Hours 25-26. Pull resistors and logic-level compatibility table. Hours
27-28. Flyback diode, return currents and decoupling. Hours 29-30. Wires, connectors, crimping
and protection selection for the actual circuit.
Hours 31-40 - practice. 2 h: pull-up switch and RC. 2 h: inductive-switch schematic, simulation
and component checks. 2 h: physical assembly of the checked circuit. 2 h: measurements, static
turn-off and log. 2 h: pinout, unpowered connection checks and verification report.
Intermediate acceptance: another person can use the schematic to trace on/off current paths,
identify flyback-diode polarity and find protection ratings. Documentation supports all voltages and
permissible operating conditions. If hardware is not ready, software block C proceeds
independently; physical items remain open without being falsely marked complete.

Work sequence: hours 41-75

Block C: record a signal and verify its interpretation
Hours 41-42. Sampling, fs and Nyquist; predict an alias frequency by hand. Hours 43-44.
Quantisation, saturation, timestamps and jitter. Hours 45-46. Low-pass, high-pass and notch
filters, and causality. Hours 47-48. Moving average and IIR; calculate state after one sample.
Hours 49-50. Planar complementary filter and accelerometer-angle assumptions.
Hours 51-60 - practice. 2 h: 70→30 Hz aliasing and filtering before downsampling. 2 h: ADC
model and missing sample. 2 h: causal encoder filters. 2 h: complementary angle and body
acceleration. 2 h: error table and restart/NaN tests. Use the same reference when comparing
settings.
By hour 60, implement streaming interface update(sample,timestamp). It updates state without
future data and returns a value plus diagnostic flag. A separate saved-file analysis may use the
whole recording, but its result name and delay conclusions must reflect that.

Block D: frequencies, latency and presentation
Hours 61-62. FFT, windows, resolution and PSD. Hours 63-64. Frequency response, bandwidth
and phase shift. Hour 65. Build the ADC/sensor/transport/filter/PWM latency budget and identify
unknown times.
Hours 66-75 - practice. 2 h: spectrum and Welch parameters. 2 h: sinusoidal runs and freqz. 2 h:
final noise, error and delay table. 2 h: six error checks and reproduction. 2 h: assemble electronics
log and report, give an oral explanation, and list M06 hardware questions.
Six required failure cases: incorrect polarity detected before power-up; mirrored pinout found by
continuity checks; ADC range excess identified by calculation and simulation; aliasing not 'fixed' by
later filtering; NaN does not permanently corrupt IIR; a long gap is flagged and handled by the
chosen policy. The first three require no deliberate damage to the physical test bench.
Final new variant: change fs by a factor of two and, before running, predict changes in an
11-sample window's delay, the IIR coefficient for the same time constant and the observed alias
frequency. Verify the calculation. If the programme simply keeps the old coefficients, explain why
filter behaviour in physical seconds changes.

ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M04  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Acceptance: a measured circuit and an
explainable filter

Deliverable package
The electronics log includes schematics and revisions, selected components and documentation,
resistance/power/protection calculations, probe positions, assembly photographs and
measurement tables. The switching circuit shows current paths, flyback diode, turn-off and
measurement limitations. Connections include pinout, labels and confirmed unpowered continuity
checks.
The signal-processing report includes a reference generator, real M03 recordings, fs metadata and
timestamps, causal filters, settings, time plots and spectra, noise/delay metrics, gap handling and
tests. Do not present a smoothed real-IMU signal as unknown ground truth; calculate reference
RMSE on synthetic data, and assess repeatability and observable properties on real data.

Questions to explain
Why are voltmeters and ammeters connected differently? How does loading change divider output?
Why does an LED need current limiting? How does VGS(th) differ from a low-RDS(on) operating
condition? Where does coil current flow immediately after turn-off? Why is the common return part
of the signal path? How are fuse parameters selected, and why do they depend on wiring?
How does sampling rate differ from PWM frequency? Why cannot digital filtering restore
information lost through aliasing? What changes when the window grows? How does step delay
differ from rise time? Why is filtfilt not a streaming filter? How does body acceleration distort a
simple accelerometer-angle estimate? What are PSD units?

Completion criteria
Passing work includes a correctly assembled and protected low-power circuit after checking,
correct multimeter measurements, recognised aliasing, comparison of at least two causal filters
and a quantified delay tradeoff. Label physical experiments and simulations separately. Fill blank
templates with your own results; the document does not claim accuracy in advance.
Pass M06 the pinout, signal ranges, expected rates, error handling and low-voltage assembly log.
M07 uses current calculations and understanding of inductive loads, but its power bench requires
its own components, protection and tests after G1. State one sensor-path limitation each for the leg
and hand; for example, permissible delay remains undefined until the future loop dynamics are
known.

Assigned reading: a short route

Read only the specified passages before the corresponding experiment. References are mainly in
English; keep explanations, glossary and report in English. Reading and preparation fit within the
existing 75 hours; whole books are not required.

Core reading
1. Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits. DC volume: chapters 1-3, 6, 16. Selected
topics: voltage/current, Ohm's law, measurement, dividers, Kirchhoff's laws and RC transients.
Before tasks 1-4, draw instrument connections and calculate the circuit. For task 5, read
Semiconductors volume, chapter 3, Inductor Commutating Circuits.
2. Steven W. Smith, The Scientist and Engineer’s Guide to Digital Signal Processing.
Chapter 3: sampling; chapter 15: moving average. For tasks 7 and 9, compare aliasing, noise and
delay. In chapter 15, read Noise Reduction vs. Step Response and Frequency Response; a full DSP
course is unnecessary.
3. Anant Agarwal, MIT 6.002: Circuits and Electronics, notes. Lectures 2, 4, 12: Basic circuit
analysis method; The digital abstraction; Capacitors and first-order systems. Consult after a simple
experiment to understand logic-level tolerances and finite RC settling time.

Documentation for individual experiments
Switching and protection. TI ULN2003A: pinout, typical circuit, power supply or Nexperia
AN11158: MOSFET parameters. Read the chosen option for task 5: limits, losses and flyback diode.
Every circuit component contributes to permissible operation.
Filtering. Analog Devices: Anti-Alias Filters; SciPy freqz and welch. For tasks 7 and 11, specify fs,
window, nperseg and scaling; assess causality and units first.
Bus pull-up reference. TI SLVA689, I2C pull-up calculation. Understand resistance, capacitance
and edge-rate relationships; build a real I2C bus in M06.
Understanding check. Before assembly, explain current paths when the switch turns on and off;
before filtering, identify information already lost during sampling and the cost of noise reduction.

СтраницаPage 63 · Glossary: terms and definitions
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M04  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Glossary: terms and definitions

Voltage. Electric potential difference between two points; measured in volts and always requires a
reference point.
Current. Rate of electric-charge transfer through a cross-section; measured in amperes, with sign
determined by the chosen direction.
Resistance. Voltage-to-current ratio of an ohmic element under specified conditions; measured in
ohms and limits circuit current.
Power. Rate of energy transfer; for an electrical circuit, P=U·I with consistent direction
conventions, measured in watts.
Ground. Chosen circuit reference node and current-return path; its conductors have nonzero
resistance and inductance.
Voltage divider. Series circuit producing a fraction of input voltage; connected loads change the
division ratio and must be included.
Time constant. For a simple RC circuit, τ=R·C in seconds; during τ, step response covers
approximately 63% of its full change.
Inductance. Parameter relating current change to voltage; a coil opposes rapid current changes
and stores magnetic energy.
Flyback diode. Diode providing a coil-current path after the switch opens; supply configuration
determines its polarity and ratings.
MOSFET. An insulated-gate field-effect transistor; gate-source voltage controls channel
conductance, and switching requires changing gate charge.
Pull-up. Resistor between signal line and supply that establishes a high level when the input or
open drain is high impedance. At a low level, it limits current.
Fuse. Component that breaks a circuit under a specified current-time load; protects the selected
wiring path within its rated characteristics.
Sampling. Representing a continuous signal by samples in time; fs=1/Δt on a uniform time grid.
Aliasing. Frequency ambiguity after sampling in which different continuous signals produce
identical samples, causing information loss.
Quantisation. Replacing a continuous value with one of a finite set of levels; introduces amplitude
error distinct from temporal sampling.
Causal filter. Filter using only present and past inputs; future samples are unavailable during
streaming.
FIR and IIR. FIR has a finite impulse response; IIR usually uses feedback and may respond for an
unlimited duration.
Power spectral density (PSD). Distribution of signal power over frequency; integrating a band
gives its mean-square contribution under consistent normalisation.
Complementary filter. Combination of estimates with complementary frequency responses, such
as slow accelerometer tilt and rapid gyroscope angle changes.

Equipment, installation and checks

Complete preparation within the first study blocks in place of another general overview. The
budget remains 75 hours; delivery waiting time is excluded. Statuses below specify actions for you
to take, not purchases or installations already completed.

Use existing equipment
Use the MacBook Pro M4 and Python/SciPy from M02-M03, plus sensor recordings or synthetic data
for filtering. Reuse listed tools if already available and working.

Buy before the first circuit experiment
1 each: a multimeter measuring DC voltage and resistance, with continuity, diode test and a fused
current input; a set of working probes. Supplement this measurement guide with your model's
manual. Connect across a circuit for voltage and in series for current.
1 CC/CV bench supply with adjustable voltage, current limit and independent output switching. A
guideline for the shared M04-M07 bench is approximately 0-30 V and up to 5-10 A at the required
voltage. These are supply capabilities; calculate each experiment's low-voltage, low-power
operating point. Do not route full supply power through a breadboard.
1 low-power circuit kit: breadboard and jumpers; several each of resistors from 330 ohm to 100
kohm, LEDs and buttons; 100 nF and 10-100 µF capacitors; 1 low-power, low-voltage relay with
unloaded contacts, 1 compatible switch and flyback diode. Select final values, powers and voltages
from tasks 1-5 and documentation before ordering.
1 connection kit: adjustable soldering iron or station with stand, solder, flux and fume extraction;
side cutters, wire stripper, tool for the chosen crimp contacts, wires, connectors, heat-shrink,
holder and suitable fuses. Consumable quantities should cover one bench and task 6 samples.

Install and check now
macOS ARM: LTspice for macOS for RC and switching circuits; verify your macOS version and
Apple Silicon support in the selected release. SciPy.signal is already available. Test: RC step
response reaches about 63% at t=RC, freqz displays a Hz axis, and welch reproduces after restart.
Before power-up: continuity and polarity checks, correct multimeter sockets, calculated supply
limits and protection ratings; then test a low-power resistive load according to the supply manual.
M04 needs neither a motor nor MCU firmware. An oscilloscope remains optional: simulate fast
transients and explicitly state that no physical measurement was made.

СтраницаPage 65 · Motion fundamentals: what a sampled sensor
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M04  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Motion fundamentals: what a sampled sensor
sees

Compulsory, within 75 hours. Use 1 h from 63-64 and 2 h of practice 66-75, 'sinusoidal runs and
freqz'. Use existing generators and the filter from tasks 7, 9 and 11; this is their combined physical
interpretation. Before starting, calculate Δt=1/100=0.01 s and convert 20 ms to seconds.

Motion continues between samples
Let a joint in a fixed plane have angle q(t)=0.20 sin(2π·2t) rad relative to the horizontal axis. Its
velocity q̇=0.80π cos(4πt) rad/s reaches 2.513 rad/s. For link L=0.12 m, maximum endpoint speed
L|q̇|≈0.302 m/s. The sensor measures q, not foot velocity directly; calculation supplies geometry
and differentiation.
The example recording also contains sinusoidal interference e(t)=0.01 sin(2π·70t) rad. At fs=100
Hz, its samples match −0.01 sin(2π·30k/100): 70 Hz appears as 30 Hz with a different phase. This
sequence cannot establish the original continuous oscillation. A later filter may attenuate 30 Hz but
cannot restore lost information; antialiasing is needed before sampling or reducing its rate.

Why a smoother angle may arrive too late
Consider a causal five-sample average: q_f[k]=(q_m[k]+…+q_m[k−4])/5, where q_m is measured
angle. Output is issued at kΔt although the window centre is two samples earlier. In steady state at
2 Hz, delay is (5−1)Δt/2=0.020 s and phase shift is −2π·2·0.020=−0.2513 rad, or −14.4°.
The amplitude of the desired sinusoid is multiplied by sin(5πf/fs)/(5 sin(πf/fs))≈0.98428 at f=2 Hz.
Thus the smoothed angle nearly preserves amplitude but describes earlier motion. Treating it as
current gives endpoint position error of scale |v|·0.020≈6 mm during rapid motion. This is a local
delay-effect estimate, not an accuracy tolerance for a finished leg.

Checks for the future control loop
1. Compare sampled 70 Hz interference with a negative 30 Hz sinusoid; repeat at fs=250 Hz. Save
overlaid sequences and label true frequency only where known from the generator. A measured
spectral peak does not establish a mechanical cause.
2. On clean 2 Hz motion, measure the five-sample filter's amplitude and phase after the transient
and compare with freqz. For a unit step with zero prehistory, output first exceeds 0.5 at 20 ms after
the first changed input sample. Add these values to the task 11 table; account for transport delay
separately.
Do not shift streaming data backwards in time to claim less delay: an earlier timestamp does not
speed publication. Feedback suitability depends on the future M10 loop dynamics, not plot
smoothness. All motion here is synthetic; no motor is needed.
Read before calculating: Steven W. Smith, DSP Guide: chapter 3, The Sampling Theorem;
chapter 15, Noise Reduction vs. Step Response.

СтраницаPage 66 · A parametric leg: from sketch to measured
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M05  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

A parametric leg: from sketch to measured
part

M5 • 31 Jan 2027 - 24 Feb 2027 • 75 hours

M05 outcome
During this month, create a parametric CAD assembly of a leg with three degrees of
freedom, drawings, a bill of materials and test specimens. This is the first physical part of
the future walking robot: links, brackets, shafts, fasteners and the cable route. At this stage the leg
may be passive, with joints moved by hand; the actuator test rig and force control belong to later
modules.
The tasks require you to justify the design: how link length determines part dimensions, which
components transfer the load to the body, how to provide access to a screw, how tolerances affect
backlash, and why print orientation changes a part's properties. The same approach will later apply
to robotic fingers, but designing the complete hand is outside M05.

Learning object and model boundaries
Use three consecutive revolute joints: the first turns the leg in the horizontal plane, and the second
and third bend it. In the zero configuration, align the first joint axis with z and the next two axes
with y; label the local coordinate frames. Initial link lengths, for example 35/80/100 mm, are only
starting geometry. You may change them after checking the layout; these are not the final
dimensions of the future robot.
Until a motor is selected, create a separate parametric component representing its envelope.
Explicitly mark mounting dimensions that still need confirmation. If the actual actuator has already
been selected, use dimensions from its drawing. A provisional motor model does not establish
mounting compatibility. A physical passive assembly can use separate shafts and bushings without
applying power.

Tools and organisation
Choose one CAD environment: FreeCAD or Fusion if you already know it. Do not learn both
simultaneously. Prepare callipers or a ruler, your existing FDM printer, available material, suitable
fasteners and a simple fixture for small static loads. Use a validated profile for your printer; the
printer model does not automatically determine hole accuracy.
Create cad/native, cad/export, drawings, bom, calculations, coupons and tests. For every print,
record the CAD revision, material, orientation, profile, mass and date. M02 covered forces, torques
and units; M03 covered ways to describe measurement variability; M04 covered cable-routing
requirements. Full kinematics, dynamic walking and actuator operation are not required here.
