ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M07  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Measure an actuator on one joint first

M7 • 04 Apr 2027 - 30 Apr 2027 • 75 hours

Main deliverable
Over the month, produce a single-actuator test rig and a model relating torque, speed, current and
temperature. The result answers a specific question: can the selected actuator perform the work of
a leg or finger joint over the required motion and load range? A catalogue torque at stall does not
mean the actuator can hold the robot's body continuously. Define requirements, measure an
available sample, separate known parameters from estimates and validate the model on new data.
Decide whether to buy a complete actuator set only after testing one sample.

What must already be ready
From M6, bring the controller, synchronised telemetry, error counters, timestamps, command
limits, physical stop and verified prevention of automatic restart. From M5, bring link geometry,
mountings and approximate mass. Identify where angle is measured: at the rotor, after the
gearbox or by a separate output-link sensor. This determines whether gearbox backlash is
observable. Entry check: convert degrees to radians, revolutions per second to rad/s and grams to
kilograms, and explain force versus torque. Calculate the static torque of a known mass about an
axis.
Select equipment around the available actuator and its documentation. You need a securely
mounted sample, compatible driver or the smart servo's built-in control interface,
angle/current/temperature measurement, a current-limited supply and a guarded fixture. If these
are unavailable, first complete requirements and a digital model; clearly separate calculated
characteristics from measurements. A bracket may be made on the existing 3D printer after
checking geometry, material and load. A printed part does not automatically have the strength of
an industrial mounting.

Scope of the month
Study the differences between DC, BLDC and smart servo architectures, but experiment with one
type. You do not need to develop your own FOC driver, rewind a motor or buy 12/18 actuators. A
smart servo's internal loops may be closed to the user; measure its external behaviour and
explicitly identify inaccessible internal signals. Low speed, holding and backlash matter for a hand;
loaded torque, repeatability and heating matter for a leg. The method is shared, while
requirements differ.
The final report must show the operating region supported by measurements and the modes for
which data remains insufficient. This plan specifies no universal current, temperature, voltage or
mass limits: derive them from the motor, driver, gearbox, supply and mounting documentation.

СтраницаPage 97 · How to allocate 75 hours
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M07  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

How to allocate 75 hours

Balance study and experiments
Hours 1-20: actuator comparison, requirements and preliminary model; 10 hours theory and 10
hours practice. Hours 21-40: measurement fixture, encoder, current, temperature and rig checks;
10+10. Hours 41-60: control loops, limits and repeatable response; 10+10. Hours 61-75:
identification, validation on new data and model boundaries; 5+10. Total: 35 hours of reading,
calculation and analysis, and 40 hours of practice. Count evaluation of raw measurements as
practice, and equation derivation and experiment selection as analysis.
Divide each ten-hour theory block into five 2-hour sessions. In each session, study one mechanism,
calculate its effect for your joint, then prepare an experiment. Schedule ten-hour practical blocks
on Sundays, divided into stages with breaks; 10 hours means active work. The final 5 theory hours
are split 2+2+1. Dates on the first page are the periods in the original overall plan. Shared
boundary dates, rest, holidays and integration reviews are unchanged; place steps in available
study hours without double counting.

A separate record for each experiment
State motor model and revision, gearbox, firmware, controller gains, supply voltage, ambient
temperature, mounting, current sensor and temperature measurement location. Record command
and measured angle, speed, current, voltage and temperature on one time axis, or document
synchronisation. The commands file contains what was actually sent after limiting, rather than only
the original desired profile. Save stop causes and missing-data intervals so fault periods remain
visible in plots.

Repository organisation
Create requirements/ for joint calculations, fixture/ for CAD and assembly, acquisition/ for collection
code, experiments/ for configurations, data/raw/ for raw runs, models/ for parameters and reports/
for plots and limitations. Split data into training (train) and validation sets by whole runs before
fitting. Randomly splitting one run into nearly identical neighbouring training and validation points
is not independent validation. Begin with a simple model and retain it as the baseline before adding
nonlinearities.
If time is short, reduce the number of brands compared, omit an additional actuator type and
simplify the interface. Requirements, measurement path, motion limits, thermal observation and
validation on an independent run remain compulsory. Keep missing hardware measurements as
open items rather than replacing them with arbitrary numbers.































M7 • 04 Apr 2027 - 30 Apr 2027 • 75 hours                                                                          2 / 15
СтраницаPage 98 · Joint requirements and architecture selection
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M07  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Joint requirements and architecture selection

What to study
Compare brushed DC, BLDC with a separate driver, and smart servos with integrated control.
Consider motor, gearbox, sensor and interface separately: a convenient bus does not guarantee
suitable torque, and a powerful motor does not solve feedback problems. Study the torque-speed
curve, efficiency, rotor inertia, permissible gearbox load, encoder resolution, backlash and
transmission compliance. Distinguish continuous and short-duration operation, and electrical,
thermal and mechanical limits.

Task 1. Load profiles for a leg and finger
Start with the M5 mass and geometry; express unknowns as ranges. For a link with a horizontal
lever arm, use τ=mgr, with m in kg, g in m/s², r the perpendicular lever arm in metres and τ in
N·m. 1. Draw a free body with force direction. 2. Calculate three link positions and two payload
cases. 3. For the leg, add a support scenario with load distribution explicitly assumed; do not divide
robot mass by leg count without describing the support phase. 4. For the finger, use desired
fingertip force and lever arm. Save the requirements table and sensitivity to mass and length.
Check that doubling the lever arm at constant force doubles static torque. Edge case: zero force
lever arm.

Task 2. Compare actuators under relevant operating conditions
Select three architectures or available candidates with primary documentation. Build a comparison
table: torque in the required mode, loaded speed, mass, reduction, sensor, backlash, current
control, diagnostics, supply, interface and unknown characteristics. 1. Reject any option that fails a
hard requirement. 2. Separately assess uncertainty from missing data. 3. Choose one sample for
the rig and describe an experiment that could disprove that choice. Prepare a decision justifying
each criterion; an arbitrary weighted score is no substitute. Check that every important conclusion
has a source, calculation or future test, and that stall torque has not been used as continuous
torque.

Reduction and inertia
Fix the definition N=motor speed/output-shaft speed. In an ideal transmission, output speed is
divided by N, torque is multiplied by N, and load inertia reflected to the motor is divided by N².
Actual efficiency and backlash impose additional limitations. For the chosen geometry, calculate
how increasing the ratio changes speed and reflected inertia. These calculations are hypotheses for
measurement; gear tooth counts alone cannot establish actual holding accuracy.






























M7 • 04 Apr 2027 - 30 Apr 2027 • 75 hours                                                                          3 / 15
СтраницаPage 99 · Measurement rig and calibration
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M07  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Measurement rig and calibration

Task 3. Fixture for one actuator
The aim is repeatable motion without movement of the motor housing. Inputs: mounting drawing,
load direction and the sample's permissible operating characteristics. 1. Draw the load path from
shaft through mounting to base. 2. Position travel stops, motion-area guarding, access to the stop
control and cable strain relief. 3. Check alignment and free travel without powered motion. 4.
Perform the first powered run at the minimum justified command, increasing it in predefined steps.
Deliver CAD, photographs, a fastener list and the verification record. Edge case: the cable must not
become taut and alter measured torque at the travel limits.
Create one table of permissible values for the supply, driver, wires, connectors and fuse. The
weakest component determines the limit, considering operating mode, cooling and documentation.
A fuse and a software current limit serve different purposes. Separately establish behaviour during
braking and energy return to the supply: a supply capable of delivering energy may be unable to
absorb it during braking. Do not command sharp acceleration or braking until this behaviour is
understood.

Task 4. Encoder angle and speed
Check counts per revolution, quadrature decoding mode, gear ratio and sign. 1. Apply a known
manual displacement with the actuator disabled, if its construction permits back-driving. 2.
Compare counts with output-link angle. 3. Estimate velocity from angle differences over a known
interval and, alternatively, from time between edges if pulses are available. 4. Compare noise and
delay at low and higher speeds. Deliver the conversion factor and plots of both estimates. Check
that a full revolution or available reference angle produces the expected count. Edge cases:
overflow, reversal, zero speed and a missed edge.

Task 5. Current and temperature
Establish what the sensor measures: supply current, winding current or current in the control
coordinate frame. These quantities are not automatically interchangeable as I in τ=K_t I. Measure
zero-current offset, compare known points with a reference instrument and retain uncertainty.
Record temperature with the sensor location and settling time: housing and windings heat
differently. Deliver calibration coefficients and a description of limitations. Fault: a missing or
saturated instrument must not permit continuation of an experiment that depends on its readings.



































M7 • 04 Apr 2027 - 30 Apr 2027 • 75 hours                                                                          4 / 15
СтраницаPage 100 · Position control and bounded commands
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M07  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Position control and bounded commands

Control-loop architecture
Determine who closes the current, velocity and position loops: your code, the driver or smart-servo
firmware. Use SimpleFOC and ODrive resources to draw the cascade and label the input and output
units of each block. An external controller must not duplicate an unknown internal loop without
understanding its mode. PID relates error to control action; feedforward predicts the required
action. Command limiting introduces nonlinearity: the integrator can continue accumulating error
when the actuator can no longer meet the request.

Task 6. Repeatable position response
Initial conditions: a checked rig, known limits and a small motion profile away from stops. 1. Begin
with an available simple mode and a reproducible initial state. 2. Apply a smoothly changing
command with specified limits; save position, speed and actual control action. 3. Change one gain
or profile parameter while keeping load constant. 4. Repeat the best configuration several times.
Deliver reference/measurement plots, steady-state error, overshoot and settling time. Define the
settling band beforehand in angle units; measure the time until the response stays within it. Edge
case: reversal and return to zero.

Task 7. Saturation and anti-windup
Begin in simulation of the simple joint. 1. Limit available control action. 2. Apply a command that
cannot be achieved quickly. 3. Compare an ordinary integrator with the chosen anti-windup
method: integrator limiting or back-calculation. 4. Restore an achievable reference and measure
recovery time. Save two plots of control action and integrator state under identical conditions.
Check that you can explain why controller gains cannot remove a physical limit. Confirm on
hardware only with a smooth motion profile inside the operating region; deliberately jamming the
shaft to demonstrate saturation is unnecessary.

Task 8. Motion profile and stopping
Set position, speed and acceleration limits from rig requirements and documentation. Generate a
bounded trajectory between two angles and compare it with an abrupt step in simulation. Use only
the permissible profile on the rig. Measure maximum speed, current, error and behaviour near the
software limit. Reject or limit an out-of-range command under an explicit rule and log it; a
mechanical stop is not a routine way to end every motion. Communication loss and restart use the
tested M6 state machine, while the mechanism's subsequent state depends on its load and
construction.






























M7 • 04 Apr 2027 - 30 Apr 2027 • 75 hours                                                                         5 / 15
СтраницаPage 101 · Identification: friction, delay and backlash
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M07  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Identification: friction, delay and backlash

A testable model
Start at the output joint: J·q̈+b·q̇+τ_c·sign(q̇)+τ_g(q)=τ_a. Here J is inertia about the axis in kg·m²,
b is viscous resistance in N·m·s/rad, τ_c approximates dry friction, τ_g is gravitational torque and
τ_a is actuator torque. Near zero speed, the sign model is inadequate: rest, breakaway and
backlash require separate observations. If torque is unavailable, use the stock actuator command
as input and identify the closed-loop command-to-angle system, explicitly stating that the model
includes the actuator and its internal controller.

Task 9. Backlash and dead zone
The aim is to understand why a finger ignores a small command and why a leg reverses with a
delay. 1. Reproduce slow motion in both directions over one range. 2. Record input command and
angles before and after the transmission if both sensors are available. 3. Plot output against input
in both directions and identify the region where input changes produce no measurable output. 4.
Repeat with another permissible load. Save dead-zone and backlash estimates with sensor
resolution. If only the motor encoder is available, output-link mechanical backlash cannot be
claimed as directly measured; a separate observation method is required.

Task 10. Steps and frequency excitation
Prepare small bounded steps and a smooth chirp within the region authorised beforehand; chirp
means excitation frequency changes over time. First calculate maximum profile speed and
acceleration to ensure they remain within limits. 1. Record raw responses. 2. Identify delay and
characteristic response time. 3. Fit a minimal model to the first group of runs. 4. Validate it with
another profile and initial position. Save parameters, applicability limits, raw data and residuals. Do
not increase frequency into dangerous oscillation merely to extend the measured bandwidth.

Why not fit everything at once?
Friction, delay, an inaccurate torque constant and a velocity filter can explain similar errors. Check
units and measurement delay first, then a simple linear model; add one mechanism only when its
effect has independent evidence. Save parameters with units, estimation method and a confidence
range or observed spread. Lower error on the training record is not success if a new record is
predicted worse. Show one case the model reproduces and one where it predictably loses
accuracy.

СтраницаPage 102 · Torque, speed, heating and the operating
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M07  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Torque, speed, heating and the operating
region

Task 11. A verifiable torque characteristic
If an independent force sensor and known lever arm are available, estimate torque as τ=F·r_perp.
Begin with a secured rig, small justified loads and known geometric accuracy. 1. Check sensor zero.
2. Measure several safe operating conditions with different loads and speeds. 3. Repeat in both
directions. 4. Compare torque with measured current, accounting for current type and
transmission. Deliver characteristic points with variability and operating limits. If torque is not
independently measured, give a calculated estimate and a method for later verification; do not call
a smart servo's internal “load” indicator an accurate torque sensor without manufacturer
confirmation.

Task 12. Thermal experiment with controlled duration
Choose a repeated profile resembling leg work or finger holding, within documented limits. 1. Begin
from a known thermal state. 2. Record ambient and available-sensor temperatures, current,
operating mode and fraction of time under load. 3. Stop at the preset duration or an earlier
documentation-based stop condition. 4. Record cooling after the experiment. Save temperature
rise above ambient and load duty cycle. A short record showing continued heating does not
establish an acceptable steady-state thermal regime.
The simplest thermal model relates temperature rate of change to dissipated power and heat
removal. In the first version, estimating characteristic heating and cooling times and explaining
applicability limits is sufficient. The I²R loss approximation requires the appropriate current and
resistance; supply current and unknown internal commutation may not provide this information. Do
not infer unmeasured winding temperature from an external sensor without a justified
thermal-coupling model.

A combined operating-range map
Plot measured points in the speed-torque plane, marking current, temperature, duration and
limiting factor. Display catalogue limits separately from your measurements. For a leg, state the
supported profile and tested duration; for a finger, separately assess holding and repeated small
motions. Check repeatability after cooling. An actuator with a different gearbox, voltage or cooling
arrangement is a different configuration requiring verification. The final map informs robot design;
it does not guarantee every future operating mode.

СтраницаPage 103 · Fault tests and numerical criteria
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M07  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Fault tests and numerical criteria

Measurement path
F1: encoder sign reversed. Detect the error in a software test and an initial small motion before
continuing closed-loop control; record expected and actual direction. F2: incorrect counts per
revolution. Comparison with an independent angle must reveal the scale error. F3: current or
temperature data disappears. Mark the run invalid and stop it if the relevant parameter is a safety
condition for the experiment. Do not reuse the last available value as fresh protective information.
F4: timestamps jump or frames are lost. Do not treat angle differentiation across a corrupted
interval as reliable velocity.

Control and mechanics
F5: target angle beyond the software limit. Check the chosen command rejection or limiting rule;
log requested and applied commands. F6: control action saturates in simulation. After an
achievable reference returns, anti-windup restores normal operation according to a defined metric;
retain the saturation interval in the report. F7: communication loss during permissible motion. Test
the M6 stopping procedure and prevention of automatic restart. F8: small reversal. Compare the
expected dead zone with instrument resolution; the program must not infer absence of mechanical
motion from a single unchanged count.

Validate the model on another record
F9: a model fitted to one profile receives another profile, load or amplitude within its declared
region. Compare angle RMSE, maximum absolute error and transition-time error.
RMSE=sqrt(mean((q_model-q_measured)²)); its unit matches the angle unit. F10: load or
temperature goes beyond the identification region in simulation or existing data. The report must
explicitly label extrapolation rather than conceal it in an overall mean error. F11: power restoration.
Motion must not resume solely from a saved reference.

Set thresholds before the experiment
Choose angle tolerance from the joint's future function and measurement capability; do not specify
“0.1 degree” without reference to the encoder and backlash. Define a settling band and required
time within it before measuring settling time. Compare model error with a simple baseline, such as
a first-order system with constant delay; a more complex model must improve independent
validation. For each experiment, retain maximum measured current and temperature with
duration, sample rate and measurement location. Preserve a failed run with its stop cause and do
not assess it as a fully completed run.

First 40 hours: requirements and rig

Hours 1-10: determine what must be measured
1-2: break leg and finger requirements into position, speed, torque and operating duration. 3-4:
study DC, BLDC and smart servo architectures; draw a motor-gearbox-sensor-controller diagram.
5-6: calculate task 1 static torques and their geometric dependence. 7-8: study the torque-speed
characteristic, reflected inertia and efficiency; plot simple expected trends. 9-10: read
documentation for available candidates and list unknown parameters. Finish by selecting the
question the rig experiment must answer.

Hours 11-20: document requirements and prepare the experiment
11-12: complete task 1 load scenarios and unit table. 13-14: build the task 2 comparison table with
sources and characteristic conditions. 15-16: create a simple joint simulation with bounded control
action; save parameters and hypotheses. 17-18: design the task 3 fixture geometry and check load
transfer, stop access and cables. 19-20: prepare test commands, acquisition configuration and the
first experiment procedure. If the sample is not yet known, remain at interface level and explicitly
mark parameters TBD; do not copy another motor's limits.

Hours 21-30: measurement and protection
21-22: study the supply, driver, wiring, fuse and braking behaviour from the exact components'
documentation. 23-24: study the encoder and velocity-estimation methods; calculate the smallest
observable angle change. 25-26: establish current measurement location and type, sensor offset
and range. 27-28: study thermal modes, temperature-sensor location and housing/winding
temperature differences. 29-30: prepare calibration procedures, initial states and stop conditions.
Finish this block with a usable measurement procedure, rather than notes alone.

Hours 31-40: first physical dataset
31-32: assemble and check the fixture without powered motion, then perform the first
smooth-motion run. 33-34: verify task 4 angle scale and sign. 35-36: compare velocity estimates
and retain stationary noise measurements. 37-38: calibrate current and temperature channels for
task 5. 39-40: repeat a short profile, check synchronisation between fields, stopping and recreation
of the plot from raw data. Saving results is included in every step. Without a real sample, complete
equivalent software tests and leave physical acceptance open until the next available session.

Hours 41-75: control and modelling

Hours 41-50: theory through your joint
41-42: draw the actual inner and outer loops; label inputs and units. 43-44: study P, I, D and
velocity measurement; explain the effect of each gain. 45-46: study action limits, integral
accumulation and anti-windup; prepare a simulation comparison. 47-48: calculate a profile with
speed and acceleration limits; distinguish a software boundary from a physical stop. 49-50: define
response metrics, repeatability, settling band and communication-fault behaviour. Do not attempt
complex tuning until feedback sign and angle scale are verified.

Hours 51-60: control practical
51-52: run the smooth task 6 profile; save the baseline response and several repeats. 53-54:
change one control parameter and compare under identical conditions. 55-56: complete task 7
simulation of saturation and recovery. 57-58: verify the task 8 bounded profile on the rig, including
a request outside the software range. 59-60: perform task 9 slow reversals; assess dead zone and
whether backlash can be measured. Freeze the working configuration at the end; identification
runs must not mix different controller gains without labelling them.

Hours 61-65: prepare identification
61-62: derive the simple joint model and choose a measurable input: torque, current with a
justified conversion constant or an external smart-servo command. 63-64: divide future runs into
fitting and validation sets; choose task 10 excitation and task 11 torque-measurement conditions;
calculate permissible profile limits. 65: finalise the task 12 thermal procedure, report format and
sample-suitability criterion. Split these 5 hours 2+2+1; all following 10 hours are practice, keeping
the total at 75.

Hours 66-75: experiments and independent validation
66-67: record bounded steps and an available frequency profile; estimate delay and initial
parameters. 68-69: obtain available torque measurements or an explicitly labelled calculated
estimate; verify directions and repeatability. 70-71: run the thermal profile for the predefined
duration and also record cooling. 72-73: fit the model and validate on another run; compare
residuals with the baseline and explain one systematic error. 74-75: assemble the operating region,
model limitations and decision on the suitability of one sample. If time is insufficient to reach
steady temperature, state that in the report; a short experiment's results cannot be transferred to

ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M07  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Presenting the result and moving to
mechanics

What the final package must contain
Requirements for the chosen joint with load scenarios; architecture comparison and sample
justification; CAD and photographs of the guarded rig; supply, stop and limit descriptions with
sources; angle, current and temperature calibration; raw synchronised recordings; controller
parameters; a torque-speed-current-heating model within available measurements; independent
validation and a fault list. For every model parameter, state units, estimation method, operating
range and confidence level. Unmeasured torque or winding temperature remains unknown even if
software can plot it.
Completion criteria from the original plan: selection rests on measurements, electrical and thermal
parameters stay within justified limits, and a set of 12/18 actuators is not selected from one
catalogue number. A negative decision is valid: the sample may be unsuitable because of heating,
backlash, speed, mass or diagnostics. This is a useful completed result if evidence supports the
reasons and requirements for the next sample are stated. Publishing the report here means
preparing a reproducible package; no external sharing or posting is required.

Self-check questions
1. Why is supply current not always the current that determines torque? 2. What changes when the
reduction ratio doubles? 3. How does backlash differ from elastic deformation? 4. Where is the
encoder, and which error can it not observe? 5. Why does a good unloaded response not resolve
leg-support requirements? 6. What does the integrator do during saturation? 7. Why can the same
PID produce a different response after heating? 8. What exactly constitutes independent model
validation? 9. How can measurement delay be distinguished from actuator delay? 10. Why does
housing temperature not guarantee a known winding temperature? Each answer needs your own
plot, calculation or explicit data limitation.

Handover to M8 and M9
Pass axis geometry, permissible angle ranges, sign, zero, resolution and measured dead zone to
M8. Kinematics must generate achievable references within these limits, but does not itself
establish sufficient torque. Pass the identified joint, masses, inertia estimates, friction, delay, input
interface and independent recordings to M9. Keep motor and link parameters separate to avoid
counting the gearbox or inertia twice. When mechanics, load or cooling changes, flag the need for
new validation because the previous operating region may change.

Assigned reading: a focused reading route

Books and notes may be in English; keep the plan, definitions and your explanations in English for
this edition. Read only the specified sections within the existing 75 hours.

Core reading and one reference route
1. Core: K. Lynch, F. Park, Modern Robotics, §8.9. Actuation, Gearing, and Friction: motor, gearbox
and reflected inertia. Read for tasks 1-2 and 9 and explain why motor and output-joint parameters
differ.
2. Core: K. J. Åström, R. Murray, Feedback Systems, 2nd edition. Chapter 11 PID Control: Basic
Control Functions and Integrator Windup. Read for tasks 6-8; draw your loops and compare
saturation with anti-windup. Other editions have different numbering.
3. Core, selectively: R. Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics: System Identification. Sections on least
squares and dynamics identification. For tasks 9-10, list measurable inputs, unknown parameters
and a separate validation recording; skip complex models.

Documentation for the practical work
ESP-IDF: Pulse Counter - Channel Actions and Glitch Filter for the encoder; SimpleFOC: Current
Sensing - motor versus supply current for task 5.
ODrive: Controller - cascade diagram and Trajectory Control for tasks 6-8. This is an architectural
example; obtain your driver's limits only from its own datasheet.

Complete the reading with an action
After each section, perform one calculation or short experiment. Save the actuator, driver and
instrument datasheet revisions. For tasks 10-12, use the familiar SciPy least_squares: check
parameter physical meaning and residuals on new data. Buying printed books is optional.

СтраницаPage 108 · Glossary: terms and definitions
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M07  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Glossary: terms and definitions

Torque. The turning effect of force: τ=r×F; torque about a specified axis is the projection of τ onto
that axis, in N·m.
Gear ratio. The ratio of input to output speed; here N=ω_motor/ω_joint, with rotation direction
specified separately.
Efficiency. The ratio of useful output power to input power under stated conditions; it depends on
speed and load.
Torque constant. Coefficient Kt relating motor electromagnetic torque to current under the
adopted model, in N·m/A.
Back EMF. Voltage generated by motor rotation that opposes the supply; proportional to speed in
a simple model.
Stall current. Current in a stationary motor at a specified voltage; this is a limiting condition, not
an allowable continuous current.
Continuous torque. Torque permissible continuously under specified cooling, speed and
temperature conditions; the manufacturer's conditions must be confirmed.
Reflected inertia. Inertia referred through a gearbox to a chosen shaft; rotor inertia at the output
scales as N².
Backlash. The relative angular travel between mating components over which a reversal is not
immediately transmitted to the load.
Static friction. Contact resistance before motion starts; it takes the required value only up to the
maximum holding limit.
Viscous friction. An approximation of motion resistance as torque proportional to angular velocity
and opposing it.
Quadrature encoder. A sensor producing two phase-shifted A/B signals from which angle
increments and rotation direction can be determined.
Counts per revolution. The number of counted signal transitions per revolution of the specified
shaft; it depends on decoding mode and gearbox.
Feedback loop. A path using measured output to change a command in order to reduce a
specified control error.
Saturation. Limiting actual control action at a physical or software boundary, even when the
calculated command is larger.
Anti-windup. A rule correcting integral state during output limiting, reducing excessive error
accumulation and recovery delay.
System identification. Determining model parameters or structure from recorded inputs and
outputs under explicit assumptions.
Residual. The difference between measured output and model prediction for the same inputs,
time and initial state.
Thermal time constant. A characteristic temperature-change time in the adopted thermal
model; it depends on heat capacity and heat transfer.
Check the relationships: P_mech=τω; for an ideal gearbox, ω_out=ω_in/N and torque increases
by a factor of N. Losses and heating require separate treatment.

СтраницаPage 110 · Motion fundamentals: what a gearbox
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M07  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Motion fundamentals: what a gearbox
provides

Required: connect joint requirements with the motor
Angle specifies the desired pose, but holding and acceleration require torque. For a leg, foot load
and link weights matter; for a finger, the object's force on a phalanx matters. Before calculating,
draw the axis and lever arm: force in N and torque in N·m differ. If the force's line of action passes
through the axis, its torque about that axis is zero.

A minimal transmission model
For one revolute joint, q is output angle and v=q̇ is velocity in rad/s. Choose shaft signs so that
N=ω_m/v>0. Then v=ω_m/N. With power transmitted from motor to load and gearbox efficiency η,
output torque is approximately τ_out=ηNτ_m. Hence τ_out·v=ητ_m·ω_m: a gearbox changes
torque and speed but does not create power.
At an illustrative operating point, let N=20, η=0.75, Kt=0.04 N·m/A, winding current i=1 A and
ω_m=100 rad/s. Neglecting losses within the motor itself, τ_m=Kt·i=0.04 N·m, v=5 rad/s and
τ_out=0.6 N·m. Mechanical power is 4 W at the motor shaft and 3 W after the gearbox. Supply
consumption requires separate measurement of the electrical path.
Separately draw a horizontal link: x right, y up, axis +z and positive torque anticlockwise. A mass
m=0.5 kg at lever arm r=0.1 m produces gravitational torque -mgr=-0.4905 N·m at g=9.81 m/s².
Rest requires compensation of +0.4905 N·m, excluding link weight. The difference
0.6-0.4905=0.1095 N·m does not by itself establish actuator suitability: operating speed, heating
and continuous holding differ.

How inertia affects rapid motion
Acceleration also requires torque I_joint·q̈, with I_joint in kg·m². Rotor inertia reflected to the output
is N²I_motor; load inertia reflected to the motor is divided by N². High reduction therefore helps
produce torque but changes dynamics and sensitivity to contact. Constant η is an approximation
for the specified motoring condition; do not transfer it to rest or reverse energy flow without
verification.

Checks within existing tasks 1 and 11
Build a calculation table and power balance. In the same exercise model, change N to 40: velocity
becomes 2.5 rad/s, torque 1.2 N·m, output power remains 3 W and reflected rotor inertia increases
fourfold. Then insert your confirmed M7 parameters and label unknowns separately. Check
gravitational torque using r×F and the existing task 11 experiment; without an independent
instrument, retain the result as a calculation.
Included in the 75 hours: 1 hour from 7-8 for transmission and inertia; 1 hour from 11-12 for the
load table; 1 hour from 68-69 for checking the existing run. This refines deliverables already
prepared. Exercise values are not specifications for the purchased motor and must not be sent as
commands.
Reference: Lynch/Park, Modern Robotics, §8.9.1 DC Motors and Gearing; §8.9.2 Apparent Inertia.
Read only the relationships between torque, speed, power and reflected inertia; FOC development
is not added here.

СтраницаPage 111 · Geometry that turns a target into joint
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M08  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Geometry that turns a target into joint
angles

M8 • 02 May 2027 - 03 Jun 2027 • 75 hours

Outcome of the month
Create a verified kinematics library for a planar two-link arm and a leg with three degrees of
freedom. It will answer four questions: where the mechanism's endpoint lies for given angles,
which angles reach a target point, how joint velocities relate to endpoint velocity, and how an
external force relates to joint torques. This directly prepares for moving a walking robot's foot and
a fingertip. Deliver code, a geometry specification, visualisations, automated checks and clear
explanations of inverse-kinematics failure.

What you should already understand
Prerequisites from earlier months are vectors, matrices, trigonometry, derivatives, Python, NumPy
and tests. Bring the CAD leg's dimensions and axes from M5 and the available joint's sign, zero
offsets and angle ranges from M7. Before starting, manually evaluate sin and cos at 0, π/2 and π;
multiply a rotation matrix by a basis vector; convert millimetres to metres. Even if a numerical
library performs everything, explain the result's direction on a drawing. The main errors this month
usually arise from inconsistent conventions rather than difficult equations.
The first reference is a planar 2R mechanism: two revolute joints, lengths l1 and l2, and motion in
the x-y plane. The second is an exercise yaw-pitch-pitch leg: base rotation about z and two bends
in a radial vertical plane. If the M5 CAD model uses a different first joint axis, such as abduction,
write a separate transform chain from CAD; do not insert its dimensions into another mechanism's
formula. Reference models verify the mathematics, while adaptation to the actual leg must retain
its real axes and offsets.

What M8 does not require
Kinematics describes geometry, but does not establish sufficient torque, body stability or collision
freedom for every part. First calculate and visualise commands; permit transmission to a real
actuator only through M6-M7 limits and after a separate rig check. A complete gait planner, force
control and dynamic balance belong to later modules. For a hand, 2R can model two phalanges, but
tendon transmission and object contact require additional models.
At the end, check forward/inverse kinematics (FK/IK) consistency, verify the Jacobian numerically
and ensure predictable failure for unreachable targets. Declare numerical-test tolerances
separately from actual mechanical accuracy: a small computational residual does not remove
backlash, encoder-zero error or incorrect dimensions.

ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M08  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Project structure and 75 hours

Allocation across four blocks
Block A, 1-20: coordinate frames, rotations and transforms, 10 hours theory and 10 practice. Block
B, 21-40: link models and forward kinematics for 2R and 3-DOF, 10+10. Block C, 41-60: analytical
and numerical inverse kinematics, 10+10. Block D, 61-75: Jacobians, force, singularities and
acceptance checks, 5+10. Total: 35 hours of study and analysis, 40 hours of implementation and
experiments. Theory includes your own derivations on paper; practice includes code, plots, tests
and investigation of specific errors.
Divide ten-hour theory blocks into 2-hour sessions: one mechanism, one hand-worked example and
one software check. Schedule ten-hour practical blocks on Sundays and divide them into small
stages; breaks add to calendar time. Split the last 5 theory hours 2+2+1. Calendar boundaries
from the overall plan may overlap adjacent modules; retain rest days, holidays and integration
reviews. Allocate the hours below to available sessions without counting them again in the
neighbouring month.

Library organisation
Create geometry/ for transforms, models/ for 2R and the leg, solvers/ for IK, validation/ for
reference poses, visualizations/ for drawings and reports/ for results. Begin with a clear
Python/NumPy implementation. Add a C++ core only for a small, already verified interface if time
allows; a Rust port is optional. For every array, state shape, units and coordinate frame. Do not
give two different types of point the same name p without specifying their origin and the basis in
which they are expressed.

Conventions document
In conventions.md, record right-handed frames, body and joint axis directions, positive angle,
length and angle units, quaternion ordering, the meaning of T_AB, multiplication order and chosen
IK branch. Recommended convention: T_AB transforms coordinates from B to A, so p_A=T_AB·p_B
for a homogeneous point. Check every CAD export and library adapter against this document. Do
not fix an inverted leg by inserting an arbitrary minus sign before finding the cause.
For every experiment, save mechanism parameters, inputs, expected result and
random-configuration generator seed. Use error statuses UNREACHABLE, LIMIT_VIOLATION,
SINGULAR, NO_CONVERGENCE and INVALID_INPUT. Never return the final numerical approximation
as a successful command without verification: residual and status are part of the API result.

СтраницаPage 113 · Coordinate frames and composition of
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M08  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Coordinate frames and composition of
motion

What to study about transforms
Rotation R specifies basis orientation, and translation p locates its origin. A homogeneous matrix T
combines them: the upper block contains R and p, and the bottom row is [0,0,0,1]. For a pure
rotation, RᵀR=I and det(R)=+1. A matrix with det=-1 is a reflection, not an admissible rigid-body
rotation. Under the chosen convention, T_AC=T_AB·T_BC. Transform order matters: rotating a local
vector and then translating the result is generally different from reversing these operations.
Modern Robotics §3.3.1 establishes notation; follow frame indices rather than the words “left” and
“right”.

Task 1. Foot coordinates in different bases
Inputs: a drawing of body, hip and foot with simple known offsets. 1. Define T_body_hip and foot
coordinates in hip. 2. Calculate body-frame coordinates by hand. 3. Verify with the matrix in code.
4. Apply the inverse transform and recover the original point. Deliver an axis drawing and tests for
several poses, including a π/2 rotation. Check that a rigid transform preserves distance between
two points. Edge case: incorrect multiplication order must fail a test with nonzero translation and
rotation, even if the case without rotation appears correct.

Task 2. Translation of a point and a direction
The aim is to avoid adding hip position to a force or velocity vector. Take a contact point and force
direction in one frame. 1. Transform the point including translation. 2. Transform the free vector
using rotation only. 3. Compare results when base position changes without a change in
orientation. 4. Add separate transform_point and rotate_vector functions, or types that prevent
confusion. Save the test and illustration. Check that shifting the coordinate origin changes point
coordinates but not a free vector's components when the basis is unchanged.

Active and passive interpretations
A matrix may rotate a physical object or describe that same object in another coordinate frame;
either use needs consistent frame indices and inverse-matrix definitions. Draw two diagrams: body
rotation relative to the world, and a stationary world point expressed in the rotated body's frame.
Label what physically moves. For a leg, this explains why holding a foot fixed in the world while
tilting the body changes the local target point. Whole-robot IK is not yet needed; demonstrating the
correct transformation of one point is sufficient.

СтраницаPage 114 · Rotations, quaternions and the mechanism
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M08  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Rotations, quaternions and the mechanism
tree

Essential SO(2) and SO(3)
SO(2) describes planar rotations and SO(3) spatial rotations. Learn basic rotation matrices and
composition, then axis-angle orientation and a normalised quaternion. Euler angles are readable
but depend on axis order and have degenerate configurations. Quaternions q and -q describe the
same orientation; comparing components as ordinary points is insufficient. Record the chosen
order, for example [x,y,z,w] in your adapter, and check every external library's requirements,
including SciPy Rotation.

Task 3. Verify orientation representations
Use identity orientation, a π/2 rotation about each axis and a compound rotation. 1. Write expected
axis directions by hand. 2. Convert matrix to quaternion and back. 3. Check orthogonality,
determinant and angular error. 4. Supply q and -q and confirm the physical result is identical.
Deliver reference orientations and an adapter test. Edge cases: a zero quaternion, NaN and a
strongly non-unit input. The API must reject or normalise it according to an explicit policy, without
concealing invalidity.

Task 4. Coordinate-frame tree of the CAD leg
For each M5 part, specify parent, joint origin, axis, joint type, zero position and fixed offset. 1. Draw
the tree from body to foot. 2. Separate fixed mounting transforms from rotations q. 3. Assemble
the chain and visualise every local axis. 4. Check the zero pose and move each joint individually.
Save geometry in machine-readable form and images of at least four poses. Check that one joint
moves only its descendants; the body and parent links stay fixed. Error: an axis exported in world
coordinates must not be treated as local without transformation.

Two ways to describe one chain
Understand what a Denavit-Hartenberg table specifies and why standard and modified versions use
different conventions. An explicit transform chain matching CAD is convenient for the first
implementation. Then study the product of exponentials: fixed screw axes and the home
configuration define FK through a product of exponentials. Derive one planar revolute example and
compare with explicit matrices. Do not rewrite the entire project in three notations; the goal is to
read other models and recognise differences in conventions.
































M8 • 02 May 2027 - 03 Jun 2027 • 75 hours                                                                         4 / 15
СтраницаPage 115 · Forward kinematics of the arm and leg
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M08  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Forward kinematics of the arm and leg

Task 5. Planar 2R arm
For links l1,l2 and relative angles q1,q2 in the x-y plane, derive x=l1·cos(q1)+l2·cos(q1+q2),
y=l1·sin(q1)+l2·sin(q1+q2). The second link's world angle is q1+q2, not q2. 1. Derive the formula
from a drawing. 2. Implement analytical FK and an independent matrix chain. 3. Compare straight,
bent and folded poses. 4. Build a grid of permissible angles. Deliver two implementations and a
reachable-point map. Check that at q1=q2=0 the endpoint is (l1+l2,0); with equal lengths and
q2=π, it reaches the base. Handle zero and negative lengths according to geometry-validation
rules.

Task 6. Exercise leg with three axes
For yaw-pitch-pitch, define q1 about z and q2,q3 as angles in the vertical plane, with positive pitch
raising the link. Let l0 be a fixed radial offset and r=l0+l1·cos(q2)+l2·cos(q2+q3). Then
x=r·cos(q1), y=r·sin(q1), z=l1·sin(q2)+l2·sin(q2+q3). 1. Draw this exact mechanism. 2. Build an
independent transform chain. 3. Compare both forms at random permissible angles. 4. Add
T_body_hip and find foot coordinates in the body frame. Save a 3D view of the leg with axes and
tests. If CAD uses another mechanism, use its own chain and a separate reference model.

Comparison with CAD and a library
Choose at least five numerically specified poses and measure endpoint position in CAD or the
saved geometric representation. Compare values with your implementation and Robotics Toolbox
or an independent matrix implementation. State what is compared in the table: coordinates, units
and basis. A large error may arise from millimetres instead of metres, another joint zero, axis
ordering or a different point on the part. Find the cause one transform at a time from root to
endpoint, rather than compensating for the final error with an arbitrary offset.

Accuracy checks
For a purely numerical reference, choose tolerance in advance relative to mechanism length and
machine precision; for example, around 10⁻⁶ m may be a reasonable starting target for a
metre-scale model in double precision, but it is not the robot's mechanical accuracy. Check
geometry scaling and errors at boundary angles. Save the maximum norm of the difference
between implementations and the poses where it occurs. Random checks supplement, rather than
replace, hand-worked reference poses.

СтраницаPage 116 · Inverse kinematics and solution branches
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M08  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Inverse kinematics and solution branches

Analytical solution for the planar arm
For target (x,y), define c2=(x²+y²-l1²-l2²)/(2l1l2). If |c2| is substantially greater than 1, the target is
unreachable; a small round-off excess may be clipped only within the declared numerical
tolerance. For both branches, obtain q2=atan2(±sqrt(1-c2²),c2), then
q1=atan2(y,x)-atan2(l2·sin(q2),l1+l2·cos(q2)). Geometrically reachable points lie between circles
of radii |l1-l2| and l1+l2, but joint limits further reduce the workspace. Degenerate lengths and
folded configurations need explicit handling rules, rather than division by zero.

Task 7. Both branches and joint limits
1. Select a target with two permissible solutions. 2. Calculate both branches and check FK for each.
3. Add angle ranges from geometry and M7; remove solutions that violate them. 4. Choose a
solution close to the previous q while respecting the permitted range, rather than merely the
shortest angular difference around a circle. Deliver an API returning permissible solutions and a
failure reason. Check that FK(IK(p)) is close to p for all accepted points; IK(FK(q)) need not return
the original branch. Edge case: a target on the outer boundary where the two branches coincide.

Task 8. Foot targets for the 3-DOF leg
For the exercise yaw-pitch-pitch leg, first calculate q1=atan2(y,x), then solve the planar problem at
(sqrt(x²+y²)-l0,z). This branch assumes a selected radial-projection direction; the model must
explicitly bound additional configurations and ranges. 1. Transform the target from body to hip
coordinates. 2. Calculate solutions and check limits. 3. Verify them with full FK. 4. Follow a short
foot-lift-and-lower trajectory while retaining the selected branch. Save animation, angles and
maximum geometric residual. At x=y=0, yaw is undefined: return a special status or retain a
permissible previous yaw according to the interface rules.

A failure must not become a command
Distinguish no geometric solution, range violation and numerical failure. Return status,
q_candidates, residual, chosen branch and a diagnostic message. Do not silently replace an
unreachable point by the nearest one: projection must be a separate explicitly requested mode
returning the target actually reached. For a robot, the difference matters: an unnoticed change in
support point changes body position, and a fingertip may fail to reach the object.



































M8 • 02 May 2027 - 03 Jun 2027 • 75 hours                                                                          6 / 15
СтраницаPage 117 · Numerical IK and library design
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M08  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Numerical IK and library design

Task 9. Iterative approximation
The aim is to solve a kinematic problem whose analytical formula is inconvenient and learn to
diagnose convergence. First use the familiar 2R model as a reference. Error e=p_target-FK(q).
Linearisation gives e≈J·Δq; solve the system or use a pseudoinverse instead of explicitly inverting a
matrix. For damped least squares, Δq=Jᵀ·(J·Jᵀ+λ²I)⁻¹e, where λ controls attenuation of large steps
near degeneracy. Implement with solve, a step limit and a finite iteration count. Do not present this
method as a guarantee of a global solution.
1. Begin with a central reachable target and several initial q values. 2. Record error norm and step
size at each iteration. 3. Add joint limits and a termination condition for lack of improvement. 4.
Compare with analytical IK on the same targets. Save convergence plots and a table of successful
and failed runs. Return SUCCESS only after checking final FK and limits. Edge cases: unreachable
target, poor initial seed, nearly straight arm and maximum iteration count. Do not return the last
approximation with a large residual as an executable command.

Unified robot-kinematics v1 interface
The model needs forward(q), inverse(target,seed,limits), jacobian(q), validate(q) and a geometry
description. Inputs must not be changed silently. forward returns position and, when required,
orientation with its basis specified. inverse returns a structured result rather than an unexplained
NaN array. Specify the input coordinate frame explicitly. Use one reference dataset for the
analytical implementation, numerical method and library comparison. A C++ wrapper may follow
these checks; porting to three languages is not the month's goal.

A small integration scenario
Place the body in several known poses and define one stationary world support point. Transform
that point to the hip frame, solve IK and recover world foot coordinates. Then repeat for the 2R
finger: a small target-point contour in its working plane. Plot target, reached point, angles, status
and distance to limits together. This checks geometric consistency across components. Velocities
and torques require separate calculations; a smooth-looking animation does not establish physical
feasibility of the profile.







































M8 • 02 May 2027 - 03 Jun 2027 • 75 hours                                                                           7 / 15
СтраницаPage 118 · Jacobians, forces and singular configurations
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M08  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Jacobians, forces and singular configurations

Task 10. Calculate foot velocity from joint velocities
For position FK, matrix J contains partial derivatives of coordinates with respect to q; each column
describes endpoint motion from a small motion of one joint. Linear velocity v=J(q)·q̇. Derive J for 2R
by hand, then obtain it for the leg analytically or using rotation axes and the vector to the foot
expressed in one coordinate frame. Begin only with the 2×2 or 3×3 position Jacobian; a spatial
velocity (twist) has 6 components and its Jacobian is 6×n. Specify linear/angular component
ordering separately.
Central-difference check: column i is approximately [FK(q+h·e_i)-FK(q-h·e_i)]/(2h). Compare several
h values, for example 10⁻⁴, 10⁻⁵ and 10⁻⁶ rad, at random and boundary poses. Save maximum
error norm and a plot against step size. An excessively small h amplifies round-off, while an
excessively large h increases linear-approximation error. Then specify q̇ and compare predicted
endpoint velocity with a small actual FK step. Edge case: derivative expressed in the wrong basis
with a nonzero base rotation.

Task 11. Foot force and joint torque
Fix the meaning of F: external force applied at the mechanism's endpoint, expressed in the same
basis as J. The corresponding generalised torque is τ=JᵀF; to balance this load, the actuator
generally provides the opposite contribution while accounting for other forces. 1. Check one joint
using r×F. 2. Compare with JᵀF for the arm. 3. Repeat for the leg and several force directions. 4.
Check virtual work, τᵀδq≈Fᵀδp. Deliver a static-load calculation and sign test. The formula itself
excludes link mass, acceleration and friction; M9 adds these.

Task 12. Map proximity to singularity
A singularity is a loss of Jacobian rank relative to its normal maximum. For 2R, compare bent and
fully straight poses. Over a grid, calculate the smallest singular value and available velocity
directions; state normalisation and units explicitly. Request motion along the direction lost in the
straight pose. Save the map and explain why a small target displacement may require a large Δq.
Add status checks and step limits to IK. Proximity to singularity does not itself mean collision, but
requires special command-handling rules.

Work sequence: hours 1-40

Hours 1-10: conventions and manual checks
1-2: review vectors, radians and matrix rotations; create conventions.md. 3-4: study homogeneous
transforms and work a body/hip example by hand. 5-6: understand active and passive transform
meanings and the point/vector distinction. 7-8: study SO(2), SO(3), axis-angle and quaternion
representations; fix component ordering. 9-10: draw the CAD leg tree and initial axis positions. At
every stage, calculate at least one reference without a ready-made robotics library; adding one
later provides an independent comparison.

Hours 11-20: geometry practical
11-12: implement transforms and task 1's coordinate round trip. 13-14: perform task 2, separate
points and directions and add a negative test. 15-16: verify task 3 orientation representations and
invalid-input handling. 17-18: build the task 4 tree and visualise local axes. 19-20: compare four
known poses with a drawing or CAD, save references and correct conventions before continuing.
Do not proceed to IK with even one unknown axis direction; its error becomes harder to diagnose
there.

Hours 21-30: derive forward kinematics
21-22: derive 2R equations geometrically and check zero angles. 23-24: derive the 2R matrix chain
and compare with the formula. 25-26: study yaw-pitch-pitch and its difference from the actual CAD
leg. 27-28: explore DH and the product of exponentials; reproduce one revolute example. 29-30:
define reference poses, tolerance scales and comparison rules for an external library. Separately
list fixed offsets that must not be confused with link lengths.

Hours 31-40: two verified models
31-32: implement task 5 and the planar arm workspace grid. 33-34: implement the task 6
exercise-leg FK and body transform. 35-36: adapt the chain to actual M5 geometry if axes differ,
retaining separate reference-model tests. 37-38: compare five poses with CAD and one
independent implementation. 39-40: run random tests, check units and export, and freeze
baseline-fk. Finish every step by saving verification results; correcting a discovered geometric error
belongs within this block and takes priority over animation styling.

Work sequence: hours 41-75

Hours 41-50: the inverse problem
41-42: derive analytical 2R IK from the triangle, including both branches. 43-44: study reachability,

СтраницаPage 121 · Acceptance, negative tests and self-check
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M08  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Acceptance, negative tests and self-check

Required scenarios
F1: rotation and translation applied in reverse order. The task 1 reference pose detects it. F2:
millimetres treated as metres. Scale checking and a known length reveal the discrepancy; relative
error between functions sharing the same mistake must not produce a false PASS. F3: target
beyond the outer radius or inside the unreachable inner circle of 2R. Return UNREACHABLE. F4:
geometrically reachable point requires a forbidden angle. Return LIMIT_VIOLATION. F5: fully
straight arm. The Jacobian loses rank and IK must not return an unbounded jump as a permissible
command.
F6: two neighbouring requests each have two solution branches. The continuity policy retains a
permissible branch or reports the need to switch. F7: poor seed for numerical IK. At the iteration
limit, return NO_CONVERGENCE with residual. F8: NaN, zero length or zero quaternion. Reject input
according to interface rules. F9: q and -q. The orientation check treats them as equivalent. F10:
force expressed in a different basis. The virtual-work test detects inconsistency. F11: incorrect
encoder-zero sign. Testing the joint adapter in a known calibration configuration reveals the error.

Completion conditions
Both models have documented geometry and automated tests. For accepted IK solutions, the norm
of FK(q)-target lies within the declared numerical tolerance and joint angles remain in range. State
maximum Jacobian error relative to numerical differentiation with the method, steps and pose set.
Include hand-worked references, random checks and independent comparison; two functions with
a shared error do not sufficiently validate each other. Unreachable and singular requests return
clear status, and reproducing results does not require manual file corrections.

Review questions and handover to M9
Explain what T_AB means; why a point and force transform differently; why 2R q2 is relative; why
IK need not recover the same branch; how numerical convergence is defined; why rank matters
more than one large J component; what sign the torque balancing an external force must have; and
how geometry error differs from backlash. Show answers in your drawings and plots. Pass lengths,
local axes, zero offsets, FK, Jacobians and permissible configurations to M9. Masses, centres of
mass, inertias and contacts will be added separately; do not conceal their absence behind a
successful kinematic animation.

Assigned reading: a focused reading route

Books and notes may be in English; keep the plan, definitions and your explanations in English for

Core reading and one reference route
1. Core: K. Lynch, F. Park, Modern Robotics. §3.3.1 homogeneous transforms; §4.1.1 product of
exponentials; §5.1-5.3 Jacobian, statics and singularities; §6.2 numerical IK. This is the route for
tasks 1-12: read the relevant section before deriving equations yourself.
2. Reference: S. LaValle, Planning Algorithms. §3.2 Rigid-Body Transformations and §3.3
Transforming Kinematic Chains. For tasks 1-4, compare the geometric explanation of transforms
and chains; one 2D chain and the transition to 3D are sufficient.
3. Core, selectively: R. Tedrake, Robotic Manipulation: Basic Pick and Place. Named sections
Forward kinematics and Differential inverse kinematics. For tasks 9-10, connect endpoint
coordinates with joint velocities; subsequent motion planning is outside this module.

Documentation for the practical work
SciPy Rotation - apply, inv, from_quat and as_quat; check component ordering and q/-q
equivalence in task 3.
SciPy least_squares - bounds, jac, tolerances and status; an independent numerical-IK check.
Robotics Toolbox: DH models - optional reference for fkine, jacob0 and DH conventions.

Complete the reading with an action
Finish reading by drawing axes, deriving a formula and checking one known pose. Do not transfer
CAD leg dimensions to yaw-pitch-pitch without checking axes and zeros. Separately explain why

СтраницаPage 123 · Glossary: terms and definitions
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M08  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Glossary: terms and definitions

Coordinate frame. An origin and ordered axes relative to which point coordinates or
physical-vector components are expressed.
Pose. A combined description of body position and orientation relative to an explicitly named
coordinate frame.
Rotation matrix. A matrix R preserving lengths and basis handedness; for spatial rotation, RᵀR=I
and det(R)=1.
Homogeneous transform. A 4×4 matrix combining rotation and translation of a point between
two specified coordinate frames.
Composition. Sequential application of transforms; frame indices determine matrix multiplication
order, which generally affects the result.
Degree of freedom. An independent parameter needed to specify a mechanism's configuration
under its geometric constraints.
Configuration. A set of independent mechanism coordinates; for the open chain considered here,
the joint-angle vector q.
Kinematic chain. Rigid links connected by joints whose relative transforms determine the position
of each successive link.
Home configuration. A predefined configuration at zero joint coordinates, serving as the
geometric reference.
Joint axis. An oriented geometric line of rotation or direction of translation, expressed in a
specified coordinate frame.
Forward kinematics. Calculating a selected link's pose from joint configuration and fixed
mechanism geometry.
Inverse kinematics. Finding configurations that achieve a specified pose or point, accounting for
joint limits and solution accuracy.
IK branch. One of several distinct configurations or continuous configuration families that achieve
the same target pose.
Workspace. The set of reachable points or poses of a selected mechanism endpoint under
specified geometry and joint limits.
Quaternion. A four-component, unit-norm orientation representation; quaternions of opposite sign
describe the same rotation.
Jacobian. A matrix relating joint velocities locally to selected endpoint coordinates; its dimensions
and units depend on the task.
Singularity. A configuration with loss of Jacobian rank in which some endpoint-motion directions
become locally unavailable.
Pseudoinverse. A generalisation of matrix inversion for linear least-squares problems that selects
a minimum-norm solution.
Damped least squares IK. A regularised local solution that suppresses excessive joint-coordinate
changes near degeneracy at the cost of residual error.
Check the relationships: ṗ=J(q)q̇; with consistent signs, the generalised force from an external
action is JᵀF. Do not confuse it with a holding command.

Equipment and environment for kinematics

NO NEW PURCHASES REQUIRED
Use the existing MacBook Pro M4, CAD and measured M5 dimensions, and M7 calibrations and one
rig joint. The existing 3D printer is needed only for fixture checks if necessary; select a profile for its
exact model. A complete leg and additional actuators are unnecessary for this mathematics.

PREPARE FOR HOURS 1-20
Save a geometry description: parent/child, joint origin, unit axis, joint type, angle sign, zero, limits,
foot point and units. Specify that axis is expressed in the joint frame. Explicitly convert CAD exports
from millimetres to metres; use the same conventions when creating URDF later.
Keep the reference 2R, reference yaw-pitch-pitch and actual CAD chain separate. Changing lengths
does not turn one kinematic architecture into another. For physical illustration, reuse the M7 rig
only after checking commands in the model.

INSTALL NOW
No new mandatory packages. On macOS ARM, use pinned Python, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib and
pytest from M2-M7; SciPy already includes Rotation and least_squares. The existing editor and
project JSON/YAML suffice for geometry descriptions. ROS, RViz and Gazebo enter later in the
programme.

OPTIONAL, IF NEEDED
If an additional library FK reference is useful, add robotics-toolbox-python in a separate
environment using the official Introduction instructions. First check dependencies on macOS ARM
or the chosen Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64. The main route uses your own matrix FK and SciPy; a MATLAB
licence is unnecessary.

INSTALLATION AND INPUT CHECKS
From a clean directory, import the libraries, print versions, perform a π/2 rotation and its inverse,
and compare q with -q. Then check FK at the 2R zero pose, FK/IK round trips back to the target,
joint limits and the Jacobian using central differences. Save a three-pose plot and a
machine-readable pytest report.
For independent comparison in task 5, use Robotics Toolbox or a separate implementation based
on saved transforms; for task 9, use SciPy least_squares. Preparation and checks replace
duplicated setup within the 75 hours.

СтраницаPage 125 · Motion fundamentals: from a point to joints
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M08  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Motion fundamentals: from a point to joints

Required worked example: FK → IK → velocity → force
Use two rigid links in the planar part of a leg with a fixed base. x points right, y up and +z towards
the viewer; angles are anticlockwise. Measure q1 from +x and q2 relative to the first link. Check
200 mm=0.2 m. Here v=q̇, in rad/s; endpoint velocity ṗ, in m/s, is a different quantity.
For l1=l2=0.2 m, add link vectors: x=0.2cosq1+0.2cos(q1+q2), y=0.2sinq1+0.2sin(q1+q2). At
q=(0;π/2), endpoint p=(0.2;0.2) m. FK applies known rotations in sequence; IK solves the inverse
geometric problem. The cosine rule gives cosq2=(x²+y²-l1²-l2²)/(2l1l2)=0. The branches are (0;π/2)
and (π/2;-π/2); both reach the point, but joint limits may exclude one.

The Jacobian: local motion and its limits
Rotation of joint i moves the endpoint tangentially. Thus a position-Jacobian column is z_i×(p-o_i):
axis z_i and the vector from joint o_i to the endpoint are expressed in one basis. At our pose,
J=[[-0.2; -0.2]; [0.2; 0]] m/rad. With v=(0.5;-0.25) rad/s, ṗ=Jv=(-0.05;0.10) m/s. This is an
instantaneous relation; a finite path requires recalculating J as q changes.
At the straight pose q=(0;0), both tangents are vertical, the x row of J is zero and rank is 1.
Instantaneous velocity along x is unavailable, although a bent chain can change x. This is a
singularity: a small requested point displacement does not guarantee small joint velocities. IK step
limiting and damping do not create the missing direction.

Force uses the same geometry; dynamics comes later
In a separate static experiment, apply f_ext=(0;-5) N at the endpoint: this is the environment's
force on the robot. With link masses and friction excluded, τ_ext=Jᵀf_ext=(-1;0) N·m, and holding
requires τ_act=-τ_ext=(1;0) N·m. Torque at the second joint is zero because the force's line of
action passes through its axis. Link weight and acceleration change the requirement according to
the M9 model; successful IK does not establish motion feasibility.

One check connects tasks 5, 7 and 10-12
Save a drawing of both branches, a p/J value table and tests. Compare J columns with central
differences of FK at h=10⁻⁴ and 10⁻⁶ rad, then repeat at the straight pose. Independently calculate
each torque using r×f_ext. Check power at the stated v: f_extᵀṗ=τ_extᵀv=-0.5 W. This explains the
transpose of J and the external-action sign; it is a calculation, not a torque command to a
position-controlled servo.
Included in the 75 hours: 1 hour from 21-22 for this reference FK/IK example; 1 hour from 63-64
for force and singularity; 2 hours from 66-69 for existing Jacobian and virtual-work tests. Retain all
other tasks; no new laboratory sessions are added.
Read selectively: Lynch/Park, Modern Robotics, chapters 4 and 6: introductory FK and Analytic
Inverse Kinematics; §5.2 Statics of Open Chains. Study the 6×n spatial Jacobian and 6-component
twist after the position Jacobian J.

ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M09  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

From link position to the physics of motion

M9 • 03 Jun 2027 - 06 Jul 2027 • 75 hours

What you will produce by the end of the month
The deliverable for this month is a joint model using the parameters identified in M7, together with
a dynamics simulation of a two-link mechanism or leg. Check dimensions, the energy balance and
agreement between calculations and measurements. The kinematics from M8 finds the angles that
place a link endpoint at a specified point; dynamics relates motion to the required torque and
actuator limits. For a leg, it describes the effects of link masses, body motion and foot contact; for a
finger, it describes phalange acceleration, load holding and the reaction when touching an object.
Begin with one link, then add a second link and contact.

Inputs
Bring the geometry, coordinate frames, FK and Jacobians from M8. From M7, bring angle, command
and current measurements and the available actuator model, including friction, delay and the
limits of identification. From M5, bring CAD-part masses and centres of mass, provided they were
determined correctly. Label each quantity as measured, calculated in CAD, taken from
manufacturer documentation or specified for an illustrative example. Inertia calculated in CAD
using a default density is not the measured inertia of a printed part. Account for fasteners, wiring
and actual infill; if data are unavailable, state the uncertainty of the estimate.
Initial self-check: distinguish kg from N, N from N·m, velocity from acceleration, and inertia about
the centre of mass from inertia about the joint axis. Check the work done by a force through a
small displacement and calculate the energy of a load at a known height. Make sure you know the
axis from which q is measured and the direction of gravity. An incorrect potential-energy sign can
produce smooth simulated motion that contradicts physics.

Scope and evidence
M9 does not require the dynamics of a complete multi-legged platform with gait control. The basic
model has a fixed base, two links and explicitly selected contacts. Increase complexity only after
checking simple limiting cases. Simulation can confirm the correctness of the equations and
numerical method, but agreement with a real actuator requires comparison against a separate
measured run. If M7 did not produce physical measurements, complete the computational work
and mark the comparison with the real actuator as unfinished.
Prepare a working integrator and a description of the model’s limits of applicability. State the
angle, velocity and load ranges and contact modes that you have checked. Separately describe the
conditions under which backlash, saturation, compliance, heating or an unknown internal actuator
controller become significant. Subsequent modules will use this information to choose control laws
that account for model accuracy.

СтраницаPage 127 · 75 hours: from simple models to complex
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M09  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

75 hours: from simple models to complex
ones

Four blocks
Hours 1-20: Newton’s and Euler’s equations, mass, centre of mass, inertia, forces and energy; 10
hours of theory and 10 hours of practice. Hours 21-40: Lagrange’s equations, equation structure
and two-link dynamics; 10+10. Hours 41-60: normal contact, friction, impact and static support;
10+10. Hours 61-75: use of the M7 identification results, model validation, sensitivity and error
assessment; 5+10. This totals 35 hours of study and analysis and 40 hours of implementation and
experiments. The allocation includes documenting results rather than leaving the report to
uncounted time.
Divide each of the first three 10-hour theory blocks into 2-hour sessions: reading a section, deriving
equations by hand, checking units and preparing an experiment. Schedule the 10-hour practical
blocks on Sundays, allowing breaks between stages. Split the final 5 hours of theory as 2+2+1. The
module dates establish its place in the overall calendar; retain the boundary dates, rest days,
holidays and separate integration checks. Hour numbers express the workload: do not count the
same time twice when placing sessions in the calendar.

The dynamics-lab project structure
parameters/ contains masses, lengths, centres of mass, inertias and their provenance. models/
contains the single-link, 2R-mechanism and contact models. experiments/ stores inputs, initial
states and integration settings. data/measured/ preserves the M7 data unchanged; data/simulated/
stores computational results. validation/ contains comparison results and runs for independent
validation; reports/ contains energy balances and model limits. Each simulation records the
equation version, solver step size or tolerances, duration, input signals and termination reason.

When to increase complexity
First, check the energy of one link without friction or external input. Second, add a known torque
and compare its work with the energy change. Third, introduce viscous friction and check that
energy decreases. Fourth, repeat these checks for two links. Fifth, add contact and account for
energy losses. Sixth, use the real actuator model from M7 and an independent measurement
recording. If a basic check fails, find the cause first; do not try to remove the discrepancy by
increasing damping or fitting a physical parameter.
Separate measurement uncertainty from numerical error. Changing mass explores sensitivity to a
physical parameter; reducing the integrator step explores numerical error. Include both
experiments in the report; one cannot replace the other. At the outset, choose several simple
motions that you can explain without a computer, and revisit them after adding each new equation
term.
