СтраницаPage 193 · Testing the model under faults
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M13  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Testing the model under faults

Physics and sensors
F1 - Incorrect inertia or axis. Change one entry and check a known configuration or a small input.
Numerical geometry or dynamics checks must detect the discrepancy before complex motion. Give
the corrected model file a new version; visual resemblance to the robot does not compensate for a
failed check.
F2 - Unstable contact. Increase the step, reduce friction or change the foot contact geometry.
Expect to detect penetration, sliding or energy growth; repeating with a smaller step and the
original geometry should explain the source. Record the physics engine and parameters, since the
same SDF can behave differently in another implementation.
F3 - Delayed IMU data and an empty depth map. The sensor supplies old timestamps or rendering
fails to produce a valid map. The controller or test must detect stale or missing data; ground truth
must never silently replace readings. Specify the frequency of valid messages and the fraction of
missing or non-numeric values; explain the total used as the denominator.

Execution and the hardware boundary
F4 - Loss of reproducibility. Repeat one seed after changing the thread count or platform. Compare
defined metrics and tolerances rather than claiming unconditional bitwise equality. If contact
events differ, isolate a minimal scenario and state which conclusions are materially affected by that
instability.
F5 - Data corruption or loss of physical communication. Drop a packet in the HIL stream, alter its
CRC or disconnect the line using the method specified in the test. An invalid command must be
rejected and data age must increase; the hardware controller and host must record a consistent
cause and transition to fallback mode. Specify which side checks CRC and which side decides what
to do if communication fails in one direction.
F6 - The simulator cannot keep up. Add computational load or a sensor and measure real-time
factor together with data age and deadline compliance. Expect failure of the timing criterion to be
recorded even with a normal average RTF. A powerful computer and RTF≈1 do not guarantee
freedom from isolated long delays.

Decide how to address each failure
Distinguish a model defect, an interface defect, an environment limitation and missing physical
data. Change one factor when correcting a failure. Repeat the reference scenario and preserve the
original failure as the basis of a regression test. If a discrepancy remains unexplained, add it to the
unresolved fidelity issues with a specific measurement that will distinguish possible causes.
"Simulation is imperfect" is too general to support an engineering decision.

























M13 • 26 Oct 2027 - 21 Nov 2027 • 75 hours                                                                         8 / 15

Hours 1-40: model physics and sensors

Hours 1-20: simulation foundations
Theory 1-10: 1-2 - SDF structure and the selected engine; 3-4 - mass, inertia and integration; 5-6 -
contact and friction; 7-8 - joint limits, damping and actuator model; 9-10 - analytical reference
cases and convergence criteria. End each of the five two-hour sessions with a prediction of a
specific physical quantity.
Practice 11-20: 11-12 - run a minimal Harmonic world; 13-14 - complete Task 1; 15-16 - repeat with
two steps; 17-18 - complete Task 2; 19-20 - save the contact failure and reference configuration.
Do not spend the ten-hour practical building a complex robot before the simple cases pass.
Progression criteria: free-fall and pendulum results agree with the chosen analytical calculation,
contact has numerical criteria, and the physics step is selected from changes in results and
computational cost.

Hours 21-40: model and sensors
Theory 21-30: 21-22 - Xacro and mirroring; 23-24 - inertial/collision and transmissions; 25-26 -
gz_ros2_control interfaces; 27-28 - IMU, contacts, depth and ground truth; 29-30 - operation
without a GUI, component readiness and time bases. Before installing additional packages,
establish that a specific sensor needs them and that the selected environment supports them.
Practice 31-40: 31-32 - verify one leg; 33-34 - complete Task 3 with four legs; 35-36 - connect the
sensors; 37-38 - complete Task 4 without a GUI; 39-40 - test an incorrect axis and a missing depth
map, and record the manifest. If graphics are unavailable, retain working physics and IMU tests and
separately mark depth verification as incomplete.
Progression criteria: the quadruped exists as a verifiable model, joint names match the ROS stack,
ground truth is separated from sensors, and missing data is detected explicitly.

Hours 41-75: SIL, PIL, HIL and fidelity

Hours 41-60: the controller inside the loop
Theory 41-50: 41-42 - SIL, PIL and HIL boundaries; 43-44 - state reset and seed; 45-46 - simulation

communication, delay and disconnection; 70-71 - complete Task 8 on an available secured rig or

СтраницаPage 196 · Acceptance checks, limitations and further
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M13  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Acceptance checks, limitations and further
work

Demonstrate model suitability
Begin the demonstration with an analytical test and a leg-coordinate check, then show the sensor
reference world without a GUI. Next, demonstrate one SIL scenario, PIL computation on the target
processor and HIL with a physical communication channel. Identify the real and modelled robot
components in each experiment. Finish by comparing a physical recording with the model and
listing properties that this twin cannot yet predict.
Acceptance requires geometry, inertia and limit checks; recorded contact and timing violations;
separate sensor readings and ground truth; a GUI-free test with a timeout; a manifest; a
host-versus-target comparison; an HIL log; and unresolved fidelity issues. If hardware is unavailable
and HIL or physical comparison has not been completed, record partial readiness and the specific
open item. A hil directory or a connected USB cable does not itself establish that the criterion is
met.

Self-check questions
1) How does visual differ from collision and inertial? 2) How can you tell whether the physics step is
small enough? 3) Why does identical SDF not guarantee identical contact in a different engine? 4)
How do you check the axis of a mirrored leg? 5) How does sensor noise differ from delay? 6) Why
must ground-truth state be withheld from the operational state estimator?
7) How does a server without a GUI differ from camera rendering without a window? 8) Where does
the controller run in SIL, PIL and HIL? 9) Why does RTF≈1 not establish compliance with every
deadline? 10) How can you measure communication delay without synchronised clocks? 11) What
does HIL with a modelled actuator verify, and what does it leave unverified? 12) Why should
digital-twin fidelity be described by subsystem? Answer using your own tests and hardware
boundaries.

Handover and selection of physical experiments
Pass the worlds, sensor models, actuator settings, scenario catalogue and list of permitted uses to
later stages. For example: the model is suitable for interface and delay testing, has limited
suitability for tuning small movements and is not yet validated for impact contact. Plan separate
tests of heating, backlash, foot forces, friction on the actual surface and emergency-response
delay; these cannot be inferred solely from a gait simulation.
If time is short, reduce visual mesh detail, the number of worlds and use of the additional MuJoCo
engine. Retain the four-leg structure, one thoroughly verified dynamic leg, sensor reference scenes
and the hardware loop. Do not add a new gait algorithm, RL or a complete arm model to these 75
hours. Turn model errors into specific engineering tasks with an expected measurement, rather
than a general doubt about the simulator's usefulness.

Assigned reading: a focused route through
the sections

The literature is mainly in English; the programme and definitions are also in English. Read the
selected sections before the relevant task, rather than entire books. Core reading is included in the
existing 35 analysis hours; consult references as needed.

Core reading
E. Renard, ROS 2 from Scratch (2024). Book and contents. Ch. 13 Simulating a Robot in
Gazebo: How Gazebo works, Adapting the URDF for Gazebo, Spawning the robot in Gazebo. Before
Tasks 3-4, understand the relationship between model, world and plugin. Use commands
appropriate to Jazzy/Harmonic.
K. Lynch, F. Park, Modern Robotics (2017). Learning resources. §8.1.3 Understanding the
Mass Matrix, §8.2 Dynamics of a Single Rigid Body and §8.5 Forward Dynamics of Open Chains.
Before Tasks 1 and 8, check inertia, the justification for the pendulum reference case and the
meaning of forward dynamics.
R. Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics, MIT notes. Multi-Body Dynamics. Sections The
Dynamics of Contact and Compliant Contact Models. Before Task 2, establish the relationship
between penetration, stiffness, friction and integration step; calculate the condition for the onset of
sliding.

Implementation references
SDFormat specification - model/link/inertial, joint/axis, world/physics and sensor. In Tasks 1-4,
record the schema version and check which fields the selected engine uses.
Gazebo Harmonic: Sensors - IMU sensor and Contact sensor. For Task 4, study frequency,
coordinate frames, plugins, noise and separation of sensor readings from simulation ground truth.
gz_ros2_control Jazzy - Add ros2_control tag, demos and Notes on the command interface. In Tasks
3 and 5, check which quantity the interface commands: torque, velocity or position.

What to record in the laboratory log
Give a source for every parameter: CAD, specifications, measurement or an assumption with a
range. After reading, identify one numerical physics test and one boundary it does not establish.
HIL requires a real controller and channel; conclusions about mechanics require a separate physical
experiment.

СтраницаPage 198 · Terms and definitions
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M13  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Terms and definitions

Digital twin. A model of a specific system tied to its geometry, parameters and measurements
within a declared domain of applicability.
SDF. A format describing simulation worlds, bodies, joints, physics and sensors; tag semantics
depend on the supported schema.
Inertial parameters. A body's mass, centre of mass and inertia tensor, expressed relative to a
specified coordinate frame.
Collision geometry. Geometry used to detect collisions and contacts; it may differ from the
model's detailed visual surface.
Forward dynamics. Calculation of accelerations from state, forces and constraints; an integrator
then updates the state over time.
Integration step. The increment of simulation time between numerical updates; it affects error,
stability and computational cost.
Step-size convergence. Stabilisation of a selected result as the step is progressively reduced;
checked with identical conditions and duration.
Contact. Interaction between surfaces that come together, involving normal and possibly
tangential forces; contact can allow sliding.
Normal force. The contact-force component perpendicular to the surface; in a unilateral contact
model, the surface pushes but does not pull.
Friction coefficient μ. The dimensionless ratio of limiting tangential force to normal force in the
adopted model; it depends on materials and contact regime.
Penetration. Calculated overlap of contacting surfaces; in a compliant model it determines force
together with stiffness and damping.
Compliant contact. A model in which force depends on deformation and its rate; high stiffness
places stronger demands on the integrator.
Ground-truth state. The model's true internal state, used to calculate errors; the operational
state estimator must not receive it.
Seed. The initial state of a random-number generator; it fixes the random sequence, but not every
effect of parallel execution.
SIL. A closed-loop software experiment in which a host-computer controller acts on a model and
receives its response.
PIL. An experiment using controller code on the target processor and a plant model; coordinated
stepwise execution is permitted.
HIL. A closed-loop experiment with a real controller and channel, checking explicitly declared
hardware boundaries and timing requirements.
Real-time factor. The ratio of simulation-time and wall-time increments; it does not describe
command latency.
Round-trip time. The time for an outward-and-return exchange measured using one clock;
without further assumptions it does not give one-way delay.
Model validation. Checking predictions against independent measurements for a specified task;
it does not establish applicability in every operating regime.

Equipment and setup for this month

Use existing equipment
MacBook Pro M4, Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64 in UTM and the Jazzy environment from M12; ESP32-S3, a
USB/UART/CAN channel, analyser and power supply from earlier modules. HIL requires a real
microcontroller (MCU) that calculates control, and a real channel. The M7 bench motor remains
suitable for repeating joint measurements.

Purchase after verifying the selected actuator
A separate physical 3DOF leg requires compatible actuators from the selected family. If one
actuator has already passed torque, speed, heating, feedback, protocol and shutdown checks, buy
another 2, making 3 in total. If there is no verified candidate, first buy and test 1; order the next 2
only after it passes acceptance. The bench DC motor does not automatically count as that
candidate.
For the approved leg CAD model and BOM, prepare 1 set of printed links, fasteners, bearings and
wiring to the final geometry, plus 1 restraining fixture. Use the existing 3D printer with a profile for
its exact model. Do not yet buy complete sets of 12/18 actuators or an onboard Pi/x86 computer.
Single-leg readiness is established by measurements, not the G2 date.

Install now
In the same Ubuntu guest, install Gazebo Harmonic, ros_gz/bridge, gz_ros2_control and the demos.
Follow the official ROS/Gazebo pairing and Jazzy plugin installation; use ros-jazzy-gz-ros2-control.
Do not mix Harmonic with Gazebo Classic. Retain ESP-IDF, firmware and the protocol from M6-M12.

Check the installation and its limitations
Run the cart demo, check joint states and position changes, then verify free fall and the pendulum
with dt and dt/2. Separately check depth-map rendering without a GUI: a server without a window
does not establish that depth frames exist. In UTM, check USB exchange and measure dropouts
and round-trip time; if timing cannot be maintained, leave the HIL criterion open.
Simple HIL with a microcontroller and model does not require a physical leg, but it does not
validate mechanics either. Purchasing three actuators serves the separate physical experiment in
Task 8. Preparation fits within the 75 hours in place of repeated setup; delivery time is outside
study hours. Power on new actuators only after matching the supply, limits and mounting.

СтраницаPage 200 · Motion fundamentals: contact and model
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M13  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Motion fundamentals: contact and model
fidelity

Required: why touching the ground does not ensure support
A foot can touch the floor while sliding, and a contact that appears rigid can still allow penetration.
Before moving on to the leg, check these effects with a simple body. Before calculating, resolve
gravity into normal and tangential components and explain why static friction need not equal μFn.

A minimal friction model on an incline
A block of m = 1 kg neither rotates nor tips. The plane is stationary at angle α; the local t-axis
points downhill and n points outwards. g = 9.81 m/s². Fn ≥ 0 and Ft are the forces exerted by the
plane on the block, in N; acceleration along n is zero: Fn = mg cos α; m at = mg sin α + Ft.
Friction coefficients are dimensionless.
Rest requires Ft = −mg sin α and |Ft| ≤ μs Fn, where μs is the coefficient of static friction. During
downhill sliding, Ft = −μk Fn, where μk is the coefficient of kinetic friction. The normal force does
not oppose motion along the slope; the boundary of static equilibrium here is tan α = μs.
Let μs = 0.40 and μk = 0.30. At α = 20°: Fn = 9.218 N, mg sin α = 3.355 N, and the friction limit is
3.687 N. Thus Ft = −3.355 N is admissible, and a block initially at rest remains stationary. The
actual friction is smaller than its limiting value.
At α = 30°: Fn = 8.496 N, the downhill force is 4.905 N, and the limiting static-friction force is 3.398
N. Rest is impossible; during sliding, Ft = −2.549 N and at = 9.81(sin 30° − 0.30 cos 30°) =
2.356 m/s². Friction dissipates mechanical energy: Ft·vt ≤ 0. The wrong sign would cause energy
to grow.
In the spring model, Fn = kδ, where k is stiffness in N/m and δ is penetration in m. At rest on a 20°
incline with k = 10 000 N/m: δ = 9.218/10 000 = 0.000922 m, or 0.922 mm. This is consistent
with the adopted compliance; a zero visible gap is not an accuracy criterion.
Increasing k changes the physical model and raises the oscillation frequency; reducing the step Δt
changes numerical accuracy. Compare Δt and Δt/2 with identical mass, friction, stiffness and
solver. If the engine uses a different contact law, first map its parameters: δ = Fn/k may not apply.

Two experiments within existing Tasks 1-2
1. Start the block from rest at 20° and 30°; save forces, velocity and acceleration after the
transient. Verify rest or sliding, the sign of Ft and the numbers above. If the engine uses a single μ,
set μs = μk and recalculate the prediction; record the settings explicitly.
2. For 30°, compare two steps over the same interval of established sliding. Save mean at, Fn,
penetration, kinetic energy K and potential energy U. The teaching target for at is a difference from
the analytical value and between steps of ≤ 2% of 2.356 m/s² with the original μs and μk. Check
that K may increase as U decreases; total mechanical energy, including the contact spring,
decreases through friction.
Time: 1 theory hour from 5-6 (contact), plus 1 practice hour each from 15-16 (two steps) and
17-18 (Task 2). These calculations and checks are included in the 75 hours. The block validates the
selected contact regime; the complete leg and physical HIL require their own checks.
Read: Lynch, Park, Modern Robotics §12.2.1: Friction; Tedrake, Multi-Body Dynamics → Compliant
Contact Models.

СтраницаPage 201 · Monthly outcome: the robot measures the
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M14  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Monthly outcome: the robot measures the
visible scene

M14 • 21 Nov 2027 - 19 Dec 2027 • 75 hours

Build a reproducible RGB-D processing pipeline: use colour images and depth to determine the
geometry of a floor, a step and an object on a table. For a walking robot, this will provide heights
and information about unknown regions ahead of a foothold; for an arm, it provides the position of
a surface and a potential grasp object. The M14 deliverable contains calibration files, reference
scenes, classical and learned methods, measurements of geometric error and latency, and a failure
log.

What you need to understand before starting
Review coordinate transforms, rotation matrices, the 4×4 homogeneous matrix, measurement
noise, NumPy, testing and ROS 2 recording from earlier modules. Check your understanding with a
small task: transform a point from the camera frame into the body frame and back; the recovered
point must match within the chosen numerical tolerance. Separately explain how a pixel differs
from a metre and why the RGB timestamp may differ from the depth measurement time.

Working setup and boundaries
The main option is recorded RGB-D scenes or a simulator with known geometry; your own camera
is useful but optional. Create three scenes: a flat surface, a box representing a step, and an object
for a future grasp. TUM data is suitable for testing loading and geometry; prepare separate
"support" and "obstacle" labels for your tasks. Do not attribute semantic annotations to the original
dataset if it does not contain them.
Use Ubuntu 24.04 and ROS 2 Jazzy from previous months. Use Python for experiments, OpenCV
and Open3D for geometry, and PyTorch for a small learning experiment. If necessary, port only a
stage whose high computational cost has been demonstrated by measurement to C++. On the
Mac, continue using the existing Linux environment. For every result, identify the CPU, architecture
and accelerator used.

What understanding looks like
You can show how an incorrect depth scale distorts the estimated box height, and how a low error
on training images can conceal poor calibration. Distinguish a recognised "floor" from geometrically
verified support. Full SLAM, step selection and a real closed-loop walking controller belong to later
stages. In M14, processing outputs describe only the observed scene and data reliability.

СтраницаPage 202 · 75 hours: work sequence and time
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M14  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

75 hours: work sequence and time
accounting

Four work blocks
Hours 1-20: camera geometry, calibration, units and time; 10 hours of analysis and 10 hours of
practice. Hours 21-40: colour, edges, features, RANSAC and tracking; 10+10 hours. Hours 41-60:
point clouds, filtering, normals, ICP and heights; 10+10 hours. Hours 61-75: CNNs, transfer
learning, comparison and acceptance; 5 hours of analysis and 10 hours of practice. Total: 35 hours
of theory and analysis and 40 hours of practice, with no hours added beyond the programme.
Divide theory in each of the first three blocks into five 2-hour sessions; divide the final 5 hours as
2+2+1. Organise practice into four Sunday blocks of 10 hours, with breaks outside study time. A
practical block may be split across available intervals with the same total duration. Roadmap
calendar boundaries may overlap between neighbouring modules; retain rest, holidays and
separate integration checkpoints without counting hours twice.

One experiment, one testable version
At the start of a session, record a question such as "How does voxel size affect estimated step
height?" Then identify the parameter to change, the fixed input dataset and the expected sign of
success. At the end, save the configuration, dataset hash, plot and failure explanation. An
experiment that changes calibration, image size and network weights simultaneously cannot
establish the effect of one factor.
Organise the project as follows: calibration/ - K, distortion and procedure; datasets/manifest - data
provenance and splits; geometry/ - depth processing; perception/ - masks; tests/scenes - reference
scenes; reports/ - metrics. Store large raw recordings separately from code, preserving exact
names, checksums and acquisition instructions. The entire dataset must be reprocessed with one
command, without manually selecting successful frames.

Working as an experienced developer
Read until you can answer the current question, then move to measurement. For each new
algorithm, work through a few points by hand, build a small test and only then process a full
recording. "It did not work" is insufficient: identify the stage, input, version and symptom. If
package installation exceeds its allotted time, replay a prepared recording and reduce the
experiment's scale; retain calibration and unit checks.

































M14 • 21 Nov 2027 - 19 Dec 2027 • 75 hours                                                                        2 / 15
СтраницаPage 203 · The camera: from pixel to geometric ray
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M14  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

The camera: from pixel to geometric ray

Topics to study
Study the pinhole model: u = fx·X/Z + cx, v = fy·Y/Z + cy. Coordinates X,Y,Z are in metres in the
optical frame; u,v and fx,fy,cx,cy are in pixels. Matrix K describes the intrinsic parameters. Radial
and tangential distortion alter observed pixels; the extrinsic transform relates the camera to the
body. Do not confuse lens calibration with the camera's pose on the robot.
Study stereo depth using Z = f·b/d: focal length f is in pixels, baseline b in metres and disparity d in
pixels. At small disparity, the same pixel error produces a larger depth error. Compare two
distances with the same error in d: a distant surface is less suitable for precise foothold selection.
For RGB-D, understand scale, channel alignment and the representations of missing or invalid
depth values. Hand-eye calibration relates camera and link motions: study AX=XB and the
eye-in-hand/eye-to-hand distinction. M14 requires a measurement scheme and understanding of
the necessary extrinsics; a separate solver is not required.

Task 1. Check the camera model
Input: synthetic 3D points in front of the camera and a specified K. Project the points, recover X,Y
from known Z values, then test the image centre, doubling Z and a point behind the camera.
Output: a projection-and-reconstruction round-trip test and a drawing of the rays. For synthetic
data, specify a relative numerical tolerance, such as 10⁻⁶, as a computational requirement. Z≤0
and missing depth must cause rejection rather than produce a point at the origin.

Task 2. Calibrate for the working field of view
Use at least 15-20 varied chessboard images: include image edges, different tilts and distances. If
you have no camera, use published OpenCV images; document square size as either a known value
from the source or an arbitrary unit. Split images by capture pose into a parameter-fitting set (fit)
and a held-out set. Find and refine internal corners, estimate K and distortion parameters, and save
a list of excluded images with reasons.
Check by overlaying reprojected points, calculating RMS pixel distances and reporting each image's
errors separately. On a held-out image, estimate only the board's position and orientation while
keeping K and distortion fixed. Repeat using only central views and compare edge errors.
Document all checks; one final number is insufficient. A small RMS does not establish correct
physical scale or the correct camera-to-body transform.


































M14 • 21 Nov 2027 - 19 Dec 2027 • 75 hours                                                                          3 / 15
СтраницаPage 204 · Classical vision: a baseline and its limits
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M14  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Classical vision: a baseline and its limits

Sections to cover
BGR/RGB and HSV colour spaces; smoothing, gradients and Canny; binary masks, morphology and
connected components; local features and matching; geometric models and outliers. Separate the
signal from the decision: an image edge is not the edge of a step expressed in metres. A
homography is sufficient for a textured planar surface; one homography cannot describe an
arbitrary 3D scene.

Task 3. Find an object and a surface edge
Input: 30 images from three scenes, with a manual object mask and marked edge. Build an HSV
mask, then an edge-based alternative; fix thresholds using the training portion. Remove small
components and save the object contour and bounding rectangle. Output: masks, overlays and a
detection-results table. Evaluate IoU = intersection area / union area on the same dataset, and the
fraction of images with no detection.
Change lighting, add a similarly coloured object, then add a shadow on the plane. Do not adjust a
threshold to fix one image after inspecting the test set. A false object detection beside the arm and
a missed edge ahead of a leg have different consequences; annotate these cases in the report.
Separately test an empty mask, an entirely white mask and an object cropped by the image
boundary.

Task 4. Robust matching and tracking
Find features in a pair of images of a flat board, match descriptors and estimate a homography
using RANSAC. Introduce a controlled fraction of deliberately incorrect pairs. Save the number of
matches and model-consistent matches (inliers), the geometric error of reference points and an
"insufficient data" flag. Test a degenerate, nearly collinear configuration and a repeated pattern.
Do not accept a matrix simply because the function returned one.
Next, run Lucas-Kanade on selected corners in a short video: compare forward and backward
motion and reject unreliable point tracks. Save the tracks and a plot of the number of points that
remain tracked. Blur or switching off the light must reduce confidence in the estimate. Tracking
establishes correspondence between images; without geometry and depth, it does not yet provide
metric body velocity. Save original images and the RANSAC seed so that repeated runs are
comparable.

СтраницаPage 205 · Point clouds: the surface in the robot frame
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M14  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Point clouds: the surface in the robot frame

What to study and check by hand
For an aligned depth map: Z = depth/scale, X = (u−cx)·Z/fx, Y = (v−cy)·Z/fy. First exclude missing
and invalid values. Transform into the body frame with p_body = R_body_camera·p_camera +
t_body_camera. Record the direction of every transform and check which inverse is required.
Optical axes differ from body axes, so check labelled basis vectors and a point directly in front of
the camera.
Filtering includes cropping to the working region, voxel-grid downsampling and outlier removal. A
normal describes the local surface direction; neighbourhood radius affects results near an edge.
For a plane n·p + d = 0, normalise n to unit length so that the residual is in metres. ICP reduces
correspondence error with a suitable initial estimate, but does not guarantee correct registration of
every scene.

Task 5. From depth to a plane and a step
Use a synthetic scene with a known box height, then a real recording. Convert depth to points, crop
the area in front of the body and compare three voxel sizes. Use RANSAC to extract a support
plane, estimate normals and build a height grid with an observation count per cell. Output: a point
cloud, plane.yaml, a height map, an unknown-cell map and height error over reference regions.
Check that synthetic height is recovered within a tolerance chosen beforehand; for recordings, use
a measured reference and its uncertainty. Mark empty cells unknown; do not substitute zero. Add
10% random outliers and a region of missing depth at the edge. Compare median absolute height
error and the fraction of cells without an estimate. Choose the threshold in metres to reflect scene
scale and sensor noise.

Task 6. Register adjacent observations
Create a pair of clouds with a known translation and rotation. Run point-to-point and then
point-to-plane ICP from identical initial conditions. Report transform error, correspondence fraction,
residuals and time; classify small residuals with an incorrect displacement as a failure. Repeat on a
single plane, in a symmetric corridor and with a poor initial estimate. Explain how incorrect
registration would shift an object for the arm and create a false support height for the leg.

СтраницаPage 206 · Learned vision: a small comparison
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M14  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Learned vision: a small comparison
experiment

The minimum theory for the week
Study convolution, receptive fields, feature maps, backbone weights and the output head. Learn
training and inference, train/eval modes, transfer learning, learning rate and overfitting. The aim is
to design an experiment without developing a large network. Compare methods on the same task
and annotations: for example, segment a specified class of object on a table or a region of flat
surface.
Image classification, bounding-box detection and pixel segmentation produce different outputs.
Choose a compact segmentation model with a pretrained backbone and fine-tune only a small
head, or use a ready-made detector for a supported class. In the latter case, perform a separate
transfer-learning experiment on a small classifier of cropped image patches; do not describe an
unchanged ready-made model as fine-tuned. Limit annotation of your own scenes to 60-100
temporally separated images.

Task 7. Train without data leakage
Split data by scene or capture session rather than randomly distributing neighbouring images.
Initial split: train 60%, validation 20%, test 20%. Save each file's assignment and check overlaps
using hashes and timestamp proximity. Apply augmentations only to train; transform images and
masks consistently for geometric changes. Do not flip a scene vertically unless those conditions are
physically possible in the intended setting.
Limit head-training time, save the best version according to the validation set and fix the threshold.
Prepare weights, preprocessing parameters, the training log and manifest. Check train/eval modes
on the same input; during inference, results must not depend on test-image order. Explicitly define
behaviour when the required class is absent or the image is corrupted.

Task 8. Quality, confidence and latency
Compare results with Task 3 on the test set using precision, recall and IoU. State the counting unit:
a pixel or a detected object. For five confidence bins, tabulate mean model confidence and the
actual fraction of correct results; note the small sample size. Measure classical and learned method
latency over the same complete processing segment. A CNN may improve recall yet fail on a new
material; reflect this in the report. Permit unknown outside the studied conditions so uncertainty
does not become a robot command.

СтраницаPage 207 · Integration laboratory: surveying terrain and
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M14  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Integration laboratory: surveying terrain and
a table

Specification
The replay command accepts an RGB-D manifest, calibration.yaml, frames.yaml and method
parameters. For each image it outputs the measurement timestamp, frame_id, a valid-depth mask,
a plane, a height grid, an object mask, diagnostic status and processing time. Add a small ROS 2
message adapter to the existing project. The computational core must process recordings without
a connected robot. Preserve the original timestamp; do not replace it with processing-completion
time.

Assembly sequence
1. Load an RGB/depth pair and check size, encoding and scale. 2. Match timestamps within a
specified tolerance and reject unpaired images. 3. Apply the correct calibration; update K
consistently when image size changes. 4. Generate points and transform them into the body frame.
5. Compute geometry and the semantic mask independently. 6. Combine results in a report while
preserving reasons for unknown values. 7. Check reproduction with one command.

Task 9. Verify what the outputs mean
In scene A, the robot looks at a level floor; in B, a box is ahead; in C, the camera observes an object
on a table. For each, define 5 reference regions with known roles: floor, box top, edge, a region
without depth data and background. Compare height, normal and the fraction of valid
measurements. Output: a region table, overlays and an explanation of where the network
disagrees with geometry. Do not allow a "floor" mask to remove a geometric obstacle
automatically.
For future foothold selection, propose only candidate regions: visible flat cells with estimated
heights. Leg reachability, load-bearing capacity, friction and stability are not checked here. For the
arm, propose the observed object surface; grasp orientation and collision freedom will be checked
in M17. This establishes which conclusions the data supports.

What to include in the deliverable
Save a README with commands, environment and library versions, input data or acquisition
instructions, calibration and the coordinate-frame chain, a table of all scenes, numerical metrics, at
least six failure or boundary cases and usage limitations. Add a short replay video labelled with
time and coordinates. Check results against raw arrays: video compression may conceal dropped
frames, so video does not replace the log.

СтраницаPage 208 · Error checks: eight mandatory scenarios
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M14  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Error checks: eight mandatory scenarios

A set of controlled faults
S1 - Incorrect depth scale: multiply distances by 1000 while retaining the settings. A range check or
comparison with reference geometry must detect the error; record the stage that detects it. S2 -
Incorrect K after resizing: halve the image size while keeping the original K. Reference height or
projection must reveal a discrepancy. Restore a consistent transform and save both results.
S3 - Time offset: pair RGB and depth with offsets of 0, 1 and 3 frames in a moving scene. Measure
mask-boundary error relative to the cloud and the number of rejected pairs. S4 - Missing depth at a
potential foothold: zero depth in a square beneath the future leg position; the output must contain
unknown. Do not increase map completeness by interpolating across an unknown edge without
labelling that interpolation separately.
S5 - Geometric degeneracy: feed ICP a single plane translated along itself. Compare
position-and-orientation error with the residual; explain the lack of constraints. S6 - Changes in
lighting and material: compare the classical method and network on a fixed test set. Show false
detections, misses and model confidence. Either method may lose the comparison, provided
experiment parameters were fixed beforehand.
S7 - Data leakage: deliberately add a copy of a training image to test; the automatic manifest
check must fail before quality metrics are calculated. S8 - Overload: add delay to network
inference, then inspect counts of received, processed and discarded images. Publishing an old map
must preserve its age and diagnostic status rather than present it as fresh.

Units and metrics
Reprojection error is the RMS of Euclidean distances in pixels; do not mix it with mean norm/N from
another example. Height error is the absolute difference in metres at reference points. Measure
computation time using the end and start readings of one monotonic timer; data age requires
aligned clocks. Report median, p95, maximum and image count. Measure file loading and
warmed-up network inference separately.

Documenting a failure
Each scenario stores its original configuration, the single introduced change, the expected
observation and the actual outcome. If a check misses S1 or S4, refine data requirements before
improving the CNN. With a physical camera, separately record lighting, mounting and reference
conditions: a synthetic tolerance does not automatically become an acceptable error for the real
robot.

Hours 1-10: five 2-hour sessions
1-2: understand K, projection and units; calculate the centre and one off-axis point by hand, then
work on Task 1. 3-4: radial and tangential distortion and the meaning of internal board corners;
prepare the capture procedure. 5-6: extrinsics, optical frame and body-frame transform; check

position and orientation; save parameters. 17-18: plot residuals by image and compare

First remove a second network architecture, then detailed ICP tuning and porting to C++. Retain

Acceptance checks and the transition to
localisation

A verifiable monthly deliverable
Include K, the distortion model, image size, physical or arbitrary board scale, original images, a
held-out set and errors by viewpoint in the calibration package. Specify time, scale and pairing
rules in the RGB-D manifest. Define transform directions and units for the frame chain; check
forward and inverse conversion. Saved data must be sufficient to reproduce setup without verbal
explanations from its author.
The pipeline builds a cloud, extracts a plane and object, estimates heights, preserves unknown and
emits diagnostics. It includes at least one classical and one learned baseline, a shared test set and
comparisons of quality and latency. Scenarios S1-S8 must be reproducible, rather than only
described. Report limitations of the real sensor if one was used; clearly separate synthetic results
from physical measurements.

Self-check without notes
1. Why is fx measured in pixels, and what changes when image size changes? 2. How does a scale
error differ from reprojection error? 3. Why must zero depth not be treated as a floor point? 4. How
do you check the direction of T_body_camera? 5. When is a homography valid, and when is it not?
6. Why can ICP with a small residual give an incorrect position and orientation?
7. How does voxel size affect a step edge? 8. Why do neighbouring images in training and test sets
create leakage? 9. What does high recall with low precision mean for the arm? 10. How does model
confidence differ from the actual probability of error? 11. Why must a measurement timestamp not
become a publication timestamp? 12. What additional checks are needed before allowing the real
robot to place a foot in a selected cell?

What to pass to M15
Pass on short synchronised sequences, camera parameters, the coordinate-frame chain, ICP
settings, reference displacements and descriptions of degenerate cases. Preserve reasons for lost
point tracks and sensor dropouts: they become localisation test scenarios. Explicitly identify
artificially corrected trajectories and excluded failed images.
The final demonstration takes 5-7 minutes: one normal scene, incorrect depth scale, a region
without depth, a method comparison and a repeated launch. Separately state what the project
does not yet measure: support load-bearing capacity, physical friction, actual contact and step
stability. The next stage can use the described geometry, but must make motion decisions under
its own constraints.

Assigned reading: a focused route through
the sections

The literature is mainly in English; the programme and definitions are also in English. Read the
selected sections before the relevant task, rather than entire books. Core reading is included in the
existing 35 analysis hours; consult references as needed.

Core reading
R. Szeliski, Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications, 2nd ed. (2022). Author's page.
Ch. 2 Image Formation; selected parts of Ch. 7 Feature Detection and Matching and Ch. 9 Motion
Estimation. For Tasks 1-4: camera rays, robust correspondences and Lucas-Kanade; record the
conditions under which a method ceases to be meaningful.
R. Hartley, A. Zisserman, Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision, 2nd ed. (2004).
Book and authors' contents. Ch. 6 Camera Models; only two-view geometry from Ch. 9 Epipolar
Geometry and the Fundamental Matrix; triangulation from Ch. 12 Structure Computation. Before
Tasks 1-2, learn to distinguish calibration, baseline, depth and uncertainty.

For the small deep-learning experiment
I. Goodfellow, Y. Bengio, A. Courville, Deep Learning (2016). Authors' online book. Ch. 9
Convolutional Networks: convolution and pooling; Ch. 11 Practical Methodology: metrics and model
selection. Before Tasks 7-8, understand the backbone and head, data splitting and the
experiment's time limit; the remaining chapters are not needed yet.

Three implementation references
OpenCV: Camera Calibration - Calibration, Undistortion, Re-projection Error; Task 2, fixed K and
distortion with separate held-out images.
Open3D: ICP registration - Point-to-point and Point-to-plane ICP, evaluation. In Task 6, compare the
residual with the error of the known transform.
PyTorch: Transfer Learning - ConvNet as fixed feature extractor and Train the model; Task 7, a
small CPU experiment with saved preprocessing settings and weights.
After reading, explain why a small reprojection error does not establish scale, why ICP can fail
despite a small residual, and why model confidence does not equal the probability of a correct
decision without checking calibration.

СтраницаPage 213 · Terms and definitions
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M14  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Terms and definitions

Pinhole projection. An ideal camera model in which image coordinates are determined by the
ratios of a point's transverse coordinates to its depth.
Intrinsics. The focal scales and principal point in K; they determine the mapping from camera rays
to pixel coordinates.
Extrinsics. Rotation and translation between the camera and another coordinate frame, with an
explicitly stated transform direction.
Distortion. A systematic deviation from the selected ideal projection caused by optics and
described by a calibration model.
Reprojection error. The distance between a measured pixel and the projection of an estimated
point; usually expressed in pixels of the selected image.
Disparity. The coordinate difference between corresponding points in a rectified stereo pair;
together with baseline and focal length, it determines depth.
Stereo baseline. The distance between camera optical centres in metres; it establishes the
metric scale of stereo depth.
Depth scale. A factor converting a stored depth code into physical units; the data format
determines the direction of conversion.
Homography. A projective mapping of a plane between images; one homography is generally
insufficient for a scene with different depths.
Feature descriptor. A vector describing a local image region for matching; descriptor similarity
requires subsequent geometric verification.
RANSAC. A model-estimation method using random minimal subsets, checking consistency of the
remaining data and rejecting outliers.
Inlier. An observation whose model residual is within a threshold; this does not yet establish that
the correspondence is correct.
Optical flow. A field of apparent image displacements between times; by itself, it does not define
metric body velocity.
Point cloud. A set of spatial coordinates of measured or reconstructed surfaces, expressed in a
common frame and physical units.
Voxel downsampling. Reduction of cloud density by combining points within spatial cells; cell
size determines the loss of detail.
Surface normal. A direction perpendicular to the local tangent plane; its estimate depends on the
neighbourhood and may be ambiguous at an edge.
ICP. Iterative refinement of a transform through cloud correspondences; it requires suitable
initialisation and may converge to an incorrect solution.
Segmentation. Assignment of a label to each pixel; distinct from whole-image classification and
detection of rectangular object regions.
Transfer learning. Use of pretrained weights while adapting selected layers to a new task and
dataset.
IoU. The ratio of intersection area between predicted and reference regions to their union area; the
rule for empty regions is specified separately.

Equipment and setup for this month

Use existing equipment
MacBook Pro M4, Jazzy in UTM, M13 data and geometry, a ruler, callipers and mounting hardware.
Recorded RGB-D and synthetic data are suitable for algorithm work. TUM RGB-D: File Formats
specifies depth scale, timestamps and the ground-truth format; saved images can be analysed on
macOS.

Purchase before recording your own data
Select 1 RGB-D camera providing metric depth and RGB, accessible intrinsics and extrinsics,
timestamps, a mask of missing and invalid depth, and a driver for the selected Jazzy/Ubuntu
ARM64 environment. Orbbec Gemini 2 is one candidate whose compatibility still requires
confirmation. Before ordering, check the exact model, firmware, SDK branch and ARM64 support
against the official Orbbec ROS 2 table. Separately verify USB in UTM using an available sample or
a confirmed configuration.
Prepare 1 suitable USB data cable and 1 stable mount; use a powered hub only if testing
establishes a need. Make 1 flat calibration board and measure its square size. Choose range and
field of view for the workbench and scene, rather than maximum specification values. If
compatibility is unconfirmed, continue with recordings and defer the purchase.

Install now
Install OpenCV and Open3D in a separate Python environment. Open3D: installation and platforms
- select a wheel for your Python version and architecture; open3d-cpu targets x86_64 Linux. If no

In the Ubuntu guest, configure the camera ROS driver and USB access according to the specific

fix a small backbone, head and weights. The Mac M4 is not a CUDA device; purchasing a GPU or

СтраницаPage 215 · Motion fundamentals: from pixel to target
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M14  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Motion fundamentals: from pixel to target

Required: why a visible point is not yet a leg target
A pixel defines a ray rather than a unique point: without depth, distance along that ray remains
unknown. After reconstructing XYZ, you need the camera's pose on the robot and the body's
position and orientation at image time. Check the prerequisite: explain the difference between
rotating a vector and translating a point, and label the optical axes C and body axes B.

Model and worked example
Use a rectified image without distortion. u,v are pixels; fx,fy,cx,cy are parameters in pixels; Z is
depth along the optical axis in metres, not range along the ray. Then X=(u−cx)Z/fx, Y=(v−cy)Z/fy.
With fx=fy=600, cx=320, cy=240, (u,v)=(370,240) and Z=1.2 m, we obtain p_C=(0.1; 0; 1.2) m.
For an error of 1 pixel in u and exactly known Z, the transverse error is δX=Z·δu/fx=0.002 m. A
coordinate-frame rotation preserves the length of this error vector; depth and extrinsic-parameter
errors are added separately. This is how pixel noise becomes uncertainty in a future movement.
In this example the camera faces forwards: its X points right, Y down and Z forwards; B has x
forwards, y left and z up. Therefore R_BC(X,Y,Z)=(Z,−X,−Y). The camera centre is t_BC=(0.2; 0;
0.3) m: p_B=R_BC p_C+t_BC=(1.4; −0.1; 0.3) m. Thus the object is to the right of the body, not the
left; camera depth is not height above the floor.
At image time, let the body have yaw=π/2 and p_WB=(1; 2; 0) m in world frame W. Then
p_W=R_WB p_B+p_WB=(1.1; 3.4; 0.3) m. In homogeneous notation, T_WC=T_WB T_BC: the
rightmost transform acts first. If the camera is on a moving link, T_BC depends on the joints; when
the body moves, use transforms at measurement time.

Two exercises within the existing laboratory
1. In Task 5, save three points: on the optical axis, to its right and below it. Draw frames C, B and W
and tabulate coordinates; check the inverse path W → C and reprojection. For synthetic data, set
computational tolerances of 10⁻⁶ m and 10⁻⁶ pixels. Z≤0 and missing or invalid depth must cause
rejection; they are not points at the origin.
2. Keep the object fixed and move the body 0.1 m along its x-axis without rotation. In C, Z is now
1.1 m and u≈374.55; the world point must remain unchanged. Substitute the old body position and
orientation and demonstrate a 0.1 m error. Save replays of both variants and explain how a timing
error displaces a proposed grasp point or foothold; reachability and load-bearing capacity are
checked later.
Time accounting: 1 hour from sessions 5-6 for coordinate frames and formula derivation; 2 hours
from 51-52 for these checks as a concrete implementation of Task 5. This remains within the
original 75 hours, with no new equipment or separate project.
Assigned reading: Lynch/Park, Modern Robotics §3.3.1 - composition and inverse transforms;
Tedrake, Geometric Pose Estimation: Representations for geometry - depth, clouds and coordinate
frames. Compare the camera equations with Task 1.

СтраницаPage 216 · Monthly outcome: where the robot is
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M15  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Monthly outcome: where the robot is

M15 • 19 Dec 2027 - 20 Jan 2028 • 75 hours

Compare motion-based position estimation, localisation on a known map and joint reconstruction of
a map and trajectory. Deliver a reproducible setup for 2D and visual SLAM, a trajectory-error table
and an analysis of conditions that make estimates unreliable. This introduces global navigation for
the future walking robot; a complete global-navigation implementation does not become a
prerequisite for stable walking.

Connecting the body, legs and camera
The robot moves its body, measures motion with an IMU, observes surfaces with a camera and
sometimes knows its support positions. Wheel odometry uses wheel geometry; leg odometry uses
kinematics and an assumption of stationary contact; visual odometry uses an image sequence;
inertial odometry integrates angular velocity and acceleration. For each source, record an
assumption that can fail: slip, loss of contact, lack of texture or sensor bias.

What to bring from earlier modules
You need transformation matrices, a basic EKF, ROS 2 tf/rosbag, RGB-D loading and the M14
understanding of ICP. Check the yaw sign, quaternion component order, time units and
camera-to-body transform. If these checks fail, first correct them using three known positions and
orientations. Do not try to compensate for a coordinate-frame error by tuning filter noise.

Minimum experimental setup
The main 2D experiment uses a short simulator recording containing LaserScan, odometry, IMU
and exact ground truth. Use one route: a straight section, a turn, a return to the start and a
repetitive corridor. For the visual method, use an RGB-D sequence from the same simulator or a
TUM recording with a reference trajectory. If the scenes differ, compare failure causes and
normalised measures. Incomparable ATE values do not establish that one sensor is more accurate
than another.
Continue in Ubuntu 24.04 and ROS 2 Jazzy. Use compatible versions of slam_toolbox and the
chosen visual method; save versions and parameters. You do not need to write a second complete
SLAM system from scratch: integrate an existing baseline or build a small pose graph from RGB-D
odometry and verified loop closures. Save a map, trajectory and quantitative evaluation; an RViz
visualisation alone is insufficient.

СтраницаPage 217 · Organising 75 hours and comparing methods
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M15  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Organising 75 hours and comparing methods

Time allocation
1-20: odometry, coordinate frames, EKF and error growth; 10 hours of analysis and 10 of practice.
21-40: occupancy grids, inverse sensor models, scan matching and AMCL; 10+10. 41-60: pose
graphs, nonlinear least squares, covariance and loop closure; 10+10. 61-75: ATE/RPE, degraded
data, LiDAR-versus-vision comparison and acceptance; 5+10. Total: 35 hours of theory and
analysis and 40 of practice.
Each 10-hour theory block comprises five 2-hour sessions; split the final 5 hours as 2+2+1. Place
four 10-hour practicals in Sunday work intervals or divide them without increasing the total time.
The numbers below denote module study hours. Overlapping module-boundary dates do not
double the available time; retain holidays, rest and separate integration checkpoints from the main
roadmap.

Fix the protocol before running algorithms
Save the sequence duration and boundaries, input sensors, frequencies, exact reference-trajectory
source and map resolution. State whether the algorithm knows the initial position and orientation.
Ground truth is only for error calculation; SLAM must not receive it through an accessible
coordinate frame. Accidentally supplying ideal odometry invalidates the experiment.
Create bags/manifest, configs/lidar, configs/visual, trajectories, maps, evaluation and failures
directories. For each run, save run_id, random-number seed, commit, noise parameters, data and
trajectory-alignment method. Include matched timestamps, excluded intervals and the
tracked-route fraction in evaluation, alongside aggregate metrics. Otherwise, a method that loses
half the route can appear more accurate than a reliable baseline.

Experiment without searching every combination
Change one parameter class at a time: odometry noise, scan dropouts, initial offset or loop-closure
threshold. Use three interpretable levels and retain one route. Tune on a separate sequence and
evaluate the final result on a held-out one. You do not need to study all of Nav2: use only
localisation and the map in M15. First verify visual SLAM on a short valid recording, then on one
degraded-data episode; leave analysis time after installation.

СтраницаPage 218 · Odometry and EKF: estimating motion with
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M15  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Odometry and EKF: estimating motion with
uncertainty

Essential concepts
Dead reckoning accumulates small displacements: for a planar body, x_new = x + v·cos(yaw)·dt,
y_new = y + v·sin(yaw)·dt, yaw_new = yaw + w·dt. Here v is in m/s, w in rad/s and dt in seconds.
This discretisation suits a teaching calculation with small steps; for rapid turns, check the midpoint
method or exact model integration. Bias is a constant offset, whereas noise is a varying deviation;
they affect the trajectory differently.
In odom, the local trajectory should remain continuous even as drift accumulates. The map frame
allows global map-based correction. Study the map → odom → base_link chain and the sensor's
fixed pose relative to the body. One agreed source must publish each transform. A jump in the
global estimate must not silently become a jump in the local controller's command.

Task 1. Body drift on a closed route
Generate a square trajectory with stops and saved true positions and orientations. Separately add
velocity noise, a constant yaw-rate bias and slip on one turn. Integrate odometry and plot error
against time and distance. Output: three trajectories and a parameter log. Test zero noise, dt=0
and timestamp discontinuity; no motion must mean no progress along the route.

Task 2. Fuse measurements and check covariance
Use state [x,y,yaw], a motion model and periodic absolute position measurements in simulation.
Write out prediction and correction steps, residual and covariance. Implement a compact EKF or
adapt a verified example from earlier modules; compare with configured robot_localization on ROS
data. Do not count the same information twice: position and velocity derived from the same
encoder are correlated.
Output: the estimate, uncertainty ellipses and an innovation plot. Test missing absolute
measurements, an anomalous jump and an artificially small R. For the leg, separately explain how
an incorrect stationary-foot assumption produces false confidence. The task criterion is explainable
error growth and filter responses, rather than a promise that EKF always improves the estimate. A
poor model or wrong units can make it worse than simple odometry.





































M15 • 19 Dec 2027 - 20 Jan 2028 • 75 hours                                                                       3 / 15
СтраницаPage 219 · Maps and scan matching: what
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M15  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Maps and scan matching: what
measurements provide

This week's topics
An occupancy grid stores the probability that a cell is occupied, not floor height. The inverse sensor
model uses a ray: cells before a reliable return were observed free, cells at the return are probably
occupied, and cells behind it remain unknown. Study log-odds L = log(p/(1−p)), which is convenient
for updates. Limit confidence accumulated from old observations. Define separate rules for missing
measurements and maximum range.
2D scan matching estimates a transform between scans or between a scan and a map. ICP
depends on correspondences and its initial estimate; a uniform long corridor poorly constrains
motion along its length. AMCL represents a distribution of possible positions and orientations as
particles on a known map: it localises rather than constructs a map. Compare a broad initial
distribution across the map with a precisely specified initial pose.

Task 3. Build a map from known poses
Input: 200-500 simulated LaserScan messages and true poses, available only to this reference task.
Transform laser points into the world, update free cells along rays and occupied cells at endpoints.
Output: a grid, an occupied/free/unknown legend and the resolution setting. Check one ray and a
wall by hand; do not mark the unseen side of a wall as free. Repeat with twice the cell size and
compare wall thickness.

Task 4. LiDAR recording and localisation
Run slam_toolbox on the same route with ordinary odometry; save the pose graph and map. Then
stop mapping and localise on the fixed map using AMCL or a supported localization mode. Do not
run two map→odom publishers simultaneously. Save launch and config files, two trajectories, the
map and a list of TF checks. Compare with your reference map from Task 3.
Test an incorrect initial pose, loss of 20% of scans and a laser rotation in the extrinsics. For scan
matching, create a small pair with a known displacement and measure transform error, then use an
ambiguous corridor pair. Separate mapping error from localisation error on an already known map
in the report. Successful loop closure does not establish correct local geometry along every section.

СтраницаPage 220 · Pose graphs: constraints, loop closure and
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M15  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Pose graphs: constraints, loop closure and
false links

Sections to study
A graph vertex represents the robot's position and orientation, or pose; an edge represents
measured relative motion or another constraint. Optimisation adjusts poses to reduce weighted
residuals. Weights relate to uncertainty: using identical numbers for metres and radians without
justification creates an arbitrary trade-off. Fixing one initial pose removes ambiguity in overall
translation and rotation, but adds no measurements of the surroundings.
Loop closure recognises a previously visited place and adds a constraint. The optimiser reconciles
constraints but does not verify correspondence truth. A robust loss reduces the influence of large
residuals; it does not replace geometric verification and may fail to protect against a consistent
false closure. Treat covariance as a local estimate within model assumptions, rather than the
probability that the whole map is correct.

Task 5. A small graph you can understand
Create 20-30 planar poses around a square, noisy odometry edges and one correct loop-closure
edge. Use GTSAM Pose2 or a small educational solver. Show initial and optimised trajectories,
residuals and the method used to anchor the common coordinate frame. Save graph.json, noise
settings and plots before and after optimisation. Test zero noise and a disabled prior; explain why
absolute coordinates are undetermined without an anchor.

Task 6. False loop closure in a similar corridor
Add an edge between different but visually similar places. Compare ordinary squared error, a
robust loss and geometric rejection of the incorrect link before optimisation. Measure ATE at the
same poses and changes in residuals of correct edges. Save three results and the loop-acceptance
rule. Show a case where the robust loss still allows map deformation; do not promise a universal
threshold.

A minimal visual-odometry experiment
Bring calibration, RGB-D recordings and pair-registration checks from M14; in M15, assemble a
short RGB-D odometry sequence. Build a graph of successive poses and add one revisit confirmed
by image or cloud geometry. Use ground truth only for error evaluation. You may use an existing
compatible visual SLAM system. If a loop closure is specified manually to test the optimiser, label it
as a manual constraint: that experiment does not test automatic revisit recognition.

СтраницаPage 221 · Evaluation: trajectory, map and tracking loss
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M15  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Evaluation: trajectory, map and tracking loss

What ATE and RPE measure
ATE compares estimated absolute poses with a reference after explicitly described alignment. For
translation, report the RMSE of distances in metres in the usual formulation. RPE compares relative
displacements between pairs of poses separated by a fixed interval, revealing local drift. Specify
the interval in seconds, frames or metres and the timestamp-matching rule. Different intervals
answer different questions and produce incomparable values.
For metric RGB-D and LiDAR, do not rescale trajectories during alignment except in a separate
scale-error study. For a monocular baseline, state whether Sim(3) was used and which errors scale
fitting conceals. Alongside aligned error, save the original trajectory, route coverage and the time
tracking was lost. Do not evaluate only a successful short fragment while omitting the lost return
leg.

Task 7. An evaluator you can trust
Create a reference trajectory, a copy with a known translation, a copy with slow drift and a
time-shifted sequence. Run evo and independently calculate several pairs. Save commands,
alignment settings, matched timestamps and an ATE/RPE table. After SE(3)/SE(2) alignment,
overall translation and rotation should disappear while local drift remains. Specify the maximum
timestamp mismatch and show the number of rejected poses.

Task 8. Map quality and robustness
In the simulated scene, compare reconstructed walls with known geometry: distances to reference
lines, passage width and occupied/free-cell fractions in a predefined region. Do not count unknown
as free. For each pipeline, report latency, tracking-recovery time and route coverage. Choose
tolerances from map resolution and the clearance required by the future body; this is a teaching
requirement, not a regulatory standard.
Offset sensor and odometry timestamps, then change the laser extrinsics; repeat with algorithm
parameters unchanged. Explain why a synchronisation error can resemble a scan-matching error.
Add a blurred section and loss of texture to the visual experiment. The overall conclusion must
identify operating conditions for each method rather than declare one algorithm best under every
condition.

Laboratory comparison of LiDAR and visual
SLAM

Inputs and outputs
Inputs: recording manifest, calibration/frames and configs for three variants - odometry only, LiDAR
SLAM and visual RGB-D SLAM. Outputs: trajectory with timestamp and pose fields, tracking status,
a map or aligned keyframes, a loop-closure log and metrics. A separate error-evaluation
programme receives the reference trajectory. For each variant, state available sensors, whether
the starting pose is known and the source of metric scale.

Task 9. One question set for three methods
1. Select a valid sequence and a held-out difficult route. 2. Check TF and time bases without
running SLAM. 3. Compute odometry alone. 4. Run the LiDAR variant and save the map and graph.
5. Run the visual method with fixed parameters. 6. Evaluate matching available intervals and full
coverage separately. 7. Repeat with one fault. 8. Assemble a report explaining the causes of
differences.
If the camera and laser were recorded in the same simulator, compare identical
reference-trajectory sections. If RGB-D comes from TUM, create two tables: metrics within each
dataset and a qualitative comparison of failures. Claims such as "LiDAR is N times more accurate"
are invalid for different routes. Tabulate comparison conditions so scene differences remain
explicit.

Task 10. Robot response to lost localisation
Create a component that receives pose with status, timestamp and uncertainty. For stale data or
lost tracking, it must output localization_unavailable and reject new global goals in simulation. Do
not restart the running local stability loop. Recovery requires a new valid estimate, reconciliation of
map/odom and an explicit return transition. Save an event log and a missing-data test.

Deliverable package
The README must describe recording processing and error evaluation; the manifest documents
data provenance; configs contains every parameter. Include ATE/RPE with definitions, map quality,
latency, route coverage and failure scenarios in the report. Add a TF-tree snapshot and example
input/output messages. For the future hexapod, state the applicability boundary: global localisation
helps follow a route but does not validate leg stability or contact reliability.

СтраницаPage 223 · Eight failure and sensitivity scenarios
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M15  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Eight failure and sensitivity scenarios

Faults to introduce
S1 - No absolute observations: disable EKF corrections and loop closures along part of the route.
Expect growing drift and increased uncertainty if the model accounts for it. Compare with zero
noise and check for false confidence despite nonzero error. S2 - Slip: add odometry error on one
turn. Save the fault time, local RPE and correction after observing the surroundings.
S3 - Corridor ambiguity: walls repeat and transverse structure is sparse. Measure errors along and
across the corridor separately; a small ICP residual does not yet establish correct displacement. S4
- False closure: connect similar places with an incorrect edge. Evaluate map deformation, ATE and
changes in correct-edge residuals with and without a robust loss.
S5 - Kidnapped robot: in simulation, instantaneously move the body elsewhere on the known map
without a corresponding odometry change. Test AMCL with local and broad initial distributions and
measure recovery time under the chosen criterion. Manual reinitialisation must not be called
automatic relocalisation. S6 - Data loss: remove scans or images for 1 and 3 seconds. The
consumer must detect estimate age and unavailability.
S7 - Time and extrinsics: shift sensor timestamps by one period, then separately rotate the sensor
by a known angle. Compare errors on straight sections and turns. S8 - Image degradation: blur, a
smooth wall or a covered camera. Measure the fraction of tracked images and test recovery; errors
on the surviving images alone are insufficient. Do not remove failed sections before preparing the
final table.

Choosing levels and conclusions
Fault levels are illustrative parameters chosen to suit the measurement frequency and scene scale;
they are not allowable limits for a physical robot. Change one cause per experiment and preserve
the seed and original bag. Evaluate sensitivity at three levels; state whether improvement repeats
or occurs only on one route.
Each scenario needs an expected-result file, actual trace, numerical criterion or manual-check rule,
and a decision: handled, detected without recovery, or undetected. The last outcome is acceptable
as an established limitation of this introductory SLAM work, but a consumer must not present an
unreliable pose estimate as current and accurate.

Sessions 1-40: motion, the filter and the map

Hours 1-10: theory in 2-hour sessions
1-2: wheel, leg, visual and inertial odometry models, with one failure-prone assumption each. 3-4:
planar-motion integration and bias; calculate a turn and return by hand. 5-6: map/odom/base_link,
transform directions and TF sources. 7-8: EKF prediction and correction, Q/R and measurement
correlation. 9-10: ground truth, error units and the Task 1 protocol. Record these principles as
implementation assumptions.

Hours 11-20: practical 1
11-12: square-route generator and an error-free check. 13-14: Task 1 - noise, bias and local slip.
15-16: Task 2 - EKF, covariance and innovation plots. 17-18: process a ROS recording, compare
with the chosen filter and check TF. 19-20: missing measurements, excessively small R and an
error report. Understand the source of drift before connecting SLAM.

Hours 21-30: theory in 2-hour sessions
21-22: occupancy, free/occupied/unknown and log-odds. 23-24: inverse laser-ray model, resolution
and invalid range. 25-26: scan matching, ICP, local minima and the corridor. 27-28: particles,
measurement likelihood and AMCL resampling through an understandable example. 29-30:
slam_toolbox modes, the difference between a map and a graph, and state saving. Select the
manual parameters needed for your scenario.

Hours 31-40: practical 2
31-32: Task 3, a map from known poses and a manual ray check. 33-34: a lower-resolution map
and the unknown/free distinction. 35-36: Task 4, process the LiDAR SLAM recording and save the
graph and map. 37-38: localisation on a fixed map, initial offset and TF transform sources. 39-40:
corridor, scan loss and a comparison report against the reference map.
By this stage, there should be three clearly understood files: a reference map for evaluation, a
reconstructed map and pose estimates. Identify their roles in filenames and the manifest. If map
processing continues after playback stops, allow the queue to finish within the practical and record
processing lag; do not compare one method's partial result with another's completed result.

Completion criteria and data for the planner

Acceptance checks
Quantitatively compare at least uncorrected odometry and SLAM on one sequence. Add a separate
visual method with a map or keyframes and failure analysis. For ATE/RPE, state definitions, units,
interval, alignment method, matched-sample fraction and route coverage. Tabulate available
sensors, reference data and condition differences. Incomparable scenes cannot establish sensor
superiority.
Find and explain examples of drift, degenerate scan matching, false closure, timing error and
sensor loss. Save settings for the valid run and modified versions. The map must contain
resolution, origin and frame_id, with unknown/free/occupied distinguished. Recalculating errors
must not require manual trajectory edits. Any component using pose must respond to stale data
and unconfirmed recovery.

Self-check
1. How does map differ from odom, and who publishes their transform? 2. Why does leg odometry
fail during slip? 3. What happens with an incorrect dt? 4. Why can an excessively small R worsen
EKF performance? 5. How does an unknown cell differ from a free one? 6. Why does scan matching
constrain some motion directions better than others?
7. How does a false loop edge change the whole trajectory? 8. What does a prior fix, and what does
it not measure? 9. How can ATE improve after failed frames are removed, and why does this distort
quality evaluation? 10. Why calculate RPE at several intervals? 11. When is scale correction
permissible? 12. Why does good SLAM not establish hexapod stability?

Handover to M16
Pass on the map, coordinate-frame chain, start and goal in one frame, an example localisation
status and a data-age limit. Add two maps: one valid and one with a known error or a passage
through an unknown region. The planner must reject a task when the pose estimate is unavailable.
A map alone does not establish whether an area is suitable as a foothold.
Demonstrate a normal circuit, a section with odometry error, a false closure and missing data.
Show numbers, then explain one failure cause without saying merely "poorly tuned". Frame the
final conclusion in terms of operating conditions: "in this scene, with these sensors and
parameters". Global navigation broadens the topics covered; local body and leg control can
develop using other state-estimation sources.

Assigned reading: a focused route through
the sections

The literature is mainly in English; the programme and definitions are also in English. Read the
selected sections before the relevant task, rather than entire books. Core reading is included in the
existing 35 analysis hours; consult references as needed.

Core reading
S. Thrun, W. Burgard, D. Fox, Probabilistic Robotics (2005), accompanying teaching
materials. Authors' slides: kalman.ppt - Bayesian filtering and EKF; mapping-occupancy.ppt -
occupancy updates; slam.ppt - joint map and trajectory estimation. Before Tasks 1-4, record states,
observations and assumptions. The MIT Press book provides detailed reference material on these
topics.
F. Dellaert, Factor Graphs and GTSAM: A Hands-on Introduction, teaching notes. Author's
GTSAM notes. §1 Factor Graphs, §3 Robot Localization, §4 PoseSLAM; for the prior example,
§2.2-2.4. In Tasks 5-6, build a small Pose2 graph with a prior and relative constraints, then add one
false closure.

Reference reading
R. Szeliski, Computer Vision: Algorithms and Applications, 2nd ed. (2022). Author's book.
Ch. 11 Structure from motion and SLAM: selected material on pose estimation, bundle adjustment
and SLAM. For visual experiments in Tasks 5-7, connect correspondences, camera motion, error
accumulation and map correction.

Documentation for your experiment
ROS REP-105 - odom, map, Relationship between Frames. In Tasks 1-2, explicitly assign each TF
source and the location of global correction.
slam_toolbox - Parameters, Localization and serialization. For Task 4, learn to distinguish a saved
map image from a graph that can support continued operation.
evo: Metrics - Absolute pose error, Relative pose error, pose relation and alignment. Before Task 7,
choose units, time association and permissible trajectory alignment.

Minimum outcome from reading
Explain using your own route: where odom drifts, how map corrects global error, what connects two
poses in the graph, and why a plausible-looking map can conceal a false closure. Downloading
large amounts of KITTI and writing a second full SLAM system from scratch are not required.
