СтраницаPage 228 · Terms and definitions
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M15  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Terms and definitions

Localisation. Estimating the robot's position and orientation relative to a known coordinate frame
or map using available measurements.
Odometry. Estimating relative motion from successive measurements; accumulated error usually
grows without external correction.
SLAM. Joint estimation of trajectory and map, linking motion uncertainty to uncertainty in
observed objects.
Prior. Information about the state before incorporating the current measurement; it may come
from a motion model or initial condition.
Likelihood. A function describing the probability of an observation for a given state and sensor
model; by itself, it is not a state distribution.
Posterior. The state distribution after combining prior information and a measurement under the
adopted probabilistic model.
EKF. A filter that approximates nonlinear models through local linearisation and represents its
estimate by a mean and covariance.
Innovation. The difference between a measurement and its prediction, interpreted with the
uncertainty of both prediction and sensor.
Covariance. A matrix of variances and joint deviations of estimate components; its units depend
on products of the corresponding component units.
odom frame. A local frame with a continuous trajectory that can gradually drift relative to the
surrounding world.
map frame. A global map frame that allows correction jumps when accumulated drift in the local
estimate is detected.
Occupancy grid. A map of spatial-cell occupancy probabilities; an unobserved cell must differ
from one confirmed free.
Log-odds. The logarithm of the probability ratio between an event and its absence; convenient for
occupancy updates.
Scan matching. Estimation of a transform from spatial measurements; it may be ambiguous with
sparse or repetitive geometry.
Pose graph. A representation of a trajectory as pose vertices and constraints between them,
obtained from motion or repeated observations.
Factor. A local likelihood or cost function relating a subset of unknown variables to a specific
measurement or condition.
Loop closure. A constraint between the current and a previously visited place, capable of
correcting drift if the correspondence is recognised correctly.
Gauge freedom. Ambiguity in the overall pose under relative constraints; removed by anchoring
or an absolute observation.
ATE. Error of estimated poses relative to reference poses after explicitly specified alignment; it
depends on time association and the selected component.
RPE. Relative-motion error between pose pairs over a declared temporal or spatial interval;
characterises local drift.

СтраницаPage 230 · Motion fundamentals: support and odometry
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M15  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Motion fundamentals: support and odometry

Required: how a leg measures body motion
When the body moves above a stationary foot, joint angles change even though world-frame
contact velocity is zero. Encoders measure relative leg geometry; body velocity can be derived by
adding leg kinematics and IMU angular velocity. Before deriving the equations, check foot FK and
the cross product: rotation produces a linear velocity ω×r that depends on the lever arm.

From position to a velocity constraint
W is the world, B the body and F a fixed material point on the foot. p_WF=p_WB+R_WB p_BF(q); q
contains only leg joint angles in radians. J_p=∂p_BF/∂q is the 3×n position Jacobian in B, so relative
foot velocity is J_p q̇. This is not the foot's complete world-frame velocity.
Let v_WB be the linear velocity of the B origin expressed in W, and ω_B the body angular velocity
expressed in B. Differentiating gives v_WF=v_WB+R_WB(ω_B×p_BF+J_p q̇). All linear velocities are
in m/s; ω_B is in rad/s. Only a stationary, non-slipping support gives v_WF=0, hence
v_WB=−R_WB(ω_B×p_BF+J_p q̇). Contact alone does not justify setting this velocity to zero.

Example with body rotation
At one instant, R_WB=I, p_BF=(0.2; 0; −0.3) m, ω_B=(0; 0; 0.5) rad/s and J_p q̇=(−0.04; 0; 0) m/s.
The rotational contribution is ω_B×p_BF=(0; 0.10; 0) m/s. This gives v_WB=(0.04; −0.10; 0) m/s.
Omitting rotation loses the lateral motion of 0.10 m/s, even though FK and encoders are correct.
If the same foot actually slips at v_WF=(0.02; 0; 0) m/s, the true v_WB=(0.06; −0.10; 0) m/s. The
incorrect zero-velocity assumption gives an x-error of −0.02 m/s. Several reliable supports allow
residual comparisons; a shared geometry error or simultaneous slip can bias estimates from all
legs.

Exercises and evidence of understanding
1. Add a short synthetic stance episode to Task 1: calculate world-frame velocity in two ways, by
differentiating p_WF and by summing the three terms. Save a table and a residual plot; halving the
finite-difference step should reduce error until rounding error dominates. Ground truth is available
only to metric calculation, not to the state estimator.
2. In Task 2, repeat the example with slipping and loss of contact. Save the innovation and
support-admissibility flag; disabling an unreliable constraint must be visible. Explain why
integrating velocities produces drift and does not by itself determine absolute position and
orientation in map.
Time accounting: 1 hour from 1-2 for the leg-odometry model; 1 hour each from 13-14 and 15-16
for examples within Tasks 1-2. The total remains 75 hours; do not add physical walking or a new
filter beyond these tasks.
Assigned reading: Lynch/Park, Modern Robotics §3.2.2 Angular Velocities and §5.1.2 Body
Jacobian. Distinguish the book's six-dimensional spatial velocity (twist) from the point-position
Jacobian used here.

СтраницаPage 231 · Monthly outcome: paths, trajectories and
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M16  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Monthly outcome: paths, trajectories and
behaviour

M16 • 21 Jan 2028 - 15 Feb 2028 • 75 hours

Prepare comparative planner tests and a small autonomous task with a behaviour tree. The robot
receives a goal, finds a valid path, builds a speed-limited trajectory along it and monitors
execution, explicitly responding when it cannot continue. This month's examples are a body route
among obstacles and a manipulator approach to an object. These foundations precede
foot-placement planning.

Three different questions
Search determines which states connect the start and goal. A geometric path q(s) describes a
configuration sequence without time. A trajectory q(t) adds time, velocity and acceleration. Task
logic decides when to plan, wait, cancel and recover. A* success does not mean an actuator can
execute the path; successful arm planning does not mean the object has already been grasped.

What to use from earlier months
Use the M15 map with unknown cells, M14 scene geometry, and link kinematics and actuator limits
from earlier modules. Check that start and goal use one frame and that angular and linear units are
consistent. The prerequisites are reading URDF, running ROS 2 actions, constructing a graph and
explaining a derivative. Review how a joint-angle trajectory produces rad/s and rad/s².

Two small experimental setups
Setup A is a 2D room map and a body with a finite planar footprint. You may use a simulated
wheeled base to learn Nav2. Setup B is a ready-made manipulator model in MoveIt 2, with a table
and a box. Choose one prepared package for each, compatible with Ubuntu 24.04 and ROS 2 Jazzy.
Do not build a complex robot model and a new environment from scratch this month.
The final package contains your Dijkstra/A* implementations, comparison of at least two methods,
a configuration-sampling experiment, trajectory checks, BT and FSM logs, and recovery scenarios.
Foothold planning, hexapod kinodynamics and contact optimisation belong to later specialisation.
Explain now why a circular body footprint and a free floor cell do not establish that a particular
multilegged step is feasible.

ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M16  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

75 hours: from the map to controlled
execution

Four work blocks
1-20: graphs, BFS, Dijkstra, A*, heuristics and costmaps; 10 hours of theory and analysis +10 of
practice. 21-40: configuration space, collision checking, PRM/RRT/RRT* and the MoveIt scene;
10+10. 41-60: time parameterisation, splines, velocity, acceleration and jerk limits; 10+10. 61-75:
FSM, BT, recovery, timeouts and MDP/POMDP foundations; 5+10. The total budget is 35 hours of
analysis and 40 hours of practice.
Use 2-hour sessions for the first three theory blocks; divide the last as 2+2+1. Sunday practical
blocks of 10 hours include implementation, measurement and reporting; breaks do not count as
study hours. The numbering below specifies study-hour order, not calendar dates.
Module-boundary dates may overlap; holidays, rest and separate checkpoints remain in the original
calendar without counting hours twice.

Repository structure
Store synthetic and input maps in maps/; algorithms and the common interface in search/; OMPL
settings in sampling/; MoveIt objects and robot parameters in scenes/; q,t files and limits in
trajectories/; the tree, FSM and adapters in autonomy/; and scenarios, seeds and results in
benchmark/. Tie every result to a map version and body footprint. After an obstacle moves, do not
silently continue using the old geometry.

One hypothesis per experiment
To test "A* expands fewer vertices", retain the same graph, cost and tie-breaking order. To test
"RRT* improves the path", compare time and cost under the same budget, including failed runs
with different seeds. To test "smoothing improves motion", recheck collisions: a spline can cut a
corner through a wall. First state the reason for the comparison, then choose the metric.
Finish GUI work by saving a machine-readable scene and launch commands. Do not rely only on
dragging a goal manually in RViz. Prepare a small reference example for each task that another
person can check without the complete setup: a known optimal path, a segment through an
obstacle, a deliberately over-fast trajectory or an expected state trace.

СтраницаPage 233 · Graph search and the cost of a body route
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M16  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Graph search and the cost of a body route

What to study
BFS finds the shortest path by edge count when edges have equal cost; Dijkstra handles
nonnegative costs; A* adds a heuristic estimate h of cost to the goal. For optimality, study
admissibility and consistency of h, vertex reopening and termination criteria. Manhattan distance is
suitable for a 4-connected grid with unit steps; recheck admissibility for different motions and
costs.
A costmap stores assigned movement costs, while an occupancy map stores occupied, free and
unknown cells. For a finite-size body, account for its footprint, or inflate obstacles by the
circular-model radius with a justified margin. Clearance must account for geometry and
uncertainty. Explicitly define unknown handling: absence of observations does not permit motion.

Task 1. Dijkstra and A* on a robot map
Create an open field, a U-shaped trap and two corridors with different costs. Implement a common
solve(start, goal, map) interface, path reconstruction and an expanded-vertex counter. Output:
path, cost, runtime, expansions and no_path status. Test start=goal, a goal inside an obstacle, an
unreachable goal and equal A*/Dijkstra cost with admissible h. Use BFS as a reference only for
equal edge costs.

Task 2. A narrow passage and a dynamic obstacle
Use a circular body model and a passage around a box. Build two costmaps for different footprint
sizes and compare passage availability. After planning, add an obstacle in the middle of the route.
Mark the old path stale, stop the simulated execution process and replan. Save map and plan
versions, the plan-invalidation log, and the new path or a correct rejection.
Check every segment against the current map; a diagonal must not pass between touching corners
of two occupied cells. Save a case where the body centre passes but the footprint hits a wall.
Explain the future distinction for a leg: the body-centre route does not define a contact sequence,
and height variation requires another state model. In M16, demonstrate this boundary and do not
call a 2D path a complete walking plan.

СтраницаPage 234 · Sampling-based search and the manipulator
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M16  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Sampling-based search and the manipulator
scene

Configuration space
Configuration q contains joint angles, body position or other system coordinates. A workspace
obstacle becomes a set of forbidden q values. Checking one endpoint does not establish the
validity of motion between points. Study joint limits, self-collision and collisions with the
environment and attached object. The configuration-space (C-space) metric must account for units
and periodic angles.
PRM builds a configuration network for repeated queries; RRT grows a tree; RRT* improves
connections to reduce cost as sampling grows. Probabilistic completeness and asymptotic
optimality hold under assumptions and a limiting budget; they do not guarantee a solution within
two seconds. A narrow passage may rarely be sampled. Post-search path simplification also
changes the result and requires checking.

Task 3. Compare sampling-based search
Start with a 2D point or disc model among rectangular obstacles in OMPL. Compare RRTConnect
with RRT* or PRM using equal time per query: at least 10 random-number seeds for three scenes.
Save the exact-solution fraction, time to first solution, length and minimum clearance; account for
PRM construction cost separately. Prepare configs, seed-list and a table of every run, including
timeouts. A missing solution must not be counted as a zero-length path.

Task 4. A MoveIt planning scene
Use a ready-made arm, table and box. Specify object dimensions, positions and orientations in one
coordinate frame; specify start and goal, and plan an approach in simulation. Then attach the
object to the gripper and replan. Save the scene, a valid path and a failure example. Check that the
attached object participates in collision checks and that its frame and scale are correct.
Separately check the path with sufficiently fine discretisation and compare with a coarse check: a
thin obstacle between waypoints must be detected. Document the limits of discrete checking;
without continuous collision checking, it is not a mathematical proof of no contact along the entire
continuous path. The future arm uses this setup to approach an object, while a future leg uses
similar checks for link motion.

СтраницаPage 235 · Trajectories: time, smoothness and actuator
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M16  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Trajectories: time, smoothness and actuator
limits

Core topics
Study linear interpolation, cubic and quintic profiles, and continuity of position, velocity and
acceleration. Jerk is the derivative of acceleration, in rad/s³ for a revolute joint. A geometric spline
may be smooth in parameter s but become infeasible after incorrect time parameterisation. Even
within velocity limits, a trajectory may require excessive torque; distinguish dynamic constraints
explicitly.
For a simple motion from q0 to q1, use q(t)=q0+(q1−q0)·s(t/T), where s(τ)=10τ³−15τ⁴+6τ⁵,
0≤τ≤1. Velocity and acceleration are zero at both endpoints. Study the derivatives: velocity scales
as 1/T, acceleration as 1/T² and jerk as 1/T³. This gives an understandable way to slow an
educational movement, but does not automatically check collisions or dynamics.

Task 5. A leg or finger joint profile
Specify q0,q1 and teaching limits in the configuration, explicitly labelling them as simulation
parameters. Calculate the profile for three T values, plot q,v,a,j and find the smallest tested T that
satisfies the limits with a margin. Output: trajectory.csv, plots, assumptions and a validator. Test
q0=q1, T≤0, non-numeric inputs and an excessively short movement. For a real actuator, obtain
limits from specifications and load tests.

Task 6. Check a path after smoothing
Take the Task 4 path, apply time parameterisation with an available MoveIt tool, and check the
complete result: joint limits, strictly increasing times, derivatives and collisions. Establish whether
the chosen library changes geometry during processing. Output: original and processed paths,
times and rejection reasons. Construct a corner near an obstacle where smooth interpolation
intersects it.
For an introduction to trajectory optimisation, focus on the formulation: variables are states and
controls; constraints are dynamics and obstacles; the objective is time, energy or smoothness.
Solve a small scalar example or study a worked solution without building a full optimiser. Selecting
path topology and continuously optimising a trajectory solve different parts of the overall task;
both outputs require checking.

СтраницаPage 236 · Autonomous behaviour: states and recovery
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M16  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Autonomous behaviour: states and recovery

Minimal task logic
Define idle, planning, executing, waiting, recovering, failed and completed states. For each, specify
inputs, actions, exit conditions and permitted cancellation. An FSM supports explicit transition
accounting; a behaviour tree supports reusable conditions and actions returning SUCCESS, FAILURE
and RUNNING. Study Sequence, Fallback, reactive condition checks and interruption of an
asynchronous action.
Recovery needs a cause and an attempt limit. For a stale map, refresh observations and replan;
endless retries do not make an unreachable goal reachable. Cancelling an active ROS action
requires acknowledgement and an unambiguous state, otherwise motion may continue after the
goal changes. Measure local timeouts with a monotonic timer; describe simulation time and
recording replay separately.

Task 7. A behaviour tree for a route
Build "check localisation → plan path → follow path", with a branch that waits for fresh data and
bounded replanning. First implement deterministic action stubs, then connect a Nav2 action in
simulation. Output: BT XML or code, a transition table and an event log. Test planner FAILURE,
endless RUNNING and user cancellation; configuration must bound the number of attempts.

Task 8. Measure recovery time
Block the path in simulation, then clear it; measure detection time, time to a new plan and time
until motion resumes. For a permanent obstacle, expect failed or waiting for the operator, rather
than a false completed. Output: a recording, BT settings, events and two plots. Do not transfer
commands from the wheeled Nav2 example directly to a walking body: it needs a separate
executor with contact checks.

MDP and POMDP through a concrete example
Describe a choice between a short unknown section, a detour and an inspection using state, action,
transition and reward. In a POMDP, the true state is hidden; decisions use a belief distribution
updated from observations. Tabulate two traversability hypotheses and update their probabilities
after a camera observation. Reinforcement learning is not required here. Account for map
uncertainty before permitting motion.

СтраницаPage 237 · Integration setup: plans have a validity
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M16  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Integration setup: plans have a validity
period

Request and plan requirements
Include request_id, current starting position and orientation, goal, frame_id, map_version, robot
model and limits in the request. The response contains exact/approximate/no_path/timeout status,
the path, its validity conditions and checking parameters. approximate status does not establish
goal attainment. Before accepting a trajectory, the executor checks map version, localisation
availability and whether the initial state is current.

Task 9. Connect search, trajectory and behaviour
1. Validate inputs. 2. Calculate an A* or MoveIt path for your setup. 3. Independently check
collisions. 4. Set motion timing and check limits. 5. Send the trajectory to the simulation executor.
6. Monitor map and status changes. 7. On a violation, block acceptance of the next segment,
cancel the action and move the BT into recovery. 8. Save the final state and its cause.
For the body route, use a path between two map points. For the arm, approach a pregrasp pose
and return to the initial state; the grasp cycle itself belongs to M17. A common validator checks
shared data requirements, but the setups have different geometry. Do not present the same point
list as a universal executor for wheels, legs and manipulators.

Task 10. Reproduce an asynchronous fault
Create this situation: plan A is delayed, the user has already requested B, and the old successful
response A then arrives. The executor must reject A using request_id and version, and the log must
show why. Repeat with delayed cancel acknowledgement and completion of the old action. Output:
a reproducible GUI-free test and an event sequence. This is an asynchronous race in robotics: a
mathematically correct path may belong to a task that is no longer current.

Final package contents
Save comparative tests under identical conditions with every seed, MoveIt and Nav2 scenes, path
and trajectory checks, the tree and FSM table, eight failure scenarios, and a README with
commands, versions and limitations. Two short videos must show normal execution and correct
recovery. Measure time from event logs rather than edited video. This software setup does not
validate the physical safety of an actuator or real workspace.

СтраницаPage 238 · Scenarios the planner must handle
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M16  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Scenarios the planner must handle

Geometry and data
S1 - start or goal inside an obstacle: return invalid_request before search and do not begin
execution. S2 - A passage narrower than the body footprint: a point path may exist, but reject the
body plan. Check the narrowest point by hand. S3 - A thin wall between waypoints: independent
collision checking must find the intersection; compare two checking resolutions.
S4 - An unknown strip across the map: forbid mode produces a detour or failure; allow is permitted
only as an explicitly labelled teaching experiment. Save both settings without silently changing
them after failure. S5 - A new obstacle during motion: cancel the old plan, increment version and
use the current scene for the new plan. Measure detection time and record the FSM response.

Timing and logic
S6 - An infeasible trajectory: shorten its duration until velocity or acceleration limits are violated.
The check must reject the result and identify the segment and measured quantity. Separately add
non-monotonic timestamps. S7 - Timeout and a stuck action: a stub returns RUNNING beyond the
limit. The tree must bound recovery attempts and finish with an understandable status. Record
attempts and waiting time even if a path is eventually found.
S8 - Cancellation and a late response: request B replaces A, then result A arrives. No segment of A
may be accepted after the change of current request is confirmed. Also test M15 localisation loss:
block new global goals, and do not mark an ended action successful merely because updates
stopped.

Metrics and comparison rules
For search, measure expansions, the number of expanded vertices; cost, the sum of specified edge
costs; and runtime, the duration of the selected code segment. For sampling methods, measure
exact-solution fraction, time to first solution, final cost, minimum clearance and number of collision
checks. Report timeout separately; show median time for successful runs together with success
fraction.
For the autonomous task, measure success fraction, recovery count, time to detect a violation and
build a new plan, and rejected stale-command count. State clocks, tick frequency and hardware.
Body-path length is the sum of segment lengths in metres. For a joint path, the sum of
angular-increment norms means something different: specify joint weights and do not compare it
with metres. Minimum clearance is calculated between geometric bodies at checked
configurations; state discretisation and units. A map may penalise wall proximity, so the shortest
path need not have the lowest cost. No collisions in a finite simulation set describes that set; it
does not prove their absence for every input, parameter and physical contact.

Acceptance: correct rejection is also a result

Required verification results
Compare at least two planners under one protocol; verify Dijkstra/A* cost on reference graphs. In
the sampling experiment, use multiple seeds, count timeouts and check the resulting path. The
MoveIt scene must include an obstacle and an attached object. Reject an infeasible trajectory with

The behaviour tree completes the task in a normal scene, recovers from a temporary obstacle and
ends its attempts when the goal remains unreachable. Cancellation works during RUNNING, and a
late result does not replace the current task. Logs connect map_version, request_id, plan and
execution. All eight scenarios are reproducible; launch instructions do not depend on the author's
manual GUI actions.

Self-check
1. When do BFS and Dijkstra produce the same cost? 2. How does an incorrect h remove A*'s
expected optimality? 3. Why does footprint size affect whether a path can be found? 4. How does
PRM usage differ from RRT? 5. Why does RRT* not promise an optimal path in fixed time? 6. What
does checking only waypoints miss?
7. How do v,a,j change when T doubles? 8. Why can a smooth spline collide with a wall? 9. How do
velocity constraints differ from torque constraints? 10. Why is RUNNING neither success nor failure?
11. How do you cancel an old task and reject its late response? 12. What additional information
does a POMDP require compared with a fully observed state?

Pass the arm scene, collision objects, pregrasp path, verified executor, limits and event log to M17.

СтраницаPage 243 · Terms and definitions
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M16  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Terms and definitions

Configuration q. A set of independent coordinates defining the robot's geometric arrangement;
velocities usually belong to an expanded state.
Configuration space (C-space). The space of all robot configurations; collisions between
geometric bodies define a forbidden region in this space.
Footprint. The planar projection of the area occupied by the robot, used in mobile-base planning
and passage checks.
Costmap. A discrete representation of obstacles and movement penalties; a cell's cost need not
be its occupancy probability.
Geometric path q(s). A configuration sequence parameterised by progress s; time, velocity and
acceleration are not yet specified.
Trajectory q(t). Motion specified over time, allowing calculation of velocities, accelerations and
actuator requirements.
Dijkstra. Shortest-path search with nonnegative edge costs, processing the smallest current cost
successively.
A*. Search selecting a node by the sum of accumulated cost g and the estimated remaining cost h.
Admissible heuristic. A remaining-cost estimate that never exceeds the true optimum; search
guarantees also depend on implementation and graph conditions.
PRM. A roadmap method using valid random configurations and checked connections between
neighbouring samples.
RRT. A search tree extended towards samples in the space; the basic algorithm aims to find a path
rather than optimise it.
Probabilistic completeness. A property in which the probability of finding an existing solution
approaches one as resources increase and assumptions hold.
Collision checking. Checking robot geometry for intersection with itself and the world; sparse
point checks may miss collisions between them.
State validity. Satisfaction of specified configuration, scene and task constraints; it does not
establish validity of an entire connecting trajectory.
Time parameterisation. Assignment of path progress as a function of time, accounting for
velocity, acceleration and other constraints.
Jerk. The time derivative of acceleration, expressed in m/s³ or rad/s³; describes how abruptly the
applied motion changes.
Behaviour tree (BT). A hierarchical structure executing actions and conditions that return
success, failure or ongoing-execution status.
Tick. A signal to evaluate a tree node; tick frequency determines the timeliness of condition
checking and action cancellation.
FSM. A finite state machine with explicit states and transitions driven by events or conditions;
defines permissible behaviour order.
Recovery. A bounded procedure following a detected failure, with a completion condition, retry
limit and a route to safe stopping.

Equipment and setup for this month

Use existing equipment
MacBook Pro M4, UTM with Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64, ROS 2 Jazzy, Gazebo Harmonic, and M14-M15
maps, scenes and recordings. The two teaching setups require simulated mobile-base and
manipulator models. No new hardware purchases are mandatory; do not order a physical arm,
wheeled base or additional actuators.

Install now
In the existing Ubuntu guest, install Nav2 navigation2/nav2_bringup, MoveIt 2 and OMPL with
dependencies for the Jazzy version in use. MoveIt: Binary Install specifies ros-jazzy-moveit for
Ubuntu 24.04; the official Nav2 repository is the starting point for package installation and
compatible bringup. Record package versions and arm64 availability; do not copy Rolling
commands without checking.
Install MoveIt 2 in M16 because the manipulator-scene laboratory runs here; reuse the stack in
M17. Initially use OMPL from MoveIt dependencies, adding a separate C++ benchmark build only
for metrics required by the task. Python bindings are not mandatory dependencies for your own
A*/Dijkstra implementation.
Use a BehaviorTree.CPP version compatible with Nav2; Reactive and Asynchronous behaviors
explains Sequence/ReactiveSequence and halt. A BT GUI editor is optional. Retain one RMW, the
RViz configuration and prepared demo packages; do not update the entire workspace merely for a
new documentation page.

Check the installation
1) In Nav2, send a reachable goal on a small map, then an unreachable one; check the action result
and cancellation. 2) In MoveIt, load a prepared model, table and box; obtain a path and reject a
collision. 3) Check availability of the chosen OMPL planners, exact/approximate statuses and
timeout. 4) Record RUNNING, tree cancellation and recovery, and final cessation of the command.
Test RViz and Gazebo in UTM with a separate small run: an installed package does not establish
working graphics. If problems occur, save console logs and paths for analysis; visual verification
remains open until the output is actually viewed. These simulation tasks do not need USB, but
reused physical peripherals still require their previous checks.
Reading and setup fit within the 75 hours. An onboard Pi/x86, GPU and physical arm kit belong to
later conditional stages; after M17, the separate OPT120 has its own CAD/BOM and single-finger
validation.

СтраницаPage 245 · Motion fundamentals: timing along a path
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M16  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Motion fundamentals: timing along a path

Required: why geometry is insufficient
The same path can be traversed slowly or abruptly. Configuration geometry determines collisions,
while velocity, acceleration and required torques also depend on time. Prerequisite: take one
revolute leg or finger joint, with q in radians, and explain q̇ and q̈ in rad/s and rad/s².

Two functions rather than one point list
A path q(s), 0≤s≤1, specifies configuration order; a monotonic s(t) specifies progress. The chain
rule gives q̇=q′(s)ṡ and q̈=q″(s)ṡ²+q′(s)s̈. The first acceleration term comes from path curvature
and the second from changes in the rate of progress. Thus smoothness of q(s) does not replace
checks of time derivatives.
For a straight joint-space path q(s)=q0+Δq·s, choose s(t)=3ξ²−2ξ³, ξ=t/T. Then q̇=(Δq/T)(6ξ−6ξ²),
q̈=(Δq/T²)(6−12ξ). Velocity is zero at both endpoints; acceleration there is nonzero and jumps
when transitioning to rest. The quintic profile in the existing Task 5 adds zero boundary
accelerations.

Numerical example and duration selection
Let q0=0, Δq=0.6 rad and T=2 s. Maximum velocity at t=1 s is 1.5Δq/T=0.45 rad/s. Maximum |q̈| at
the endpoints is 6Δq/T²=0.90 rad/s². With example limits of 0.30 rad/s and 0.60 rad/s², this profile
is too fast.
The velocity limit gives T≥1.5·0.6/0.30=3 s; the acceleration limit gives T≥√(6·0.6/0.60)=√6≈2.45
s. Thus this cubic profile requires T≥3 s. At T=3 s, the maxima are 0.30 rad/s and 0.40 rad/s²;
choose a larger T for a margin. This result applies to the chosen profile shape, not the globally
shortest time for any motion.
Foot velocity equals J_p(q)q̇ and varies with configuration; one joint limit does not specify constant
foot speed. Moreover, the torque needed to support weight does not disappear with slow motion.
After checking velocity and acceleration constraints, check dynamics, contacts and geometry;
calculating torque does not set the control mode of a position-controlled servo.

Two exercises in Tasks 5-6
1. Save q,q̇,q̈ for T=2,3,4 s in trajectory.csv. Compare analytical extrema with a dense grid and
numerical derivatives; check q(0),q(T), zero velocities and rejection of T≤0. Then use the same
validator on the Task 5 quintic profile: its maximum coefficients differ.
2. Take the arm path near the box: a monotonic change of time parameterisation alone preserves
path geometry, while waypoint-based path smoothing may change it. Show both versions and
repeated collision checking; include one correct rejection and a plot of the violated constraint.
Time accounting: 1 hour from 41-42 for the derivation; 1 hour each from 51-52 and 53-54 for the
numerical example and validator. Geometry checking remains within the existing 57-58. The
budget stays at 75 hours, with no additional setup required.
Assigned reading: Lynch/Park, Modern Robotics §9.1-9.2, part 1 - path and time; part 2 - cubic
and quintic time scaling and boundary conditions.

СтраницаPage 246 · Monthly outcome: a manipulator under
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M17  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Monthly outcome: a manipulator under
human supervision

M17 • 15 Feb 2028 - 19 Mar 2028 • 75 hours

Build a small, reproducible testbed for grasping and transferring an object. Treat it as an integrated
robotic system connecting kinematics, planning, operator actions, data, commands, updates and
engineering responsibility. The M17 deliverables are a simulated transfer of a simple object, a
study of repeatability and failures, an interface for selecting modes and cancelling actions, and a
documented assessment of threats and hazards.

Four areas of work
This month covers manipulation, human-robot interaction, ethics and cybersecurity, industrial
applications and teamwork. Allocate the manipulator work so that every topic receives attention. A
complex anthropomorphic hand, tactile skin and force-controlled grasping are not required here.
Under the curriculum, the advanced OPT block on hand mechanics and tactile sensors takes 120
hours after M17 and is separate from these 75 hours.

What to bring from M14-M16
From M14, use the object-observation format and the descriptions of coordinate frames and
uncertainty; from M16, use the prepared manipulator scene, collision checks, pre-grasp pose and
trajectory validation. In the main experiment, specify the object's position precisely in simulation to
distinguish manipulation errors from vision errors. Then deliberately offset the estimated position
and orientation. A complete vision-guided grasping system is outside this month's required project.

Testbed and working environment
Prepare an existing manipulator model with a simple parallel gripper, a table, a cube or cylinder,
and a target region. Work in Ubuntu 24.04 with ROS 2 Jazzy and a compatible MoveIt 2
configuration. You may additionally test your own mechanism once the baseline simulation
experiment works; rated limits and real contacts require separate tests. A cancel button in a
graphical interface does not, by itself, constitute a hardware emergency stop.
By the end of the month, explain why the manipulator might fail to reach its goal, who is authorised
to issue commands and how the operator knows the current mode. State which data are retained,
what happens when communication is lost and what must be checked before changing a limit. For
the future hexapod, the same questions concern body motion, leg contacts and handing control to
a human.

СтраницаPage 247 · 75 hours and a separate hand project
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M17  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

75 hours and a separate hand project

Four blocks
1-20: FK and IK, grasp coordinate frames, object transfer, contact and repeatability; 10 hours of
theory and analysis +10 of practice. 21-40: teleoperation, levels of autonomy, modes, operator
feedback and a small interface study; 10+10. 41-60: privacy, data errors, threat modelling,
authentication, encryption and updates; 10+10. 61-75: PLCs, industrial buses, standards,
requirements, verification and planning a team exercise; 5+10. Total: 35 hours of analysis and 40
of practice.
In the first three blocks, schedule reading in 2-hour sessions; in the last block, use 2+2+1. Divide
practical work into four Sunday blocks of 10 hours, or equal periods that suit your schedule. Page
dates follow the original curriculum, while step numbers indicate the learning workload.
Overlapping module boundaries, rest, holidays and separate checkpoints do not add hours; OPT120
is counted separately.

Keeping the scope manageable
Start with one robot, one object type and one scene, then introduce variations. Keep development
of custom motor control, vision and a physical hand outside this experiment. MoveIt plans the
geometric sequence of actions; assess contact and object retention using separate simulator
observations. A simplified object attachment demonstrates planning, but does not establish that
grasping force is sufficient.

Preparation in the first block
Create a model-description file: simulator and MoveIt versions, object dimensions, joint limits, table
position, coordinate frames and the source of the pose estimate. For each experiment, save run_id,
the random-number generator seed, parameters, initial object state and result. Provide observation
without issuing commands, manual control, plan execution and stopping. Maintain a shared log of
command_id, mode and actor, even while there is only one operator.
Working folders: manipulation/ for tasks and scenes; operator/ for the interface and study protocol;
evaluation/ for repeated experiments; review/ for hazards, threats and ethical decisions;
requirements/ for criteria and changes. Store secret keys and participants' personal data outside
the repository. In the report, distinguish observations, proposed causes and ways to test them: this
helps another engineering team understand the system.


































M17 • 15 Feb 2028 - 19 Mar 2028 • 75 hours                                                                         2 / 15
СтраницаPage 248 · Manipulation: poses, approach and contact
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M17  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Manipulation: poses, approach and contact

What to study
Review forward kinematics, FK: it determines end-effector position and orientation from joint
coordinates. Inverse kinematics, IK, solves the reverse problem; there may be several valid
solutions or none. Define the world, base, tool, object and grasp coordinate frames. Define the
grasp pose relative to the object and the pre-grasp pose as an offset along the approach direction.
Before connecting the planner, verify transform composition and inversion using three known
poses.
Transfer sequence: move into position → approach → close the gripper → confirm retention → lift →
transfer → lower → open → withdraw. Define geometric and logical conditions for each stage. The
attach operation in the planning scene changes the collision model, but does not measure contact.
When introduced to force and impedance control, establish how position control differs from
specifying a desired interaction; a complete force-control loop is studied separately.

Task 1. FK, IK and the grasp coordinate frame
Use an existing manipulator model and three reachable object poses. Specify the grasp offset,
calculate the tool pose and solve IK while checking joint limits and self-collisions. Calculate FK for
the solution and compare its position and orientation with the target. Save a table of poses,
solutions and rejection reasons. Test an object outside the workspace and a rotation of 180°; if no
valid IK solution exists, the limits must remain enabled.

Task 2. A complete grasp-and-transfer cycle
Use MoveIt Task Constructor or a compatible sequence of ROS actions. Save each stage and its
result, add the table and object to the scene, and check attached geometry during transfer.
Prepare a task description, configuration and reproducible demonstration. Separately verify that
the object reached the target region and was released, and that the arm withdrew: successfully
producing a plan without executing it must not count as task success.

Interpreting contact checks
For a physical simulation of retention, specify mass, friction and the gripper model; check whether
the object can fall. When using a simplified attach, label the mode a kinematic demonstration
(kinematic demo). Consider a virtual spring F=K·(x_des−x), with K in N/m, and a damper. Explain
why high stiffness and delay can increase contact forces. Specified forces and speeds are
educational parameters and do not replace checking rated specifications and conducting physical
tests.





























M17 • 15 Feb 2028 - 19 Mar 2028 • 75 hours                                                                         3 / 15
СтраницаPage 249 · Repeatability and operator interaction
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M17  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Repeatability and operator interaction

Task 3. Defining a successful transfer
Perform 10 runs with the same initial scene and 10 with small, predefined object offsets. Save
success status and failure stage, final pose, cycle time and retention state. Before the experiments,
specify the target region in metres and acceptable orientation. Present every result, mean error
and dispersion; if deterministic simulation produces identical results, explain why.
Repeatability describes how close results are under identical conditions; accuracy describes
closeness to a specified reference. An incorrect grasp offset can make the arm place the object in
the same wrong location every time: test this case. In separate experiments, introduce an incorrect
mass, friction or calibration offset and distinguish these causes. In a kinematic demonstration,
evaluate the plan and pose; such an experiment does not measure holding force.

Human-robot interaction (HRI)
Study direct teleoperation, assisted control, autonomous task execution and explicit transfer of
control. The operator needs the current mode, active goal, age of state data, reason for rejection
and available action. A mode error occurs when a person expects manual control while an
autonomous plan is active, or the reverse. Spatial interaction requires clearly indicated access
zones and the robot's future path; low speed alone does not demonstrate contact safety.

Task 4. Modes and operator intervention
Create a simple panel or CLI with view, manual, auto and stopped states. Include command_id and
mode in commands. Before a manual↔auto transition, complete or cancel the previous ROS action;
after stopped, the old queue must not resume automatically. Save the transition table, interface
and test log. Test a manual request during auto and a repeated start after communication loss.
Give the operator a scenario: position the gripper, start a transfer and stop it when the object is
wrong. Display the planned path and current stage; present debugging diagnostics separately. The
same principle applies to transferring control of gait: a human action must bring the system into a
clear state, otherwise competing commands may enter a shared topic.










































M17 • 15 Feb 2028 - 19 Mar 2028 • 75 hours                                                                         4 / 15
СтраницаPage 250 · Interface testing and privacy
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M17  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Interface testing and privacy

Task 5. Test the interface on a clearly defined task
Conduct a pilot study in simulation with two interface versions: for example, buttons alone and
buttons with explicit mode and state indications. Use the same task: start a transfer, notice an
intentionally incorrect goal and cancel the action. Explain the task and the data to be recorded to
the volunteer beforehand. Conduct this experiment without physical robot motion near a person. If
no participant is available, follow a predefined scenario yourself and state that no independent
study took place.
Prepare 3-5 attempts for each version, alternate their order and provide the same initial training.
Record the time until correct cancellation, mode errors, unnecessary actions and a brief answer to
“what is the robot doing now?”. Save the protocol, anonymised table and three observations. So
few attempts cannot establish statistical superiority; use them to correct specific unclear
indications.

Task 6. Camera data and model errors
List the testbed's data: table images, object pose, operator actions, identifiers and logs. For each
type, state its purpose and retention period, access rights and deletion method. In the
demonstration, retain only the necessary table region or use synthetic data. If people or personal
belongings appear in the frame, exclude unnecessary regions from the educational dataset in
advance; transfer to an external service requires an appropriate basis.
Return to the baseline CNN from M14 and compare errors under two lighting conditions and with
two object materials. Consider practical ethical questions: for whom and under which conditions
does the system perform worse, who knows its limitations and who can correct the result? If the
data contain no people, evaluate gaps in operating conditions and interface accessibility; there is
no basis here for demographic statistics. Good average performance does not establish
performance under unstudied conditions.

A documented decision
Write a short record: “question → alternatives → chosen decision → verification → remaining
limitation”. For example, events and anonymised errors suffice to measure cancellation time, so
operator video need not be retained. If pose-estimation confidence is low, request another
observation before grasping. Include these decisions and supporting results in the final engineering
review.
































M17 • 15 Feb 2028 - 19 Mar 2028 • 75 hours                                                                          5 / 15
СтраницаPage 251 · Command security: a threat model for your
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M17  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Command security: a threat model for your
testbed

Distinguish hazards from threats
A hazard is a potential source of harm, such as unexpected gripper motion. A cybersecurity threat
is the possibility of malicious interference, such as an unauthorised command or a substituted
update. A code error, malfunction or attack may lead to the same consequence. For each case,
record the cause, protection and test. Encryption does not correct an invalid joint limit, and a limit
switch does not determine access rights to video recordings.

Task 7. A threat model for your own testbed
Draw the testbed boundaries: operator, ROS and DDS network, control process, storage and update
channel. For each flow, identify the protected asset, sender, recipient, trust boundary and possible
violation. Analyse unauthorised commands, replay of old commands, calibration changes,
corrupted updates and log leaks. Prepare a table of 5-8 specific threats with priorities and owners
of protective measures.
In an isolated experiment, test commands containing an unknown actor, expired timestamp,
repeated command_id, NaN and out-of-range values. The expected result is rejection with an
explanation and no simulated motion. DDS certificates, identity and permissions govern admission
to the system and its channels; the application checks command freshness and prevents repeated
execution. Enabling SROS2 alone does not protect against all these threats.

Task 8. Minimum protection and an update
Study authentication, authorisation, encryption and trust in updates. On the local testbed,
configure minimum permissions for one publisher and subscriber using SROS2, or reproduce the
official example in a separate namespace. Test permitted and prohibited publication. Save a public
description of roles and permissions and verification logs; exclude private keys from the final
package.
Prepare an educational configuration-update scenario. A new version of the limits requires a
contents description, a hash and engineering review; a deliberately modified file must be rejected,
and the previous working version must be restored in simulation. Explain that a hash detects
change, but verifying authorship requires a trusted signature or channel. Parameters may change
during motion only through a defined state transition.

































M17 • 15 Feb 2028 - 19 Mar 2028 • 75 hours                                                                       6 / 15
СтраницаPage 252 · Industrial applications: the cell and its
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M17  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Industrial applications: the cell and its
requirements

What to understand at an introductory level
A PLC executes industrial cycle logic and processes inputs and outputs; the robot controller
controls drives and the programme; a supervisory computer may plan actions and exchange data.
An industrial bus connects devices and defines communication properties. Learn the purposes of
EtherCAT, PROFINET and CAN; implementing these protocols is outside this month's scope.
Distinguish ordinary control from separate protective functions.
ISO 10218 concerns industrial robots and their applications; ISO 13849 addresses safety-related
parts of control systems; IEC 61508 provides the context of functional safety and its lifecycle. In
M17, read official descriptions of scope and terminology, without claiming compliance with a
standard. Applicability, the required level and verification of a real cell require separate input data
and competent assessment.

Task 9. Sketch an educational cell
Draw the robot, table, object feed, presence sensor, operator panel and a notional PLC. Define a
ready/request/busy/done/fault state exchange with cycle_id and test it using software process
simulators. Save the diagram, I/O table and event sequence. Test a repeated request, a missing
part, communication loss and reset during busy. The done state belongs to a particular cycle_id: an
old event must not confirm processing of a new part.

Task 10. Requirements, changes and teamwork
Formulate 8-10 requirements: start conditions, acceptable scene, cancel behaviour, pose-estimate
age, operator rights, logging and rejection on recovery. For each, provide a criterion and a link to
its test. Change the grasp offset or speed and prepare a change request: reason, affected
requirements, checks and restoration of the previous version. Support engineering review with
data; label your own verification as self-review.
Plan how to gain teamwork experience: which part of the work can be submitted for review, which
questions to ask a control or mechanical specialist, and which small contribution to a robotics
project would demonstrate collaboration. Prepare a review package and a list of missing
experience, such as industrial equipment, initial hardware commissioning and working with
someone else's requirements. An educational testbed does not replace an internship or a verified
professional qualification.































M17 • 15 Feb 2028 - 19 Mar 2028 • 75 hours                                                                        7 / 15
СтраницаPage 253 · Eight checks for manipulation, the operator
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M17  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Eight checks for manipulation, the operator
and threats

Manipulator and interface
S1 - unreachable pose: IK or the planner reports failure, and the system does not enter executing.
S2 - the object touches the table during transfer: the collision model includes the attached object
and rejects the plan. S3 - incorrect grasp offset: the robot misses repeatedly, and the report
distinguishes repeatability from accuracy. In a physical simulation, add slipping; in a kinematic
demonstration, attach does not confirm retention.
S4 - mode change during auto: a manual request triggers cancel, waits for coordinated completion
and only then allows a manual command. Mode outputs are not mixed. S5 - loss of communication
or pose estimates: data age increases, and the task receives the defined stopped or uncertain
status. Network recovery does not start the old queue. Describe the simulator's actual response;
this experiment does not demonstrate a certified protective stop.

Commands, data and the cycle
S6 - repeated command or unknown actor: the application rejects the request without repeating
the cycle. Check command_id, mode and validity period separately from DDS participant
identification. S7 - configuration change: integrity checking detects substitution, the update is not
activated and the previous version can be reproduced. Separately state that without a trusted
signature, forged authorship remains possible.
S8 - late done from the previous PLC cycle: the new request has a different cycle_id, so the old
event does not count as success. Add an absent object after a claimed grasp: the hold-check stage
must report the corresponding failure. Inspect the final archive manually: it must contain only
necessary frames and events, without participants' personal data or secret keys.

Recording criteria
For each scenario, record the initial scene, triggering event, expected states, observed response,
timing and remaining risk. Justify pose and timing tolerances as parameters of the educational
task. This table does not define safe speeds for physical interaction with a person. The absence of
errors in 10 repetitions does not prove zero failure probability.
Indicate how each result is supported: simulation, logic or document review, or a required physical
test. Show the operator the reason for failure, whether motion has been cancelled and whether
restarting is possible. If the execution outcome is still unknown, state that explicitly: hidden
uncertainty prevents an accurate assessment of robot state.

ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M17  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Sessions 1-40: object transfer and the
operator

Hours 1-10: five sessions of 2 hours
1-2: review FK and IK, coordinate frames and grasp offset; calculate three transforms by hand. 3-4:
pre-grasp pose, approach, attach/detach and scene geometry. 5-6: transfer stages and criteria for
planning and execution. 7-8: contact, friction, fundamentals of force and impedance control, and
differences between kinematic and physical demonstrations. 9-10: repeatability, accuracy, test
protocol and simulation limitations. Prepare the scene for the practical session.

Hours 11-20: practical session 1
11-12: Task 1, reachable and unreachable poses with FK verification. 13-14: Task 2, initial stages
using Task Constructor or ROS actions. 15-16: complete transfer with the correct scene and
target-region checks. 17-18: Task 3, repeated trials and pose variations. 19-20: failures S1-S3,
grasp offset and cause analysis. If the physical grasp model is not ready, save the basic kinematic
demonstration and state its limitations explicitly; the remaining weeks are needed for other topics.

Hours 21-30: five sessions of 2 hours
21-22: teleoperation, automated assistance, autonomy and command authority. 23-24: mode FSM,
operator intervention, cancel and transition confirmation. 25-26: operator feedback, data age and
mode errors. 27-28: spatial interaction, zones and limitations of the educational simulation. 29-30:
pilot study, metrics, participant preparation and limitations of a small sample.

Hours 31-40: practical session 2
31-32: Task 4, a simple interface and mode table. 33-34: operator intervention during auto,
communication loss and command_id log. 35-36: Task 5, two interface versions and pilot attempts.
37-38: analyse events, cancellation time and mode errors; fix one identified problem. 39-40: repeat
the scenario and write a short HRI report stating its limitations.
If no volunteer is available, follow a previously written scenario yourself and list questions for
external testing. Study results must reflect the attempts actually conducted. A simple version can
use a CLI with prominent mode and state indications: this experiment focuses on making robot
control understandable.

ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M17  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Sessions 41-75: data, threats and project
handover

Hours 41-50: theory in 2-hour sessions
41-42: necessary data, privacy and retention periods. 43-44: machine-learning limitations,
incomplete data and responsibility for decisions; connection to M14. 45-46: hazards, cybersecurity
threats, protected assets and trust boundaries. 47-48: authentication, authorisation, encryption
and command-freshness checks. 49-50: update integrity, signatures, restoration of the previous
version and documentation of remaining risks.

Hours 51-60: practical session 3
51-52: Task 6, data inventory and checks across lighting conditions and materials. 53-54: Task 7, a
flow diagram and five specific threats. 55-56: test commands with repetitions, NaN and an
unknown actor; rejection logs. 57-58: Task 8, permitted and prohibited communication in an
isolated SROS2 example. 59-60: update and restore the previous version, inspect the archive and
review responsible engineering decisions together.

Hours 61-65: theory, 2+2+1
61-62: PLC, robot controller, industrial bus and cycle coordination; channel purposes. 63-64: official
scopes of ISO 10218, ISO 13849 and IEC 61508, requirements and supporting results. 65: change
management, engineering review and planning teamwork experience. Introductory hours cover
terminology and the limits of standards' applicability; a full compliance analysis requires separate
work.

Hours 66-75: practical session 4
66-67: Task 9, cell sketch, I/O and cycle coordination. 68-69: checks for cycle_id, missing parts,
communication loss and late done. 70-71: Task 10, requirements and a change request for one
parameter. 72-73: scenarios S1-S8, repeat the transfer after the change and restore the previous
version. 74-75: final materials package, demonstration and handover to OPT120 and subsequent
modules. The intervals total 75 hours.

How to reduce scope
If time is short, first remove the second object, complex contact model and interface decoration;
then reduce the number of configuration variants. Keep a reproducible experiment with one
manipulator, repeatability testing, operator intervention, the HRI study, threat and hazard
assessment, industrial diagram and a requirement with its test. Move hand development, tactile
sensors and force experiments to the separate OPT120 block, preserving M17 time for ethics and
teamwork.

СтраницаPage 256 · Acceptance checks and preparation for the
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M17  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Acceptance checks and preparation for the
hand project

Evidence for the four areas
Manipulation: scene, configuration, complete cycle or explicitly labelled kinematic demonstration,
FK and IK verification, and a table of repeated trials. HRI: modes, cancellation, indications and a
protocol for the participant study or self-conducted walkthrough. Ethics and cybersecurity: data
inventory, use decisions, threat model and results of isolated tests. Industrial applications: cell
diagram, I/O, requirements, change request and a plan to develop teamwork experience.
Prepare a README and a unified set of commands to reproduce the work. State in the report what
was measured physically, what was tested in simulation and what was considered only
theoretically. These experiments do not establish ISO/IEC certification, safe collaborative operation
or industrial readiness. Save observed outcomes for the eight scenarios, and supporting results or
a description of the remaining limitation for every significant protective measure.

Self-check questions
1. How does the tool pose differ from the object pose? 2. Why can IK have several valid solutions?
3. How does an attached object affect collision checking? 4. Why does attach not measure grasping
force? 5. How does repeatability differ from accuracy? 6. How does the operator know who
currently controls the robot?
7. What happens after cancel and communication loss? 8. How does a hazard differ from a
cybersecurity threat? 9. Why does encryption not replace limit checks? 10. What does a hash prove
about an update, and what does it not prove? 11. How does cycle_id prevent a false done? 12.
What external experience do you still need to work in a robotics team?

What to hand over to OPT120
Hand over coordinate-frame descriptions, the baseline arm model, scene with objects, grasp
parameters, reproducible action sequence, operator-intervention requirements and failure log.
With this foundation, the separate 120-hour block after M17 develops hand mechanics, tactile
perception, retention and physical testing. Its hours, equipment and criteria are accounted for
separately; a completed anthropomorphic hand is not an M17 deliverable.
For the walking robot, retain the rules for mode selection, command authority, command-freshness
checks and review of limits. They will be needed for external control of the body and legs. Before
use on a real robot, test these decisions with the relevant mechanics, loads and actuator
electronics. M17 is complete when you can explain and reproduce the entire testbed's operation,
including failure and recovery.



























M17 • 15 Feb 2028 - 19 Mar 2028 • 75 hours                                                                       11 / 15
СтраницаPage 257 · Assigned reading: manipulation and
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M17  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Assigned reading: manipulation and
human-robot interaction

Read the specified extracts before the corresponding tasks. Core reading explains principles;
reference reading supports implementation. Sources may be in English; prepare your explanations
and report in English. Reading is included in the 75 hours.

Core reading
1. Russ Tedrake, Robotic Manipulation (MIT, course notes). Basic Pick and Place: Monogram
Notation; Pick and place via spatial transforms. For Tasks 1-2: write down the object → grasp → tool

2. Christoph Bartneck et al., Human-Robot Interaction: An Introduction, 2nd ed., 2024.
Chapters Design, Research Methods, Robots in Society. For Tasks 4-6: one mode-indication
principle, a pilot-study protocol and a data decision; skim Spatial Interaction to define the
boundaries of the motion zone.
3. Ross Anderson, Security Engineering, 3rd ed. Ch. 4 Protocols; Ch. 6 Access Control. For

distinguish an unauthorised command, an old command and an incorrect but permitted parameter.

Mechanics reference reading
4. Kevin Lynch, Frank Park, Modern Robotics. §12.1.2 Contact Types; §12.2.1 Friction; §11.5
Force Control. For Task 3 and the transition to OPT120: distinguish touching, slipping and holding,
and position and force. Leave the full theory of force-based grasping to the separate block.

against your pinned Jazzy version. SROS2: README and tutorials on the Jazzy branch - participant

СтраницаPage 258 · Fundamental concepts in M17
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M17  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Fundamental concepts in M17

Pose. A body's position and orientation relative to a specified coordinate frame; both components
are needed to describe a grasp.
Grasp frame. A coordinate frame on the object relative to which the desired end-effector position
and orientation are specified.
Inverse kinematics (IK). Finding joint coordinates for a specified pose; a valid solution must
respect limits and be checked using forward kinematics.
Pre-grasp pose (pregrasp). Position and orientation before approaching the object; it defines
the approach direction and space for the open gripper.
Attached object. Geometry linked to the robot in the planning scene; this link alone does not
establish physical retention of the object.
Repeatability. Closeness of repeated transfer results under identical conditions; a systematic
offset may persist in every attempt.
Accuracy. Closeness of a result to a specified reference; it is evaluated relative to a defined goal,
coordinate frame and measurement conditions.
Impedance. A specified dynamic relationship between motion and interaction force; it usually
includes virtual stiffness and damping.
HRI. The study and design of human-robot interaction, including state understanding, control,
errors and social context.
Mode error. An operator action based on an incorrect understanding of the current mode or of
who controls the robot.
Hazard. A potential source of harm; the presence of a hazard alone does not describe an event's
probability or the severity of its consequences.
Security threat. A possible violation of protected system properties, such as command
substitution, data disclosure or loss of control availability.
Authentication. Verification of a participant's claimed identity or identifier by a trusted method; it
does not itself define permitted actions.
Authorisation. A decision to permit a particular action by an identified participant, considering
role, resource and access policy.
Encryption. Transforming data to conceal their content from those without the key; it does not
replace checks of command authority, freshness and admissibility.
Hash. A short computed representation of content; comparison detects change relative to a
trusted reference, but does not establish authorship.
Digital signature. Cryptographic verification of integrity and of a message's association with the
signer's key, assuming trust in the corresponding public key.
Idempotency. A processing property whereby repeating the same logical command does not
repeat the physical action or change.
PLC. A programmable logic controller that executes industrial cycle logic and processes inputs and
outputs according to its configuration.
Cycle handshake. An exchange of readiness, request and completion states under defined rules;
cycle_id links acknowledgement to a particular operation.

Equipment and software for M17

Use existing equipment
MacBook Pro M4; Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64 in UTM; ROS 2 Jazzy, Gazebo Harmonic and the MoveIt 2
configuration from M16. A virtual arm, table and object suffice for simulation. The M14 camera is
needed only for the existing data in Task 6; do not repurchase sensors or the printer.

No mandatory purchases
M17 requires no purchases. Simulation is sufficient for all ten tasks; a physical arm, PLC, industrial
bus and tactile sensors are unnecessary. The operator interface uses the keyboard and screen of
the existing computer. A volunteer participant also needs no additional devices.

Install now: additions to the existing environment
In Ubuntu ARM64, add a Jazzy-compatible MoveIt Task Constructor only if it is absent and selected
for Task 2; see Pick and Place. Pin the package, commit and dependencies, and check main against
Jazzy. A custom sequence of ROS actions is acceptable.
For Task 8, add SROS2 tools and tutorials from the corresponding branch in a separate ROS
namespace. Save the chosen DDS implementation and its security settings. The mode FSM can be
implemented in the existing code; a separate BehaviorTree library is needed only if a BT
implementation is selected.

Installation checks
Launch the previous module's MoveIt scene, solve IK for one reachable pose, and execute a short
transfer and cancel. In SROS2 with security enabled, check permitted communication and rejection
of a participant without permission; keep keys out of the report. Test the graphical interface and
networking inside UTM on your own computer, and save versions and logs.

Only after M17: the separate OPT120 block
Before building and testing the hand, prepare CAD, a BOM and requirements. Include one actuator
and one selected contact or tactile sensor in the first order for a single-finger prototype, with
suitable load capacity, power supply and interface. Determine quantities for the full hand after
testing the finger. Purchases and the 120 hours are accounted for separately.
For introductory Tasks 9-10: ISO 10218-1, ISO 13849-1, IEC 61508-1 - official scopes. This overview
does not assign a PL/SIL or establish installation compliance.
Preparation and checks use time already allocated within the original 75 hours to review reading
and setup. Delivery of possible OPT120 equipment is outside the learning workload. Check the
availability of equipment and installed components.

СтраницаPage 260 · Motion fundamentals: fingers and grasping
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M17  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Motion fundamentals: fingers and grasping

Required: touching is not yet retention
Kinematics establishes whether contact has been reached; statics establishes whether admissible
forces can balance the object's weight and moments. First draw the object and finger separately,
showing pairs of equal and opposite forces and the moment arm. For the finger, f_ext always
denotes the force exerted by the object on the robot; the robot's force on the object points in the
opposite direction.

A simple retention calculation
Consider a stationary object between two symmetric vertical fingers. Each contact has a normal
force N and upward friction no greater than μN; the weight mg acts downward. For a centred object
without an external rotational moment, 2μN≥mg is necessary. This checks that particular vertical
equilibrium; it does not prove retention against every possible disturbance.
With m=0.20 kg, g=9.81 m/s² and μ=0.50: mg=1.962 N and N≥1.962 N per finger. Choosing
N=2.5 N gives a maximum total friction force of 2.5 N. If μ falls to 0.25, the limit becomes 1.25 N
and can no longer support the weight. Equality at the boundary provides no margin; μ here is an
illustrative model parameter.
For a massless vertical link with a normal-force moment arm of 0.04 m, the holding torque
magnitude is 0.04·1.962≈0.0785 N·m; friction in this geometry acts along the link. A real finger
requires its Jacobian, mass and configuration: in statics, τ_act+τ_g+Jᵀf_ext=0, where τ_g denotes
joint torques due to gravity. Changing the external force direction also changes the sign of the
compensating torque.

Why one motor does not determine two angles
For a finger with two independent joints, one taut, inextensible tendon can impose only
Δl=r1q1+r2q2 for constant moment arms. With r1=r2=0.01 m and Δl=0.005 m, q1+q2=0.5 rad:
the pairs (0.1;0.4) and (0.3;0.2) both satisfy the command. The actual pose depends on springs,
contact and dynamics. This illustrates underactuation; when an object stops one link, the
distribution of motion in the other changes.

Two exercises for Tasks 2-3
1. In the object-transfer report, save a force diagram and a table for three values of μ and two
masses. With N=2.5 N, predict by hand whether the object will be held or will slip. Compare with
contact simulation if available; with simplified attach, label the result a model calculation. Planner
success does not establish this equilibrium.
2. Plot the line q1+q2=0.5 and add the contact condition q1=0.2 rad: this leaves q2=0.3 rad. Save
the plot and explain which physical condition determined the configuration. A full-size hand will
need separate mechanics and sensors; a calculation without purchases suffices for now. Do not
send torque commands to position-controlled servos.
Time allocation: 1 hour from 7-8 for statics; 1 hour from 17-18 to check the table as part of Task
3, and 1 hour from 19-20 to explain failure. These are within the original 75 hours. Building the
hand and working with tactile sensors belong to the separate OPT120 stage after M17.
Assigned reading: Lynch/Park, Modern Robotics §5.2 and §12.2.1 - torque and friction; Tedrake,
Fully-actuated vs Underactuated Systems: Definitions - independent coordinates and available
control inputs.

СтраницаPage 261 · Why a robot needs a learned model
ROBOTICS AND AI  /  M18  /  DETAILED STUDY PLAN

Why a robot needs a learned model

M18 • 30 Apr 2028 - 04 Jun 2028 • 75 hours

Monthly outcome
Create a reproducible classifier for foot contact with a surface and compare it with a simple rule
and logistic regression. Feed it joint and IMU measurements available to the robot, together with
leg-motion features. Its outputs are contact probability, a decision of “contact”, “no contact” or
“insufficient data”, and the time taken to obtain that decision. Save the data, dataset membership,
training configuration, model, error analysis and CPU execution-time measurements.
Learning here addresses a narrow perception task. The classifier helps determine which foot can be
trusted when estimating body state. For now, it operates on recordings or alongside a classical
algorithm in simulation. A false confirmation of contact can make the estimator treat a slipping or
lifted leg as stationary; average accuracy alone therefore does not establish the model's suitability.

What must be ready before starting
Prepare synchronised recordings from previous simulations: time, episode and leg identifiers, joint
positions and velocities, body angular velocity, foot position or velocity and an available force
estimate. Save simulator contact ground truth only for labelling and evaluation. If recordings are
insufficient, perform controlled motions of one leg: free swing, touchdown, stable support, liftoff
and slipping. Data collection does not require a complex gait.
Check that you can read CSV and Parquet, plot a time series, explain the mean and standard
deviation, calculate a dot product and differentiate squared error. Practise missing skills in the first
block. Use your development experience to describe the data format, ensure reproducibility and
investigate causes of model errors; there is no need to repeat all Python fundamentals.

What the result establishes
The main outcome is a justified educational experiment. The network is not yet permitted to control
a physical robot. The original curriculum mentions G3, and the overall calendar allocates separate
time to integration checks. In M18, prepare the data, model and limitations for that stage. Checks
are required before any physical use, regardless of the date of G3. In later modules, the classical
estimator and controller must also work without machine learning.
The connection to the hand is direct: the same process applies to estimating finger-object contact.
However, a positive “touch” label does not mean a “reliable grasp”. Use one main foot-contact task
this month; describe the differences in features and errors for transfer to a finger, without requiring
a second training project.
